021ca6c1-9f8d-5f9a-87db-f4c9193cbe1f.name: Saint John the Baptist from a Deesis Tier
021ca6c1-9f8d-5f9a-87db-f4c9193cbe1f.description: John the Baptist was the cousin of Jesus Christ and preached in the Judean desert. He lived a life of self-denial by wearing camel hair clothing and eating only locusts and wild honey. The people of the region came to him to be baptized in the Jordan River. When Jesus asked to be baptized, John proclaimed that he was not worthy of such a task and that Christ should baptize him instead. Christ insisted, however, and during the baptism the Holy Spirit descended and a voice from heaven proclaimed, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). John got into trouble when he criticized King Herod’s marriage to Herodias, who had a child from her previous marriage to Herod’s brother. Herod’s stepdaughter, Salome, convinced him to arrest John and demanded his head on a silver platter. Granting her wish, Herod ordered John beheaded. In this icon, John the Baptist stands in three-quarter profile and faces left. This icon was once part of a Deesis tier of an iconostasis and would have hung to the right of an icon of Christ in Majesty.
021ca6c1-9f8d-5f9a-87db-f4c9193cbe1f.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Sotheby's Auction in 2006. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

0268e426-50a7-5898-934e-642eb18157d3.name: Chasuble of the green Persian verstements
0268e426-50a7-5898-934e-642eb18157d3.short_description: The ground fabric of this dalamtic, a silk in wark satin, is single-coloured. The centre and sleeve ends are decorated with a silk fabric from Persia. The manufacture of precious silk fabrics had a long-established tradition in Persia when it experienced its last climax under the Safaviden dynasty (AD 1501-1736). Silk fabrics of high quality showing naturalistic designs with reference to the contemporary miniature painting were typical products of the period.
0268e426-50a7-5898-934e-642eb18157d3.dates: Persian fabric, 17th century, manufacturing: Vienna, c. AD 1750

03306ff5-668c-5706-a70c-d5ed5a3886c1.name: The Arrival of the Mahmal
03306ff5-668c-5706-a70c-d5ed5a3886c1.description: The painting is after is after Konstantin Makovsky’s 1876 work, ‘The Arrival of the Holy Carpet in Cairo’ (during this period the mahmal was often referred to as ‘the holy carpet’, or ‘le tapis sacré’ in French). It is not clear whether de Mango had seen Makovsky’s work or if he had access to the original photograph from which the painting was made. However, we do know that de Mango spent time in Cairo and was greatly inspired by life in the Middle East. An engraving of Makovsky’s work by R. Brendamour also appeared in a German periodical of 1893, and de Mango may have been aware of that version as well.
03306ff5-668c-5706-a70c-d5ed5a3886c1.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
keywords: Religion; Pilgrimage; Cairo; Egypt; Hajj

040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.name: Pieces from the Nur al-Din Zangi *minbar*.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.description:
A collection of panels formed from small and medium-sized pieces of interlocking pinewood representing all that remains of the Minbar of Nur al-Din Zangi, which was crafted in Aleppo as a good omen for the conquest of Jerusalem. The *minbar* was destroyed in a fire of 1969 which damaged some of the sections of al-Aqsa Mosque, especially the southern, *qibla*, wall. Nur al-Din Zangi ordered the production of the *minbar* while preparing for the conquest of Jerusalem but he died before he could retake the city, and Salah al-Din (Saladin) undertook the transportation of the *minbar* from Aleppo to Jerusalem in AH 583 / AD 1187.  
The *minbar* was made from interlocking pine and inlaid with mother-of-pearl, ivory and pearls. The different components that constitute it are attached to each other by means of wooden nails and, in addition, the interlocking technique (*ta'sheeq*) is employed. The *minbar* was made up of three sections: the entrance, which faced *muqarnas* tiers, a staircase and a podium, which was covered by a kiosk. The door was composed of two leafs, important sections of which remain. The entrance opened onto the staircase with a wooden enclosure on both sides, crafted in the *mashrabiyya* technique. The staircase leads to the podium where the *khatib* would deliver the sermon.  
The *minbar* is rich in vegetal and geometric decorations as well as an arrangement of star-shaped medallions, each of which forms a complete decorative unit which, with the surrounding units, forms beautiful latticework (*mashrabiyya)*. The *minbar* also has a collection of epigraphic inscriptions that contain Qur'anic verses and an endowment (*waqf*) inscription of Nur al-Din Zangi and his son al-Salih, who accomplished what his father began. This is in addition to the inscriptions which bear the name of the craftsmen who made the *minbar*. The *minbar* of Nur al-Din is considered to be one of the most beautiful of the Islamic wooden *minbar*s.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.short_description: The remains of a *minbar* destroyed in 1969 in a fire that damaged al-Aqsa Mosque. The minbar was commissioned by Nur al-Din Zangi in Aleppo as a good omen for the conquest of Jerusalem. Salah al-Din (Saladin) undertook its transportation to Jerusalem. The pieces have rich vegetal and geometric decoration, interlocking and star-shaped panels and names of the craftsmen.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.initial_owner: Nur al-Din Zangi (ruled in Syria AH 541–69 / AD 1146–74) and Salih bin Nur al-Din Zangi, Salah al-Din Ayyubi (known as Saladin, r. AH 564–89 / AD 1169–93).
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.dates: Construction of the *minbar* began in hegira 564 / AD 1169, and was completed in AH 570 / AD 1174.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.method_for_datation: The *minbar* is dated by the epigraphic inscriptions it bears, and a number of historical sources, some of the most important being those of Abu Shama (d. 665 / 1267) and Ibn al-Athir (d. 630 / 1223) and Mujir al-Din al-Hanbali (d. 927 / 1520).
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.method_for_provenance: Aleppo was narrowed down as the place of production for the *minbar*, supported by both the epigraphic inscriptions on it and by historical sources.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.provenance: Custom-made in Aleppo, Syria for al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem.
040d5edd-ece2-5d65-a462-03b30e90b3e1.obtention: The *minbar* was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum after the fire of 1969.

048c6a9d-2f1b-5deb-80ce-ba88d1053a07.name: Milas Prayer Rug
048c6a9d-2f1b-5deb-80ce-ba88d1053a07.description: Milas region is famous for its prayer rugs. This is an outstanding example of a Milas prayer rug with intensive decoration and skillful handcraft. The prayer area of the rug is decorated with a tree of life on a ground filled with rose, carnation and tulip motifs. The border is composed of highly stylized tree and dragon motifs which are locally called “leaf” and “frog”. These continuous motifs are arranged in the form of “cattle water” which is the most important decoration element of Milas rugs.
048c6a9d-2f1b-5deb-80ce-ba88d1053a07.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
048c6a9d-2f1b-5deb-80ce-ba88d1053a07.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.name: Reliquary of St. Stephen the King
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.description:
The reliquary bust of St. Stephen the King, on a base, shows the saint in royal dress. Characteristics of the Baroque style come to the fore in the saint’s head shown in the round and almost imperceptibly turned sideways, with striking features and a soft wavy beard and moustache.  
The bust was probably made by a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is the work of a contemporary Central European goldsmith.  
The Latin inscription in a cartouche nailed to the front of the base records that Cardinal Francesco Barberini, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, had this bust made in 1635 out of piety for St. Stephen. He commissioned the bust to hold the saint’s skull, endowing the relic with the reverence it deserved. Today it is still in Zagreb Cathedral dedicated to St. Stephen the King.  
St. Stephen, King of Hungary, converted the Hungarians to Christianity and in the early 11th century founded an archbishopric in his hometown Esztergom where he died. He was canonised in 1087 and his cult spread from Hungary to Croatia where it was especially widespread after the Middle Ages. At the time, Hungary and Croatia were in a union and known as the lands of the Crown of St. Stephen after the crown he wore.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.short_description: The reliquary of St. Stephen in the form of a bust shows him dressed as a king with a crown on his head. The bust was probably the work of a master craftsman from Rome, influenced by Bernini, while the crown is attributed to a goldsmith from the Central European circle. The Latin inscription in a cartouche on the front of the base verifies that the reliquary was commissioned by Cardinal Barberini in 1635, nephew of Pope Urban VIII, a member of a powerful and wealthy Roman family that died out in the male line in 1736.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.method_for_datation:
The 1915 Inventory of Zagreb Cathedral mentions the reliquary.  
A Latin inscription with the year of origin is on a cartouche on the front of the base.
05127f0b-387e-53fc-9c38-7c747e046530.obtention: Cardinal Francesco Barberini gifted the reliquary to Zagreb Cathedral.

05e51871-4d33-519c-836e-6e68090e5a80.name: Ladik Prayer Rug
05e51871-4d33-519c-836e-6e68090e5a80.description: This rug is an outstanding example of a Ladik prayer rug because of its colours and detailed decorations. Typical characteristics include, upside down tulips in the borders and three crescent motifs at the top of a triple niche *mihrab*. However, the column motifs usually present in this type of rug do not appear. This example demonstrates the variety of the Ladik prayer rugs and the broadness of its motif repertory.
05e51871-4d33-519c-836e-6e68090e5a80.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts

072908a4-0753-537a-a852-9b3ddcb4ddd6.name: Kırşehir Prayer Rug
072908a4-0753-537a-a852-9b3ddcb4ddd6.description: Kırşehir Province of Central Anatolia was an important prayer rug producing centre. This double *mihrab* prayer rug is an outstanding example of the regional style. Kırşehir prayer rugs characteristically have elaborate stepped arches above the *mihrab*, vivid colours, and detailed floral decorations. The multiple borders are filled with stylized flowers, leaves and a scrolling vine of carnations. The most important element of the decoration is the naturalist bird motif woven inside the *mihrab* area.
072908a4-0753-537a-a852-9b3ddcb4ddd6.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.name: Healing bowl
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.description: This brass talismanic healing bowl, dated to the 12th–13th century Seljuq and Anatolian Beyliks period, was traditionally used in Anatolian folk medicine for spiritual wellbeing, protection from the evil eye, and relief from night terrors and insomnia. Water placed inside the bowl was blessed through recitation, then either drunk or applied to the body to transmit its sacred power. The bowl is richly adorned on both its inner and outer surfaces with finely engraved Kufic inscriptions.
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.method_for_datation:
Date of production was determined by Islamic metal artefacts expert Güner Liman.  
The inscriptions on it were also read by Fuat Recep, an expert in Ottoman archival texts.
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.method_for_provenance:
Its date was determined by Islamic metal artefacts expert Güner Liman.  
The inscriptions on it were also read by Fuat Recep, an expert in Ottoman archives.
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.obtention: It was displayed for 20 years in the window of the antique shop of “Parisli Mustafa” in the Cevahir Bedesten (Grand Bazaar) and was sold at auction after his death.
keywords: Water; healing bowl; Seljuqs; brass

09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.name: Candlestick base.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.description: The base of a Mamluk candlestick made of beaten sheet copper that has been gilded with brass and inlaid with silver and gold. The drip-tray that would have sat on the top rim of the base is missing. The body is decorated with a wide band of *naskhi* script divided into two sections by two roundels. The main decorative fields are embellished with fine floral scrolls inlaid with silver. The inscription, which is inlayed with silver, describes the attributes of the patron who commissioned the candlestick but does not mention his name! Many such candlesticks would have been presented for use in mosques, shrines, and religious schools in Egypt. The Mamluk rulers of Egypt and Syria became great patrons of art and architecture. Cairo was their capital, which they ruled from AH 647 / AD 1250 to AH 922 / AD 1517.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.short_description: Many metal candlesticks like this one were commissioned during the Mamluk period to be presented for use in mosques, shrines and religious schools. The Arabic calligraphic script describes the titles and allegiances of the Mamluk patron who commissioned the candlestick.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.dates: Hegira, late 7th–early 8th century / AD late 13th–early 14th century.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: the titles written on the base are typical Mamluk titles of the late 7th to early 8th / late 13th century to early 14th centuries.
09c974f1-3499-5895-8d83-7f1c12a97916.method_for_provenance: The titles written on the base are typical Mamluk titles of the late 7th–early 8th / late 13th–early 14th centuries.

0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.name: Incantation bowl
0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.description:
A copper dish with a small, inverted dish at the canter, known as an incantation bowl. The entire surface, inside and out, is ornamented with religious inscriptions and talismanic numbers.  
  
The exterior rim is inscribed with Qur’anic verses: “In the name of Allah, the Gracious, the Merciful”; “Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The parable of His Light is as a niche and within it a lamp”; “Allah the Sufficient, Allah the Healer”; “In the name of Allah, the Gracious, the Merciful”; “In the Name of Allah, Who with His Name nothing can cause harm in the earth nor in the heavens, But Allah is the Best to guard and He is”; “In the name of Allah...the healer…”. The inner rim is ornamented with a band enclosed between two frames, each inscribed with repeated numbers (81 / 12).  
  
The band is inscribed with Qur’anic verse in Thuluth script: “Allah, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting by Whom all subsist, there is no god but Him. Neither slumber seizes Him, nor sleep; to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. Who is there who might intercede with Him save with His leave? He knows what lies before them and what is hidden from them, whereas they cannot attain to anything of His knowledge save what He wills them to attain. His Dominion overspreads the heavens and the earth, and their upholding wearies Him not. He is All-High, All-Glorious”.  
  
The inner base is surrounded by fifteen lobed medallions arranged in horizontal registers containing invocations reading: ”Allah the Sufficient / Allah the Healer / In the name of Allah,” repeated. At the very centre is a small, inverted dish. Its decoration begins with a band inscribed in Thuluth script repeating ”O Allah, grant us well-being”. Above it runs a row of pointed arches containing horizontally written numbers (II/II). The central surface of the dish is adorned with a star-shape formed of interlaced script reading ”O the most Compassionate, O the most Generous”.  
  
The exterior body is decorated with ornamental bands consisting of inscriptions and motifs. The outer rim begins with a band of Qur’anic verse: “Allah, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting by Whom all subsist, there is no god but Him. Neither slumber seizes Him, nor sleep; to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. Who is there who might intercede with Him save with His leave? He knows what lies before them and what is hidden from them, whereas they cannot attain to anything of His knowledge save what He wills them to attain. His Dominion overspreads the heavens and the earth, and their upholding wearies Him not. He is All-High, All-Glorious”. This is followed by a frame of repeated numbers (II/II).  
Around the outer rim of the bowl are fifteen lobed medallions arranged in horizontal registers, each inscribed with repeated invocations: ”Allah the Protector / Allah the Healer / In the name of Allah / Allah the Comforter”.  
Next comes a frame whose decoration is effaced, but traces of the number (81/12) remain visible.  
The recessed base begins with a band in thuluth script containing invocations: ”O Allah, grant us health / O Allah, be pleased with us”. This is followed by a row of pointed arches inscribed with numbers (81/12 and II/II). At the very center, a hexagram encloses the numbers (81/12).
0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
keywords: Water; incantation; religion; bowl; copper

0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.name: *Holy Sepulchre*
0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.description:
The golden thread relief embroidery for the sarcophagus-shaped *Holy Sepulchre* covers eight panels and contains 16 oval medallions bordered by gold cartouches. Within the medallions is an iconographic programme based on juxtaposing Old Testament scenes, announcing the Sacrifice of Christ, with corresponding scenes from the New Testament.  
Within the lower oval cartouches are four embroidered scenes from the Old Testament: Abraham sacrificing Isaac, Moses with the brass serpent, Moses fighting the Amalekites, and the legend of the prophet Jonah and the sea monster.  
In the triangular gables of the roof are scenes showing The Last Supper and the Resurrection  
The longer sloping sides of the roof contain five scenes from the Passion of Christ: Christ on the Mount of Olives; Seizure of Christ or the Kiss of Judas; Christ before Caiaphas; the Scourging of Christ and the Crowning with thorns, on one side, and on the other, Pilate Revealing Christ (*Ecce Homo*); Christ Falling under the weight of the Cross; Crucifixion on Golgotha; the Deposition and the Burial.  
The *Holy Sepulchre* is the work of Wolfang Jakob Stoll, commissioned from him by the Bishop of Zagreb, Petar Petretić, whom Stoll served from 1650 to 1667. Petretić was a great patron of the arts and actively promoted Croatian art heritage.  
Stoll made many superb vestments most of which are stored in the Treasury in Zagreb Cathedral. The *Holy Sepulchre* is his greatest and most complex work and probably the only preserved example of an embroidered *Christ's Sepulchre* in Europe.  
Stoll based his rendition of the biblical scenes on copperplate prints, which were at that time widespread in Europe. He worked mainly from the prints of Jan and Egidius Sadeler who found their inspiration in the paintings of Marten de Vos, Theodor Barendsz and Jacopo Tintoretto.  
The decorative elements, such as festoons, genii, baskets of fruit and flowers, belong to the ornamental repertoire of Mannerism.  
The *Holy Sepulchre* was first placed in the Cathedral in Passion Week before Easter on 13 April 1659
0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.short_description:
The golden thread relief embroidery of the *Holy Sepulchre* covers eight panels and contains 16 oval medallions bordered by gold cartouches containing scenes from the Old and New Testaments.  
The Bishop of Zagreb, Petar Petretić, commissioned it from the German embroiderer, Wolfgang Jakob Stoll.
0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.method_for_datation: Analysis of Stoll’s work includes vestments with a pluvial with the master’s name and the monogram of Bishop Petar Petretić. Contemporary documents in the cathedral archives confirm the commissions and the engagement of the above master.
0b440404-7dee-50b3-9519-121dcb0f4d35.obtention: Commissioned for the cathedral, the *Holy Sepulchre* was destined for the Treasury from the outset.

0bf9f93d-7e41-57a5-a618-9f644fa93aa1.description:
The coconut shell vessel is intricately engraved with Persian couplets using the carving technique.  
  
On the silver border, the inscription reads:  
  
"They are offered a pure drink whose end is musk \[a pleasant fragrance\]. Let those who strive, strive for this — a spring from which those near to Allah drink.”  
  
This is followed by the date AH 1234 / AD 1818 and the phrase "Amal-i Kazım" ("Work of Kazım").

0cf1a62f-ad34-5894-aee0-ed8e36e2513a.name: Triptych with '*hilya-i-sherif*' (noble description).
0cf1a62f-ad34-5894-aee0-ed8e36e2513a.description: This triptych is a typical product of Ottoman religious art of the AH 12th / AD late 18th century. It is made of wood covered with a thin layer of paper painted with various motifs and consists of three parts. The central panel, the most important part, contains a *hilya-i-sherif*, a noble description of the physical and moral qualities of Muhammad. The two side panels contain the *hilyas* of the first four caliphs and the sons of Ali, Hasan and Husayn. This piece is of particular interest as, in the lower part of the central panel, there is a mention of the illuminator, who signed Halil Kamili, disciple of Mehmed Qalyunt, and the calligrapher, Mahmud son of Mustafa, pupil of Baqqal-zade Ahmed Efendi, who died in the month of Rejeb 1200. In terms of the decoration of the triptych, its three leaves are embellished with inscriptions in various different characters, such as *thuluth*, *naskhi* and *ta'liq*, while the actual decorative motifs used include classical shoots with stylised floral motifs in the *hatayi* style, and *rumi* motifs, arabesques dominated by palmettes. The pointed pediment of the triptych shows in its centre panoramas of Islam’s two pre-eminent sacred sites: Mecca, with the Ka'ba in the foreground, and Medina, with its mosque. Particularly notable is the small, central vase from which flowers shoot, symbolising the distribution of the charismatic virtues of the prophet. The description of the physical and moral qualities of Muhammad are part of a long literary tradition that started with Ibn Ishaq’s *sira* (biography of the Prophet). Triptychs such as this one were the object of real worship and veneration, relating to the magical powers that, according to the calligrapher, could be attributed to the triptych and to belief in the magical powers of the writing.
0cf1a62f-ad34-5894-aee0-ed8e36e2513a.short_description: Triptychs were a common and important part of Ottoman religious art. This example includes the ‘noble description’ of Muhammad’s physical and moral qualities, as well as representations of Islam’s two pre-eminent holy sites: Mecca and Medina.

0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.name: *Kiswa* (tomb cover) for the Prophet of God, Ibrahim (Abraham).
0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.description:
There was a tradition in both the Mamluk and the Ottoman periods, for sultans, noble personages of state, as well as the benevolent, to interest themselves in the tombs of the prophets and the devout by offering a *kiswa* (covering for a grave or tomb), and then to renew it each year or whenever necessary. The ritual draping of tombs and shrines were popular celebrations that took place in certain seasons every year. For the most part, this occurred in order to procure the good-will and approval of visitors to the tomb or shrine, and to enhance the popularity of the *kiswa*'s donor among the general public. It was during the Ottoman period in Palestine that there was a huge unparalleled interest in the tombs, shrines and holy places that were scattered throughout the region. This was within the context of the official interest in the Sufi orders, their sheikhs, and the venues where the rituals were practiced. An example of this veneration can be seen in the context of the tombs of the Prophets Moses, Samuel and David, and their wives, in al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil).  
The *kiswa* exhibited here is made from woven green silk. The *kiswa* was produced in order to envelope the tomb completely, leaving only the tombstone visible, upon which was written the name of the deceased: “The Prophet of God, Ibrahim \[Abraham\]”. The *tughra* of the Ottoman sultan, Selim III (r. AH 1203-22/AD 1789-1807) is embroidered on the *Kiswa*, together with inscriptions that read, “This is a protector” and “revered”, in addition to other inscriptions that include religious supplications and Qur'anic verses.  
The official tradition as noted above, to send *kiswa*s to the tombs and shrines of venerated holy men and women, continued in Palestine until the end of the Ottoman period in 1916, when the tradition was officially stopped. At the popular level, however, locals who lived in the environs of these tomb sites and shrines continued preparing *kiswas* but they were no longer splendid, finely made textiles as had been the case during the period of the Ottoman sultans.
0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.short_description: The coverings of the prophets’ tombs were renewed every year in popular celebrations. The importance of these traditions increased during the Ottoman period. This covering woven of green silk envelops the tomb leaving only the tombstone on which is written the name of the deceased. The *tughra* of Ottoman Sultan Selim III is embroidered on it.
0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.initial_owner: The Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil).

0e4485e1-3fb0-5d8c-a83c-5315bc85cb66.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this piece was made in Syria or Istanbul in view of the similarities with other pieces made there, some of which are housed in Turkish museums, particularly in Istanbul.

0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.name: Mosque lamp.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.description: A mosque lamp of typical size and shape for Mamluk lamps, with flaring neck, wide body and high foot. Thick glass loops are attached for the suspension cords. It is decorated with enamelling, mostly in blue and red, with some highlights added in green, white and gold. The majority of the decoration is calligraphic. A prominent inscription states that 'This is one of the objects made for His High Excellency, our lord the great Amir, Sayf al-Din Aqbugha 'Abd al-Wahid \[officer of\] al-Malik al-Nasir'. The areas in and around the calligraphy are decorated with floral motifs and arabesques. Sayf al-Din Aqbugha's blazon, a diamond (napkin) on a rectangular field, appears in roundels on the neck. Aqbugha built an important *madrasa* at the Mosque of al-Azhar in Cairo (the Madrasa al-Aqbughawiyya) in AH 740 / AD 1340, and this lamp was probably suspended from the ceiling in that building, possibly with the very cords that are still attached to it.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.short_description: A lamp of typical Mamluk shape, decorated with enamelled glass forming inscriptions, floral decoration, and blazons. The patron, Sayf al-Din Aqbugha, founded a *madrasa* (religious school) at the Azhar mosque complex in Cairo in AH 740 / AD 1340, and this lamp may originally have hung there.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.method_for_datation: It is likely that the lamp was made for the Madrasa al-Aqbughawiyya, built by Sayf al-Din Aqbugha in 740 / 1340.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that glass lamps like this were made in Cairo, as it would have been easier and safer than making them elsewhere and then transporting them.
0e493dee-d727-519c-91a1-24aef19e5e22.obtention: Purchased by the Museum in 1869 from the collection of Dr Meymar.

0e4a2c60-95e1-53b1-b364-83013292b0c9.name: Qur’an Stand
0e4a2c60-95e1-53b1-b364-83013292b0c9.short_description:
This Qur’an stand would elevate larger holy books to prevent direct contact with the unclean surface of the ground. The pigmented wood structure from India features deep floral carvings.  
  
Mughal-style carvings with rows of florals and vines adorn the Qur’an stand in geometric precision. While Islamic woodwork in India remains widely understudied, the lobed arches of the legs remind of Mughal architecture. Furthermore, the woodwork of the Mughal Empire rarely bears inscriptions, hindering an accurate dating and study of clusters of pieces.  
  
These stands still cradle Qur’ans in affluent homes, mosques, Islamic schools (*madrasa*), and in tombs for recitation and display purposes.

100c3cd0-799a-5feb-ac7f-8516c0d5b098.name: *Saint Catherine of Alexandria*
100c3cd0-799a-5feb-ac7f-8516c0d5b098.short_description:
Under a Renaissance arch with leafy garlands and ornamented pillars, St Catherine stands on a brown tiled floor in front of a balustrade, next to a broken torture wheel. In accordance with her position as a king’s daughter, she wears a fashionable Burgundian Low Country dress with a high-girded, ermine-trimmed cloak and a crown on her long, blond tresses. In her role as a martyr, she carries the sword of justice. As a symbol of her exaltation, two *putti* hold up a draped cloth behind her, concealing part of the hilly, wooded, castle-studded landscape in the background. On the frieze of the entablature there is an inscription that reads “S katherina”, and affixed to the pillars are little frames with the date (1523) in both Arabic numerals (left) and Roman numerals (right). So far, no drawing or print has been produced that might have served as a model for this reverse glass painting.  
  
The date must be connected to an event that sparked the commission for this magnificent small painting, but there are no inscriptions nor heraldic clues as to whether it was commissioned for personal use, as a gift to a private individual, or as a donation to a private or public building. The quality of the glass support, the careful painting technique with generous application of gold leaf, and the meticulous, delicate etching as well as the high artistic merit identify it as a precious reverse glass painting that could only have been created in the context of rich patronage.
100c3cd0-799a-5feb-ac7f-8516c0d5b098.method_for_datation: By date and by stylistic analysis

1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.name: Circular chandelier.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.description:
This chandelier belongs to a series of eight found in the Great Mosque of Kairouan, and which are dispersed today among four Tunisian museums (Raqqada, the Bardo, Mahdiyya and Monastir).  
The punched cast-bronze base is in the form of a tray designed to carry 10 candles, with a flared bronze corona from which 18 evenly spaced upright arms project. These are similar in size and are all decorated with double, spread fleurons. The stylised vine-leaf motif is commonly used in Ifriqiyan art of the 3rd and 4th centuries (9th and 10th), particularly in the *mihrab*, the *minbar* and the *maqsura* of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. Nine of the 18 arms end in circular rings and the other nine have heart–shaped tops. The two types are placed in alternating sequence on the corona. The heart motif is frequently found in Kairouanese bookbinding and features in stylised form on several Fatimid sculptures. The central ring of the chandelier is surrounded by 18 horseshoe arches linking the uprights, giving the overall effect of a festooned rose. The base-tray is suspended by three chains linked to three rings.  
The Kairouanese type of chandelier has doubtless been influenced by similar Byzantine designs produced throughout the Islamic period in the Mediterranean region. Muslim craftsmen replaced the Christian cross of the Byzantine and Coptic chandeliers with the tri-lobed fleuron and the geometric motifs dear to their own creed. Prototypes similar to that of Kairouan have been found in Egypt, Syria and especially in Spain. This Spanish ancestry arouses speculation that Western Islam may have had its own school of bronze-smiths.  
Interestingly, this technique appears to have been taken up by Spanish Christians, since there is a similar chandelier from a Spanish church at the British Museum in London.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.short_description: Inspired by Byzantine art, this piece was one of a group of eight used in the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The Muslim artist has replaced the cross in Byzantine and Coptic chandeliers with a trilobed fleuron and some geometric motifs consistent with the Islamic creed.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.method_for_datation: The seven other chandeliers with which this one was kept probably date from before the Hilalian invasions of 449 / 1057. There are stylistic similarities to chandeliers from Egypt, Syria and Spain dating from the 4th / 10th century.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.method_for_provenance: This chandelier was part of the furniture of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. Along with seven other pieces, it was kept as a relic in the old library of the Great Mosque. They all date from before the Hilalian invasions in 449 / 1057. Furthermore, it can be compared to other pieces from Egypt, Syria and particularly from Elvira in Spain. Archaeological digs at the ruins of the Great Mosque in this town have revealed a chandelier dating from the 4th / 10th century whose overall design and internal rosette of horseshoe arches bear a striking resemblance to the Kairouanese chandelier. This convincing evidence unmistakably dates the Kairouanese chandelier from the same period.
1027aa27-0c29-5f12-8165-2db5e0dda881.obtention: This chandelier was displayed from 1956 at the museum of the Great Mosque of Kairouan before its acquisition by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada in 1986.

1203d512-7e1e-58c1-b5ee-087144132528.name: The Miracle of Saint George and the Dragon
1203d512-7e1e-58c1-b5ee-087144132528.description: Saint George was born to Christian parents in the 3rd century. He joined the Roman army and became a high-ranking officer at a young age, earning the respect of Emperor Diocletian. At that time, Diocletian persecuted Christians and required that all soldiers offer sacrifices to the pagan gods. Saint George publicly denounced the emperor and confessed to being Christian. He was subjected to brutal punishments but refused to renounce his faith. Eventually, he was beheaded and became a popular martyr saint. In one story of his life, he rescued a town besieged by a dragon. The townspeople had been sacrificing children, who were randomly chosen by casting lots, to the dragon. Saint George rode in just as the town’s princess was to be sacrificed. He killed the dragon, a symbol of paganism, and converted the townspeople to Christianity. In this icon, Saint George rides a white horse and slays the dragon with a spear while Christ, seen in the upper right corner, bestows a blessing.
1203d512-7e1e-58c1-b5ee-087144132528.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2003. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography

13234dce-e760-5f68-9ead-fa6944333432.name: Magic Bowl
13234dce-e760-5f68-9ead-fa6944333432.short_description:
Protective verses from the Qur’an, blessings and magic letters encase this bronze bowl. This vessel belongs to a group of objects known as magic bowls in Islamic metalworks, intended to ward off fear, evil and demons (*jinn*).  
  
While this bowl originates from Karbala in Iraq, the place of pilgrimage for Shiite Muslims, these objects have appeared in Syria, India and Iran since the 12th century. Earlier Sasanian magic bowls with Aramaic inscriptions embodied similar amuletic qualities, however were made of clay instead of metal and invoked the powers of demons and Liliths.  
  
The Throne Verse (*Ayat al Kursi*) of the Qur’an guards the exterior of the bowl in the *thuluth* style of Arabic calligraphy, granting talismanic protection. A hexagram (six-pointed star) invokes prophet Sulayman (Solomon), while the surrounding inscriptions bear blessings for one's body and the senses. Twelve panels on the vessel allude to the twelve Imams in Shia Islam. The science letters (*ilm al huruf*) ascribes magical properties to the assortment of letters marking the panels.

1433647b-a363-527b-a739-01058ae49638.name: Ritual ladle for the Taghounja festival
1433647b-a363-527b-a739-01058ae49638.description: The ritual ladle used in the Taghounja festival reflects the intersection of water, fertility, and collective ritual in Moroccan rural life. During this traditional celebration communities would gather to invoke rain, fertility, and divine blessing. The ladle, carved from wood, was used to pour or sprinkle water in symbolic gestures of renewal and abundance. Its simplicity belies a profound cultural meaning: water as the essence of life, shared collectively through ritual. Its preservation illustrates how intangible heritage and material culture merge to tell the story of Morocco’s spiritual relationship with water.

14763417-a183-5949-ac5d-11f296d400e1.name: Hanging (*sitara*) for the Mosque of the Prophet, Medina al-Munawwarah
14763417-a183-5949-ac5d-11f296d400e1.short_description: This hanging of red, yellow-golden and green silk is richly embroidered with silver and silver-gilt inscriptions and designs. Above, a lamp with invocations to Allah as the Opener or Judge (ya Fattah) appears suspended from an arched niche resting on two columns. Its spandrels display two roundels with the Islamic profession of Faith (shahada). Below, a quote from chapter 2 (Al-Baqarah), verse 197 of the Holy Qur’an appears: ‘…and the best provision is Al-Taqwa (piety, righteousness)’. In the lower half of the hanging, four roundels with the names of the rightly-guided caliphs surround the imperial Ottoman emblem or tughra of the sultan Abd al- Hamid II  (1293 H/1876 AD – 1327 H/1909 AD), who commissioned this curtain.. Hangings like this one may have been intended for the prayer niche of the Prophet’s mosque, as earlier examples of this type often include the inscription ‘this is the mihrab of the Prophet (pbuh)’.

14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.name: Namban Oratory
14d23909-007c-5bfe-ba51-0f21c11eaef4.description:
This rectangular oratory surmounted by a triangular pediment with the monogram *IHS* (the abbreviation of the Greek *IHSOUS*, or JESUS) located at the centre, has two side-panels enclosing a painting of the Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus. Although the lacquer decoration presents a predominantly Japanese ornamental grammar – especially a floral one – both its form and the iconography embody Christian cultural references. The pictorial image is itself an example of the possible interaction between the Jesuit painting school – operating in Japan since the 1580s – and the Japanese pupils that quickly demonstrated skill in Western-style painting.  
As it is, such a hybrid object, that crosses different artistic backgrounds, could only have been made during the Portuguese presence in Japan, during the period spanning approximately 1549 to 1640.  
The oratory is mentioned in the *Inventário Artístico de Santarém* (Santarém Artistic Inventory) as Indo-Portuguese lacquer work. Such misinformation reveals how, in the middle of the 20th century, such an item was unfamiliar to the European public in general, but that was not the case in the late 16th and beginning of the 17th century, at least not for the Portuguese elite. Such a statement can only be based on the remaining objects – with or without associated painting – the number of which has expanded increasingly during the last three decades (this example did not come to light until 1985). A fact that also draws attention to the demands of the Iberian market for these objects at the time.  
The Sardoal Oratory has the particularity of being associated with a religious space, thanks to an inscription located on the altar of Nossa Senhora da Esperança in the Church of Nossa Senhora da Caridade. This text, dated 1670, is the earliest known reference in Portugal to a reminiscent *Namban* object.

151fac1e-ebdf-570b-9f37-a9dcd36098e4.name: Flask: Candle holder for festival of name-giving
151fac1e-ebdf-570b-9f37-a9dcd36098e4.short_description: On the 7th day after the birth of a child, there is a candle burning naming festival in Egypt. For both boys and girls, flasks for drinking water are made of clay, and are provided with candle holders. Depending on the sex of the new-born baby, the neck of the bottle is either fashioned as a stylised female figure or ends in an implied penis. The festival is celebrated in honour of the 7 angels who stand around the new-born. On the evening of the 7th day after the birth of the child, these angels become a threat. In order to propitiate them, they are provided with a plate of food-offerings. Nearby, the clay bottle stands on a tray with beans. The beans are sprinkled with water and the candles on the flasks are lit. Each candle receives a name. The one which burns the longest is, so to speak, the "baptismal candle" of the child. The stub of the candle is then placed in a small bag, together with magical substances, and worn around the child's neck as an amulet to ward off evil.

153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.name: Parts of a *minbar*.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.description:
These elements of the facing of the *minbar* are formed by two distinctive parts. The first one consists of two longitudinal panels from the upper parts of the lateral faces of the *minbar*. Their surfaces, divided into sections and surmounted by an arch, are decorated with stacks of pinecones and acanthus rosettes borrowed from Abbasid flora. The panels are framed by a band bearing an inscription in angular *kufic* script also in an Eastern style. The inscription in the right panel, whose spandrels are adorned with half-sprays of acanthus, includes the date the Fatimids founded the *minbar*. The one in the left panel shows Qur'anic texts from verse 36 of Sura 24, 'The light'.  
The second part includes the three elements from the back.  
The top, arched panel is topped by an inscription in *kufic* script, which indicates the name of the Umayyad patron and the date the *minbar* was repaired. Its surface, framed by a border of small floral medallions, is decorated in two styles: the upper section is occupied in the centre by a rectangular panel with a poly-lobed arch with floral medallions and on the sides by festoon acanthus rosettes. The lower section is adorned with an acanthus rosette flanked by poly-lobed medallions containing polygonal knotwork based on an eight-pointed star.  
The rectangular middle part, bordered with a votive inscription, is adorned with a central motif of tiered chevrons with palm foliage and serrated acanthus rosettes inscribed in squares.  
The lower part is decorated with half-balusters in turned and painted wood, glued on a slab.  
These facings, which illustrate a historic period of Morocco when two political and religious movements fought for the hegemony of the country, play an important role in the history of Moroccan art, which, from that time forward, would be influenced both from the East and from Andalusia.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.short_description: These *minbar* parts illustrate a historical episode and the beginnings of Islamic art in Morocco, when Fatimids and Córdoban Umayyads were fighting for control of the country. The Fatimids incorporated Eastern decoration when making the *minbar*, and the Umayyads added Western elements when converting it.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.dates: Sides: Hegira 369 / AD 979; back: Hegira 375 / AD 985.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.dimensions: Back: height 146 cm, width 75 cm, depth 3–4.5 cm; panels: height 56 cm, width 20.6 cm, depth 2.5–4.5 cm.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.method_for_datation: Two inscriptions mention the dates. The date of foundation is shown on the arcature in the right panel: 'This *minbar* was made in the month of Shawwal in the year 369 \[April / May 979\]' and the date it was repaired appears on the upper part of the back: '… this is what was commissioned by the mayor of the palace …, al-Mansur, sword of the empire of the *imam* and servant of God … Hisham … Abi Amir Muhammad … son of Abi Amir … in the month of Jumada II in the year 375 \[October–November 985\]'.
153c5ddb-dd1d-5e3c-9e80-de0b66684f95.method_for_provenance: These parts were removed from the *minbar*, which remained in use at the Andalusian Mosque from its creation in 369 / 979 until 1353 / 1934.

15610349-3f4b-5d20-bbb1-76ff1816ce04.name: Kaftan
15610349-3f4b-5d20-bbb1-76ff1816ce04.short_description: Originally worn by a prince or a boyar, the present kaftan was turned at some point into an ecclesiastical cope and preserved as such at the Cozia Monastery (in southwestern Romania), where it was discovered in 1864. By the mid-1950s it was transferred to the Museum, and was later reconstituted into its original form. The long, loose garment with long sleeves is lavishly decorated with eight-petalled rosettes set against a red ground. Each rosette encircles a lotus flower. In between rosettes, a design of delicate scrolls with tiny wild roses.

159db56e-edd6-577a-b51e-40b856217129.name: Prayer rug
159db56e-edd6-577a-b51e-40b856217129.description: The rich colour palette and the contrast between the undecorated *mihrab* field and the borders with intricate geometric motifs, the so-called *Crivelli güls*, convey a sense of vitality and unsophisticated beauty. The apex of the stepped *mihrab* echoes the crenellations on the narrow panel above. Identical motifs can be found on earlier carpets, which testify to the persistence of certain patterns over more than two centuries. These motifs, drawn from architecture, appear to have lost their original meaning, much like the columns turned into flower garlands on other 19th-century rugs. Two ewers featured in the spandrels on either side of the pointed top of the *mihrab* suggest, in all probability, the ritual ablution before prayer.

15b869a4-109e-5091-8bd1-fdeab056f0c9.name: Frontal with St. Alexander pope
15b869a4-109e-5091-8bd1-fdeab056f0c9.description:
This frontal originally decorated the front of the former altar in the church of Vergiano. It is a good example of the art of scagliola, a technique of using plaster to create imitation marble or stone. This method was invented in Emilia, in Carpi, a small town near Modena, at the beginning of the seventeenth century.  
The art of scagliola is very old. In antiquity it was common to decorate surfaces in order to imitate marble, but examples of decorations made of plaster powder imitating marble start only from the sixteenth-century. Scagliola is a cheaper technique compared to precious stone inlaid. For this reason and for its rapidity of execution it soon became very popular. This explains the ample presence of scagliola artefacts in Italy made exclusively for churches and mostly altar frontals. Guido Fassi (1584–1649), an architect and engineer from Carpi, was the first to employ this technique for altar frames. Later his collaborators and pupils painted on the scagliola surface first, then imitated stone inlay thus creating in Carpi the first Italian school of scagliola.  
The artist who made this frontal, Carlo Antonio Bini, is a member of this school. He employs the typical decorative naturalistic patterns (flower wreaths, small birds, fantastic creatures) against a black background. In the middle Pope St. Alexander I is kneeling in front of a monstrance, wearing a cope.
15b869a4-109e-5091-8bd1-fdeab056f0c9.short_description: This altar frontal represents St. Alexander pope kneeling in front of the Eucharist. Against a black background one can see the naturalistic patterns (flower wreaths, small birds, fantastic creatures).
15b869a4-109e-5091-8bd1-fdeab056f0c9.method_for_datation: Inscription in the lower middle: MDCLXXX / CARLO ANTONIO BINI FE (1680/Carlo Bini made).

163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.name: Candlestick base.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.description: A cast brass, inlaid candlestick of truncated conical form; it has bevelled ridges on both the upper and lower rims. The body is dominated by a central band of *naskhi* script divided into three sections. The sections are separated by three roundels containing Mamluk heraldic emblems, the style dating to the AH 8th / AD 14th century. The main decorative fields are embellished with fine floral scrolls inlaid with silver; a black niello substance is used as inlay to fill in the background of the floral patterns, thus emphasising the fine details of the scrolls. The inscription describes the patron who commissioned the candlestick. Many such candlesticks would have been presented for use in mosques, shrines and religious schools in Egypt. The Mamluk rulers of Egypt and Syria became great patrons of art and architecture. Cairo was their capital, which they ruled from AH 647 / AD 1250 to AH 922 / AD 1517.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.short_description: This candlestick was made for presentation to a mosque or *madrasa*, and is decorated with the titles of the Mamluk patron who commissioned it, stating: 'by the most noble authority, lofty, lordly, great; the kingly, supportive, … provider of protection; the masterful, maintainer, prince al-Nassiri'.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis, together with analysis of the titles described in the inlaid scripts and the Mamluk heraldic emblem.
163ae238-7cdd-5bf2-b4ef-095207b4794d.method_for_provenance: Analysis of the Mamluk heraldic emblem and inlaid scripts.

1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.name: Mosque lamp.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.description: A glass mosque lamp with a rounded body, flared neck and attached splayed foot. The lamp is almost intact apart from the neck which has been repaired. Attached to the body of the lamp are six loops used to suspend the lamp from the ceiling. The lamp is covered in peonies outlined in red against a blue background. On the neck and underside of the body are three circular medallions of a composite vegetal design. This is a fine example of the more unusual type of Mamluk mosque lamps without inscriptions. The small numbers of similar lamps that survive are all associated with buildings constructed under Sultan Hasan ibn Muhammad. Rows of these lamps, lit up, illuminating the floral designs against a blue background would have been a spectacular sight in a mosque interior.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.short_description: An enamelled glass mosque lamp with rounded body, flared neck and attached splayed foot. Although typical of Mamluk mosque lamps in shape and technique, this lampis unusual as it has purely floral or vegetal decoration and no inscriptions.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.method_for_datation: This lamp is one of a group of lamps without inscriptions, decorated with purely floral motifs, produced in about the mid-7th / 14th century. They are associated with buildings commissioned by Sultan Hasan ibn Muhammad (r. between 747–51 / 1347–51 and again in 754–62 / 1354–61). Two similar lamps, now in the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo, were found in the Madrasa of Sultan Hasan built in 756 / 1356. Another lamp in the same museum in Cairo is inscribed with the name of Sultan Hasan.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.method_for_provenance: This lamp bears close resemblance to others produced for buildings in Egypt that were commissioned by Sultan Hasan.
1702078b-d03e-543a-b81f-2cd7344ea8f1.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by Sir Augustus Wollaston Franks in 1881.

178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.name: Processional Altar of St. John the Evangelist
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.description:
A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, which belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception, and was used in the Procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja. The social and religious significance of the Corpus Christi Day procession cannot be understated; it represents one of the greatest manifestations of the Portuguese Baroque, which once acknowledged, justifies the sumptuousness of some of the pieces used in these ceremonies. Traditionally, up until 1893, the altar was carried by farmers.  
Rectangular in shape, the *acroteria* (small bases placed at the four extremities) has a beaded edging, and four *albarradas* or ornamental vases, alternate with smaller jars in the middle. The entirety is covered with vegetable and scalloped-shell ornamentation, and St. James' crosses. The wooden carrying rods are also silver plated.  
The octagonal shaped pedestal stands over the main body, decorated with double scalloped-shell ornamentation, pear-shaped “tables” and St. James' crosses. There is also an octagonal platform with small jars placed at each corner of the pedestal.  
An iron column rises above the pedestal, covered with silk cloth embroidered with gold thread. It meets a gold and silver halo embellished with precious stones above which a gold and silver crown rests, also studded with precious stones. In the middle of the altarpiece, the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist is played out, the saint graphically shown immersed in boiling olive oil. The wooden effigy of the saint with clasped hands looks straight up at the sky. The silver boiler, standing on a silver tripod above the fire, is kept alight by two multicoloured wooden figures, kneeling at either side of the boiler. One of them is blowing and the other is using a solid-silver pitchfork.  
The patrons of the altarpiece were a group of nuns devoted to St. John the Evangelist. There was another group of nuns in the same convent that devoted themselves to St. John the Baptist and commissioned a similar processional altar in honour of the saint. In fact, both altarpieces date from the beginning of the 18th century and were made in the same workshop. They both show the same crowned stamps of the city of Lisbon and the same maker's letter “M”.
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.short_description: A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, it portrays features typical of the Portuguese Baroque at the time of King João V. Designed to represent the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist, the piece belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception and was used in the procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja, on Corpus Christi Day.

17a114d9-989f-52a9-85d5-689485ba21f6.name: Icon *The Holy Seven Slav Teachers*
17a114d9-989f-52a9-85d5-689485ba21f6.short_description: This icon represents icon-painting in Macedonia in the 19th century. This painted variant of the motif of the seven Slav teachers was enriched by Dimitar Dicho Zograf with the romantic awareness of the Macedonian Revival. The style of the most popular and most productive Macedonian painter in the 19th century follows the experience of the painters from that period. It was commissioned by the Robev family for the church of St. Nicholas Gerakomia in Ohrid. It was painted on wood with oil. It represents the Slav missionaries Ss. Cyril and Methodius and their most prominent disciples Clement, Nahum, Gorazd, Sabbas and Angelariy, in a sole composition entitled as “Sedmochislenitzi” (The Seven Holy Teachers). The saints' names are inscribed in the Old Church Slavonic language.

1911d22b-68b3-5d5e-a23a-6f0b09d5b12c.name: Dalail Al Khayrat (Dalail Al Khayrat wa Shawariq Al-Anwar fi Dhikr al-Salat ala al-Nabi al-Mukhtar)
1911d22b-68b3-5d5e-a23a-6f0b09d5b12c.short_description:
Written in *maghrebi* calligraphy in the 18th century, the *Dalail al-Khayrat* (“The Guide to Goodness”) represents a famous collection of prayers for Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) compiled by Sufi leader Imam Muhammad Sulaiman al-Jazuli in Souss, Morocco. Bound in brown cardboard with golden geometric and floral decorations, the copy embodies a book that swept across the Muslim world.  
  
Often attributed to sainthood, the Berber al-Jazuli created this literary device in the 14th century for recitation, prayer and oral remembrance of the beloved Prophet Muhammad. Intended for word recitings to enhance one’s access to the divine, the book could be read aloud or silently, alone or as a collective.  
  
The prayers are split into seven sections representing each day of the week for daily worship. Simultaneously, the book served as a *hajj* (pilgrimage) guide due to its vivid descriptions of Mecca and Medina. While the book appeals to people across socio-economic backgrounds and geographic context, the collection reflects al-Jazuli’s inclusive nature and encouragement of women to transfer Islamic knowledge and educate the future generations.

19309244-d3ba-5328-b6af-d77395f59e8e.name: Mosque Lamp
19309244-d3ba-5328-b6af-d77395f59e8e.short_description: This mosque lamp was almost certainly made for the monumental mosque and madrasa complex of the Mamluk Sultan Al-Malik Al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Barquq (AH r. 783-791 and 792-801 / AD 1382-1389 and 1390-1399) in Cairo, completed in 788 AH / 1386 AD. It presents a typical decoration for glass lamps produced in that period with inscriptions in blue enamel, gilding on the neck, and in reserve on blue background with a floral interlacing motif on the globular body. Al-Malik Al-Zahir Sayf al-Din Barquq is mentioned twice in the inscriptions on the body and in the circular medallions on the neck. The blue inscription on the neck is verse 35 from the Sura of Light (Qur’an 24), “Allahu nur al-samawati wa al-ardhi mathalu nurihi kamishkatin fiha misbahun al-misbahu fi zujajatin" (God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The Parable of His Light is as if there were a Niche and within it a Lamp: the Lamp enclosed in Glass). This quotation is often used for lamp decoration and emphasizes the sensorial, luminous aspect of the Qur’anic text. The large spaces of the mosques and madrasa founded by the Mamluks during the eighth century AH / fourteenth century AD required ample lighting. This need prompted the production of hanging lamps in Egypt and Syria and explains the relatively high number of surviving examples today.

19712bce-3702-52aa-a6e1-3f6ba2529789.name: ‘Transylvanian’ rug
19712bce-3702-52aa-a6e1-3f6ba2529789.description:
The term “Transylvanian” rug is related to small prayer rugs made in the villages of Anatolia but preserved mostly in the region of Transylvania. Commonly these are decorated with two prayer niches in mirror image and have a border filled with elongated, polygonal cartouches.  
The Kraków rug represents both these features. The red field of the double niche is ornamented with palmettes and cogwheels organised along the vertical axis, and two flowering branches flanking it. The indigo-colour spandrels are filled with an ornament of the “rosette and leaf”-type with large rosettes among lanceolate leaves. In the main border, flanked by two narrower borders, there are cartouches with lozenges, placed on the red ground.  
So-called Transylvanian carpets were very popular in Poland and many are preserved in Polish collections. We can also find such rugs depicted in Polish paintings. On the refectory ceiling in the former Piarist monastery in Rzeszów, a Transylvanian rug covers the table in a scene from “The meeting in Emaus”, painted at the end of 17th century by Łukasz Ziemecki. It looks very much like the rug in the Kraków collection. It is interesting that in the Brukenthal National Museum in Sibiu, Transylvania, a rug with almost the same design as the Kraków version is preserved. The only visible differences are colouristic. On the edge of the Sibiu rug is an inscription with the date 1675. Therefore, the Kraków rug was probably made in third quarter of 17th century.
19712bce-3702-52aa-a6e1-3f6ba2529789.method_for_datation: Comparative analysis of other preserved rugs; analysis of paintings

1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.name: Prayer rug.
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.description:
This rug belongs to the group of prayer rugs from Ghiordes, a village between Izmir and Ushak, where most of the Anatolian prayer rugs were manufactured in the AH 12th–13th / AD 18th–19th centuries. It shows in the central field a pointed niche with a half-niche on each side on a cream background. The motif of the three-arched niche derives from rug patterns of Ottoman courtly manufacturing during the AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries. In contrast to these original designs, the columns of this rug are based on stylised carnations. Edged with trefoiled blossoms they support the main niche and separate it from the half-niches. The spandrels are filled with stylised carnations on a dark-blue background. A large bouquet of flowers hangs in the apex, reaching nearly to the bottom where a row of carnations is presented. The panel above the spandrels is filled with rosette blossoms and ornaments.  
The border is formed by two horizontal and two vertical stripes showing an endless pattern of stylised plants on a dark blue background. The wavy motif of a flower scroll alternately coloured in blue, red and tan is repeated on the inner and outer guard bands.
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.short_description: Prayer rug, probably from Ghiordes. In the central field the rug shows a pointed niche with a half-niche on each side. Stylised carnations and bouquets of flowers are the most important motifs of this rug. The central field is framed with a border.
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.method_for_datation: A very similar rug is dated to the 12th / 18th century.
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.method_for_provenance: Rugs showing similar designs and colour schemes are usually ascribed to the Ghiordes group.
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.obtention: Acquired from the carpet dealer P. Willborg, Stockholm, in 1984. The rug belonged to the collection of R. Christensen, Stockholm.

1a9e5630-70cb-5d3f-a3ff-92564b210c02.name: Lamp
1a9e5630-70cb-5d3f-a3ff-92564b210c02.short_description: The Mamluks were prodigious patrons of the arts who took a special interest in building religious foundations, which they supplied with all manner of beautiful furnishings, including lamps such as this. According to the inscriptions on the lower part of the lamp, it was commissioned "By order of the most noble authority, the Exalted, the Lordly, the Masterful, holder of the sword, Shaykhu al-Nasiri", a former mamluk of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. On the upper and lower sections of the lamp is Shaykhu’s heraldic device or blazon in the form of a circular medallion bearing a red cup set between a red and a black bar. He is known to have built a mosque and a *khanqa* in Cairo in the mid-eighth/mid-fourteenth century, and this lamp was most likely made for one of these structures.
1a9e5630-70cb-5d3f-a3ff-92564b210c02.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
1a9e5630-70cb-5d3f-a3ff-92564b210c02.dates: Hegira mid-8th century / AD mid-14th century

1a9e5630-70cb-5d3f-a3ff-92564b210c02.method_for_provenance: Lamps of this type seem to have been produced exclusively for Mamluk religious foundations.

1c83b59f-bba0-5630-b9da-a13188474ac4.name: Prayer rug
1c83b59f-bba0-5630-b9da-a13188474ac4.description: Outlined on the contrasting green of the central field, the red prayer niche has a stepped arch fringed with hooks along its inner edges. Inside the niche, a floral composition encircled by 12 tiny ewers recalls the mosque-lamp motif. A recurrent motif of prayer rug designs, ewers are traditionally associated with an *aide-mémoire* meant to remind the believer of the ritual ablution required before prayer. The present rug features a main border reminiscent of the so-called Gothic border of 16th- and 17th-century carpets, and, in the upper corners of the main field, stylised vegetal motifs, which show the Western influence on Turkish art. This rather unusual blending of two stylistic sources is illustrative of the two main “forces” with a strong impact on the decorative vocabulary of 19th-century Ottoman carpets: the Turkish tradition and the influence of European art. The bright colour scheme is quite remarkable and its sharp contrasts almost shocking compared mainly to the fine colouring of the Gördes and Kula carpets that reigned supreme on the European market of Oriental carpets at the turn of the century.

1ca4ae5b-e753-59d1-a5de-423460efb5d1.name: Iconostasis in the Church of the Holy Saviour
1ca4ae5b-e753-59d1-a5de-423460efb5d1.short_description: This iconostasis was created by one of the greatest Macedonian masters of woodcarving, Petre Filipovski Garka, who formed his own group of artisans and developed his outstanding style of wood-carving, which was widely recognizable in the Balkans in the early 19th century. This exquisite piece of wood-carving was made from walnut in the technique of high relief. The iconostasis depicts scenes from the Old and the New Testament in which biblical figures are rendered wearing traditional costumes worn in Macedonia. The detail shows the self-portraits of Petre Filipovski and his associate artisans.

1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.name: Calligraphy
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.description:
Considered one of the masterpieces of Ottoman classical literature, *Su Kasidesi* (*Water Ode*) is Fuzûlî’s celebrated ode (*kaside*) written in praise of the Prophet Muhammad. The poem employs water (*su*) as its central metaphor, intertwining themes of purity, life, longing and spiritual elevation. Throughout the *kaside*, water appears as an entity filled with devotion—flowing, bowing, crying, evaporating and kneeling—mirroring the poet’s own yearning for the divine.  
  
Fuzûlî’s intricate wordplay transforms water into a symbol of both physical and spiritual life, reflecting the Islamic belief that all creation originates from water. By personifying water as an admirer of the Prophet, the poem situates natural elements within an emotional and devotional universe.  
The musical rhythm of the *aruz* metre, the repetition of sound patterns and the carefully layered imagery create an atmosphere of reverence. The poem’s rhetorical brilliance lies in its fusion of mystical Sufi thought, high literary artistry and deep emotional sincerity.  
  
*Su Kasidesi* continues to be celebrated as one of the finest examples of Ottoman poetic expression, demonstrating Fuzûlî’s mastery in blending spirituality, metaphysics and lyrical beauty.
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.method_for_provenance: Date and origin are written on the piece.
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu
keywords: Poem; Calligraphy; water; spirituality

201954ee-da8e-50a5-a061-1b9e19db7811.name: Ostrich egg pendants
201954ee-da8e-50a5-a061-1b9e19db7811.short_description: Since the early modern period, ostrich eggs have been suspended in rooms in the Christian and Islamic regions of the Mediterranean. Their purpose is to warn the faithful and to safeguard their souls against harm. In bazaars, they are hung on the fronts of street side shops, and in and above gateways. Ostrich eggs decorate the tombs of saints, churches and mosques. With the fashion for all things Oriental, they have found their way into upper class living rooms furnished "in Moorish style."

208f7a0a-f7c8-54f1-a727-726b4b64c7c8.name: Prayer chain
208f7a0a-f7c8-54f1-a727-726b4b64c7c8.short_description: Islamic prayer beads (*misbaḥa*) consist of three sections of beads separated from each other by two larger marker beads (*imām*) for easier counting. The last bead, which is usually a much larger piece in the shape of a bottle neck, is called "minaret imam" (*yad*) and stands for the greatest and secret hundredth name of Allah. The *misbaḥa* is meant for reciting prayers, praising Allah, and as a talisman.

20abb534-7f0e-5447-96ad-59b7c1f4354d.name: Pendant with The Miracle of Saint George and the Dragon
20abb534-7f0e-5447-96ad-59b7c1f4354d.description: Saint George was born to Christian parents in the 3rd century. He joined the Roman army and became a high-ranking officer at a young age, earning the respect of Emperor Diocletian. At that time, Diocletian persecuted Christians and required that all soldiers sacrifice to the pagan gods. Saint George publicly denounced the emperor and confessed to being Christian. He was subjected to brutal punishments, but refused to renounce his faith. Saint George was beheaded and became a popular martyr saint. In one story of his life, he rescued a town besieged by a dragon. The townspeople had been sacrificing children, who were randomly chosen by casting lots, to the dragon. Saint George rode in just as the town’s princess was to be sacrificed. He killed the dragon, a symbol of paganism, and converted the townspeople to Christianity. In this miniature icon, Saint George is seen atop a white horse slaying the dragon with a spear. The princess stands nearby with the town in the background. The icon has a beautiful enameled *oklad* (frame) with a silver loop at the top. It may have been worn around the neck and was probably commissioned for a military officer from a wealthy family since Saint George is a patron saint of soldiers.
20abb534-7f0e-5447-96ad-59b7c1f4354d.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Christie's Auction, London, in 2007. Gifted by Gordon Lankton to the Museum of Russian Icons in 2008.
keywords: Saints; Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography
materials: Egg tempera on wood with silver oklad, gems, enamel

2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.name: Calligraphy
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.description:
This artwork features the phrase "*Su gibi aziz ol*", written in classical Ottoman Turkish and rendered in Hasan Çelebi’s refined *sülüs* calligraphy. The expression—literally "May you be as precious as water"—is a traditional Anatolian blessing that conveys wishes of purity, value, and life-giving goodness. Water, regarded in both Islamic thought and Ottoman culture as the origin and sustainer of life, becomes a symbol of virtue, generosity, and spiritual clarity.  
  
The calligraphic composition is shaped in a fluid, droplet-like form, echoing the blessing’s meaning. Surrounding the central inscription is an intricate *tezhip* (illumination) border in deep blue and gold, reminiscent of traditional Ottoman manuscripts.  
  
The visual contrast between the delicate floral motifs and the strong, sweeping calligraphic lines highlights the harmony between ornamentation and the written word.  
Through its union of devotional aesthetics and cultural symbolism, this piece reflects the enduring legacy of Ottoman calligraphy and the masterful craftsmanship of Hasan Çelebi, one of the leading contemporary heirs of this artistic lineage.
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu
keywords: Calligraphy; Qur'an; Verse; Water

2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.name: Lamp holder.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.description: A large brass lamp holder; a hexagonal base tapers upward to an upper structure which once supported a dome, now lost, to which the suspension chain would have been attached. The bottom of the structure would have held several small glass oil lamps, accessed through a door in one of the six sides which is now missing. The sides are pierced to let the light from the lamps through, as well as engraved and inlaid with designs in which an inscription medallion praising Sultan Qaytbay is nestled among floral decoration. A large inscription band at the bottom of the lamp holder, repeated in smaller calligraphy in a parallel band at the top, declares: 'Glory to our lord the Sultan, the most noble ruler, sultan of Islam and the Muslims, reviver of justice in the world, suppressor of the immoral and rebellious, sultan of the Arabs and Persians, lord of the two seas, servant of the Two Holy Shrines, master of kings and sultans, Commander of the Faithful, Abu'l-Nasr Qaytbay, may God Almighty make his reign long'! When this lamp holder hung in a mosque it is unlikely that its decoration would have been visible; still, it is indicative of the quality of the arts under Sultan Qaytbay.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.short_description: A large brass lamp holder, the sides of which are pierced to reveal the light supplied by oil lamps held in its bottom. The decoration, executed in several techniques, includes several inscriptions naming Sultan Qaytbay. The lamp holder must originally have hung in a mosque he founded or renovated.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.method_for_datation: Inscriptions on the object name Qaytbay as Sultan and imply that he is still alive ('may God extend his rule'), the lamp holder is thus dated to his regnal dates, 872–901 / 1468–96.
2226f421-a01c-56bf-809f-7d0c2067f79e.method_for_provenance: Cairo was the Mamluk capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.

24d1b22a-7e02-5a13-97d1-ffbb62d62561.name: Fragment from the internal *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba
24d1b22a-7e02-5a13-97d1-ffbb62d62561.short_description:
This fragment comes from the internal *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba which was presented by the Ottoman sultan ‘Abdülaziz (r. 1861–1876) in his first regnal year. It was the last internal *kiswa* to be sent by the Ottomans. It remained inside the Ka‘ba until 1936, when it was replaced by an Indian-made one. Later internal kiswas were woven in Mecca.  
The section preserved in fragment represents almost half of the loom width and an almost complete vertical repeat. The latter is made up of four zigzag bands. In the first wide band is the *shahada*, followed in a narrower band by phrases in praise of God. The third band has cartouches and roundels inscribed with invocations to God. The final narrow band has *sura* *al-Baqara*, II, verse 144, in part, ‘*We see the turning of thy face (for guidance) to the heavens: now shall We turn thee to a Qibla that shall please thee. Turn then thy face in the direction of the sacred Mosque*’.

272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.name: Brass head of flagpole
272aabb1-2d59-5faa-9ce5-a28c1305a906.short_description: This mast, made of casted brass, bears an Arabic calligraphic decoration with the inscription "Oh God, Oh Muhammad". It is fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.name: Prayer rug.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.description:
This rug, dominated by the colours red, brown and white, is dedicated to prayer because of its niche motif in the central rectangular field. The niche is formed by a stepped, pointed arch and edged all around with carnations. A geometrical ornament is set against the light brown background of the area below the arch. A floral device replaces the lamp often to be seen in other prayer rugs. The spandrels are filled with five red flowering bushes. There are two transverse panels, one above the spandrels and one below the niche. Both show the same motif of a cloud-band in combination with rosette blossoms filling the spaces. The small central field is framed by a broad border consisting of an inner and an outer row of heavily stylised carnations and seven narrow stripes coloured alternately white and red.  
There were two places, Ghiordes (Gördes in Turkish) and Kula, manufacturing prayer rugs of similar patterns. This rug combines characteristic elements of both: for example, the seven narrow stripes are found in Kula prayer rugs and the niche with two transverse panels and a colour scheme dominated by red are typical of Ghiordes prayer rugs.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.short_description: Rug dedicated to prayer because of the niche motif in the central rectangular field. The floral device in the area below the arch replaces the lamp often to be seen in other prayer rugs. The central field is framed by a border of stylised carnations and seven narrow stripes.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.method_for_datation: In the 13th / 19th century, rugs from Ghiordes and Kula show a strong stylisation of the floral motifs similar to that of the rug described above.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.method_for_provenance: The rug cannot definitely be ascribed to Ghiordes or Kula. It shows characteristics of both manufacturing centres such as the two transverse panels, one at either end of the central field, typical of rugs from Ghiordes, and the seven narrow stripes which are to be found in rugs from Kula.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.obtention: Bought for the collection of Wilhelmina von Hallwyl (1844–1930) in Saloniki in 1896. Count and Countess Walther and Wilhelmina von Hallwyl donated the collection and their home to the Swedish state in 1920.

28485e93-6aee-597e-b6d4-519ba9eeb8e4.name: Caucasian Rug
28485e93-6aee-597e-b6d4-519ba9eeb8e4.short_description:
Although the Ummayad and Abbasid caliphates overthrew the Iranian empires in the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, the cultural influence of Persia remains. This Caucasian carpet displays a blend of influences from Islam and pre-Islamic Persia.  
  
Primary colours from natural dyes typically brighten carpets from the Shirvan region with blue likely representing water as a life's source. The symmetry in these textiles creates harmony with repeated shapes such as the *kubpa* (hexagonal medallion) with tooth-like edges and diamonds to protect from the evil eye.  
  
Bright colours and geometric figures adorn this rug with abstracted religious symbols. The *mehrab* (arched prayer niche) denotes the direction toward toward which Muslims pray, Mecca. The upper end of the carpet displays the date, 1281 Hegira (1864 AD). Two chequered rectangles resemble a chess board, which suggests a possible alternative use for this carpet for entertainment during travels.
