2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.name: High altar for San Pietro Cathedral of Bologna
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.description:
This complex and precious altar was donated by Pope Lambertini to the San Pietro Cathedral of Bologna. Originally it was composed of six candlesticks, a silver cross and a silver frontal depicting *Jesus Handing the Keys to St. Peter in the Presence of the Apostles*. Unfortunately, these rich objects were probably handed to the Frenchmen in 1796, after the treaty of Tolentino, signed by Pope Pius VII.  
The invoices for the high altar are registered in the *Diario Benedettino*. The pope prayed that it reached Bologna safe and sound.  
In the middle of the side there is a silver embossed oval representing *Christ Rescuing Peter from the Water*, on the sides are two smaller roundels representing allegories of *Faith*. The three bas-reliefs are framed in gilded cast bronze, with cherubs' heads and garlands against a blue lapis-lazuli background. In the corners the oval bas-reliefs represent the *Martyrdom of St. Peter* on the left and *St. Peter in Jail Visited by the Angel*. On the upper side hangs the coat of arms of the Lambertini family in silver.  
The whole altar is on show together with a sumptuous frontal donated by the pope in 1742, made of  
hemp canvas embroidered with gold thread. Against the embroidered gold background are several sewn gold leaf decorations. In the middle is a roundel of *St. Peter* half bust and on the sides the coat of arms of the Lambertinis' with the tiara and the papal keys held by angels.  
This extremely precious altar, only a part of the richer original complex, is characterised by its technical skill and high artistic quality. The Roman silversmith Angelo Spinazzi, documented from 1721 to 1767, probably made the step. On the sides a hallmark, despite being not entirely legible is believed to be that of the Roman craftsman Filippo Tofani. No hallmark is visible on the main central relief.
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.short_description:
This extremely precious altar was donated to the cathedral of Bologna by Pope Benedict XIV.  
The sides and corners are characterised by extremely detailed work: against a blue lapis-lazuli ground are intertwined coats of arms of the Lambertini family and oval bas-reliefs with figures in chiselled and embossed silver and gilded bronze. On the side, in the middle, *Christ Rescues Peter from the Water* flanked by two Allegories of Faith, on the corners *St. Peter in Prison Visited by the Angel* and the *Martyrdom of St. Peter*. The work was made in Roman workshops. The altar is completed by a beautifully worked frontal, also a gift from Pope Benedict XIV (1742).
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.dimensions: Side max. 57x380x27 cm; medallions left and right 34x25 cm, central 35x55 cm; sides 105x78 cm, 5x63 cm; capitals height 57 cm; roundels, right 30x21 cm, left 28x21 cm; frontal 104,5x355 cm
2b8bffd7-5ba3-5029-b6c5-d671a0482187.method_for_datation:
This altar was sent to Bologna and began in 1753. Work continued to 1756 although the whole complex was not yet complete.  
Spinacci, quoted many times as the author of the step, might be Angelo Spinazzi, a Roman silversmith working between 1721 and 1767.  
On the reliefs on the corners it is possible to see two hallmarks: 1) *the cipher 85 in a circle*, 2) *FT with a small cross under inside an irregular frame*. The first is used by several testers and affirms the high quality silver, following 1734 prescriptions. The second hallmark refers to the silversmith Tofani, even if this work is not cited by Bulgari in his monograph and if we don't know for sure the hallmark of this master.

2c61e46e-3c33-5e1e-acf0-98b19112c300.name: Mosque Lamp
2c61e46e-3c33-5e1e-acf0-98b19112c300.short_description:
The Mamluk glassmakers invented mosque lamps gilded and enamelled in vibrant colours between the 13th and 14th centuries. Production centres in Egypt and Syria became prominent for these mosque lamps with innovative Islamic enamelling techniques.  
  
During the 13th century, extensive trade occurred between Venice and the Mamluks, influencing the glass lamp techniques and styles. Hematite and cassiterite pigments created the pink tint in Mamluk glassware.  
  
This mosque lamp embodies an example of the vase-shaped enamelled lamps gaining popularity in Europe in the 19th century as exotic and luxurious medieval Islamic art pieces.  
  
The pink lamp reads the year 1867 along with the signature Philippe-Joseph Brocard, a renowned French craftsman fascinated with reviving, preserving and reproducing Mamluk lamps. The *kufic* calligraphy is reminiscent of the style used during the Mamluk era.

2e37ae24-5c92-5eeb-bdae-5fa66679ca7b.name: Ladik prayer rug
2e37ae24-5c92-5eeb-bdae-5fa66679ca7b.description:
Ladik, in Anatolia, had been an important carpet-making centre since at least the 17th century. Two types of prayer rug can be assigned to Ladik, but both have one charming feature: a row of elongated tulips in a cross-panel. The first group, considered to be earlier, are triple-arch prayer rugs. These have a narrow cross-panel with tulips over a *mihrab*. Another group consists of mostly 18th- and 19th-century rugs. They have a much smaller central niche and a wide cross-panel with upside down tulips beneath the *mihrab*.  
The Kraków rug belongs to the second group. The small, red *mihrab* niche is closed with a stepped, pointed arch, decorated with hook motifs. It has three elongated blossoming shrubs inside the niche that resemble the columns of the first group of Ladik rugs. The spandrels are decorated with five rosettes, a pair of lanceolate leaves and three ewers. The *mihrab* niche and ewers are symbols connected with the everyday ritual prayers of Muslims. Beneath the *mihrab* there is a wide cross-panel with two rows of arcades, upside down tulips, roses and stems with flowers. Six borders surround the field of the carpet. The main border is filled with an ornament of bold, strongly geometrised carnations.  
It is interesting that a very similar Ladik rug was depicted in a painting dating to as early as the second quarter of the 17th century. In the votive picture of the priest Tarło in one of the Polish churches, the rug can be seen beneath the altar of the prayer scene.

2ed5f331-f245-5701-b5ea-1a6aa1a79c09.name: Qur’an
2ed5f331-f245-5701-b5ea-1a6aa1a79c09.short_description:
This large-scale Qur’an manuscript from India stretches more than one meter in length. Handmade in India, these grand holy books were likely a result of domestic writings of the Qur’an and calligraphy as a form of devotion and worship.  
  
The *ayah* (verses) are composed in black ink in *naskh* script within a black frame refining the border on the delicate paper. Individual *ayah* and decorative elements also appear in liquidized gold for embellishment and emphasis. A selection of pages illustrates segments of *surah* (chapters) in bright colours from pigment in diamond and medallion shapes with floral motifs.

2f8a5281-9aad-56b2-94ab-cc71340502a0.name: Prayer rug
2f8a5281-9aad-56b2-94ab-cc71340502a0.description: Pirot kilims are woven very finely. Weave density can measure up to seven to nine grains per centimetre, like on the kilim with a *mihrab* and pots with flowers in the central field. At the top of the *mihrab* there is a lamp, and in the corners there are flower braches. Kilim has three borders and the one in the middle is narrower than the other two. Borders are decorated with vegetable ornaments, *almonds* (*bademčići*) and *octopuses* (*oktapod*). The colours used are: red, green, blue, yellow, brown and violet.

3014d292-46d6-5552-8846-8782d58e0b90.name: Foot reliquary
3014d292-46d6-5552-8846-8782d58e0b90.description: When Basel split into two half-cantons in 1833, the famous Basel Minster Treasure suffered the same fate. The new Canton Basel-Landschaft received 64 per cent of the treasure, but because it was desperately short of funds, it converted the ecclesiastical riches into cash, among them the silver reliquary of 1450, which brought the exchequer 562 francs. The reliquary has the shape of a foot, consistent with its contents – allegedly the foot bones of a young boy who was murdered in Bethlehem on Herod’s command. What chills modern viewers to the bone today, used to be the object of religious devotion to many. Through a of rock glass opening believers could catch a glimpse of the sacred relic and hope for divine assistance.
3014d292-46d6-5552-8846-8782d58e0b90.obtention: Part of the Basler Minster Treasure. Aquired by the Landesmuseum at an Auction in 1982.
keywords: Minster treasure; relic; foot reliquary; Basel
materials: Silver, chased, partially gilded; silver filigree; copper, engraved, gilded; enamel (translucent); crystal glass beads; mother-of-pearl; oak wood

301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.name: Candlesnuffer.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.description:
A candlesnuffer that resembles a pair of scissors, made from gilded iron and with decorative painting. Although the form resembles an ordinary pair of scissors one of its arms contains a small chamber (a rectangular box section) to extinguish lamps and candles. The second arm (which has a flat edge), when closed, enters inside the chamber and snuffs out the lamp or candle. The arm with the chamber extends into a tapered shape not unlike an ordinary pair of scissors, while the flat-edged arm is shorter, cut-off at the level of the chamber. The piece is completely gilded and is decorated with a multiplicity of forms the most prominent being located on the two sides of the chamber. Each of the long sides of the chamber is decorated with two confronting birds, possibly pigeons, and they appear to hold a leaf in their beaks. On each of the two small sides of the chamber are lions. Some of the decoration and gilding has worn off as a result long-term use.  
This snuffer has been used to extinguish not hundreds, but thousands of candles and lamps which would have illuminated al-Aqsa Mosque, Dome of the Rock, the plazas and other buildings within the Haram al-Sharif in Jerusalem.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.short_description: The Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock were lit by thousands of candles and lamps which required implements for lighting and extinguishing. This candlesnuffer takes the form of elegant scissors made from gilded iron. It is decorated with zoomorphic and vegetal forms, minutely portrayed to fit the small scissors.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.method_for_datation: The snuffer was dated by comparing it with the design and techniques of manufacture of other pieces whose dates have been tentatively pin-pointed.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.method_for_provenance: It is possible that the snuffer was produced in Istanbul since there are similar pieces known to have been produced there, but there is no firm evidence to confirm this.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.obtention: The piece was transferred from al-Aqsa Mosque to the Islamic Museum but it is not known when.
301e4bad-ae28-55b7-8175-5f828d2c5939.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Gilding; iron; candles; candle-snuffer; scissors

310e79cc-ee2c-5e1c-89d1-fcfcb20cf00e.name: Curtain for the door of the Holy Ka‘ba in Makkah al-Mukarramah
310e79cc-ee2c-5e1c-89d1-fcfcb20cf00e.short_description: This curtain, known as *sitara*, *burdah* or *burqa* and embroidered with qur’anic quotations, forms the most elaborate part of the *kiswah* textile cover which encloses the Holy Ka‘ba in Makkah. This example was made under the patronage of King Fahd ibn Abd al-Aziz al-Saud, who ascended the throne in AH 1405 / AD 1985.

32629ea7-5978-5c34-ac5e-6fa3012db355.name: Reliquary Chest of St. João de Brito
32629ea7-5978-5c34-ac5e-6fa3012db355.description:
The Portuguese established trading posts along the coasts of India and China where merchants could trade and store their merchandise, extending their authority into the hinterland. While the traditional political structures of local chieftains remained, the elite profited by reselling European wares. In addition to trade, the Portuguese sought to spread Christianity among the local Asian populations with Franciscan, Dominican and later Jesuit missionaries preaching to the indigenous peoples. The Christian missionaries learned the native languages, familiarised themselves with the indigenous cultures and even their religions; in this effort, the Jesuits were extremely dedicated. St. João de Brito was sent as a member of the Jesuit Order to the mission of Maduré, in India, in 1673. His aim was to convert the higher castes, in order to better establish Christianity in the region. He became a *pandaraswami*, an Indian ascetic. One of his converts, Prince Tadaya Theva upon becoming Christian, was rejected by one of his wives. She complained to her uncle, the Raja of Marava, who had the Jesuit executed in Orbyur, India, in 1690.  
This chest, with a pyramidal lid engraved in low-relief, features scenes of St. João de Brito's life and martyrdom. The bas-relief on the top features the saint in Indian dress, with sandals and a staff. Several winged cherubs in chiselled silver flank the lid. The body of the chest presents two sculpted winged angels on each side in true Baroque expression. Four elaborate feet in gilded silver hold the main body. Commissioned by King Pedro II of Portugal as a royal homage to the Jesuit saint, the Portuguese coat of arms is seen in the centre testifying to the royal provenance.  
The presence of the *Agnus Dei* on the top may have been a later addition by the Jesuits, who used it on special occasions as a Eucharistic tabernacle for the veneration of the Blessed Sacrament.

32db9874-813f-566f-afe8-d3adcab6c80a.name: Saint Georges
32db9874-813f-566f-afe8-d3adcab6c80a.short_description:
This stained glass was commissioned from the artist Yoki by the Association “Semper Fidelis” to commemorate the entry of the canton of Fribourg into the Swiss Confederation in 1481. Although officially presented to the Fribourg cantonal authorities, this piece of glass art was designed for the Musée du Vitrail (now Vitromusée Romont), which opened in 1981 as part of the celebrations for the 500th anniversary of the canton joining the Swiss Confederation. For a long time it was exhibited in the attic of the museum, where a special opening was created to display it.  
  
This glass in concrete depicts St. George in armor and nimbus, riding a white horse, holding a spear in both hands and piercing the mouth of the dragon lying at his feet, which turns its head to look at him.

33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.name: Fragment of a basin.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.description:
Fragment of a basin sculpted in low relief, triangular in shape, both parts of which have been restored. Two of the sides are flat, the third is curved.  
The scene on the basin, of which only a part has survived, depicts hawking. The torso and part of the thigh of a horse rider can be distinguished, clothed in a pleated tunic belted around the waist by a large belt, and holding a white weapon in the right hand. Behind him, a falconer, whose face is mutilated and whose lower limbs have been amputated, and who is wearing a tunic that is open in front and tightened at the waist by a narrower belt, holds a dead hare. In his left hand, he holds up a falcon, of which only one foot and a bit of the tail can be seen above the horse's rump, the lower part of which is missing. A section of tree trunk, which could belong to a palm tree, appears behind the falconer.  
To the left of this scene lies an inscription consisting of two lines in *kufic* lettering. The first line is rather difficult to interpret ; the second reads as follows: ' …*ine wa arba'ou maya … amal ibn* …' (…four hundred…the work of Ibn…). '*ine*' cannot be translated as it is the last syllable of a number that could just as well be forty as seventy or even ninety.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.short_description: Fragment of a sculpted white marble ablutions basin, the two halves of which have been pieced back together. The bas-relief scene shows a falcon hunt. On the left-hand side there is an inscription in *kufic* characters. This object was originally from Andalusian Morocco.
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.holder: National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Arts

33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.method_for_datation: The object features a date which is missing the numerals representing single units and units of tens, and thus can only be placed somewhere between 440 and 489 (1048 and 1096).
33034cbb-75d9-5619-8b7f-cac29ec681b4.method_for_provenance: Through comparing this bas-relief fragment to basins from al-Andalus, Marçais was able to attribute this fragment to a basin, which could have been used for ablutions, of the same origin.

336e6afb-8f0e-5f3a-a491-c18e56f13628.name: *Hag Al Layla'* celebration
336e6afb-8f0e-5f3a-a491-c18e56f13628.description: *Hag Al Layla'* takes place in Sha’ban, the month before Ramadan. On this night, families hand out sweets and nuts – peanuts, almonds, *meez* and *nakhi* (chickpeas) – to the neighbourhood children. The children recite *dua’as* (verbal prayers) as they collect treats inside handmade cloth bags, however, should their neighbour refuse to hand out treats they may express anger toward that person. Traditionally, women give out the sweets, which are kept in a *geffah* (palm leaf basket), while sitting outside their front door. Each child would take care to visit every house in the neighbourhood.

keywords: shaban; ramadan; hag al layla

33fb43d3-39d9-5067-a872-1b4b9314584b.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
33fb43d3-39d9-5067-a872-1b4b9314584b.description: During the Mawlid (Feast of the Birth of Prophet Muhammad), people from all over Damascus rush to buy the first gift of this occasion, the *Mulabbas*, distinguishing the capital from other Syrian cities. This sweet, made of roasted almonds coated with sugar, is linked to the emotional history of the people of the capital because it is white, symbolising new birth, as in the birth of the Prophet. Many shops in the historic Buzuriyya market in Damascus are filled with sweets and chocolates in preparation for Mawlid al-Nabawi. According to one of its makers, the *Mulabbas* industry in Damascus dates back more than 150 years, and its main sales area is centred in the historic Buzuriyya Market.

3481e842-be03-549a-be65-9ec6969a8ba5.name: Marasali prayer rug
3481e842-be03-549a-be65-9ec6969a8ba5.description: A Caucasian Marasali prayer rug woven in 1253 Hijra (1838 AD) with the quintessentially Azeri flaming buta motif. The main, and very dark blue, field of this pile carpet is occupied by rows of multi-coloured pear-shaped leaf motifs with serrated edges.  These motifs are better known as flaming butas (also botehs or Paisley pattern motifs), and are here alternately coloured across the horizontal rows, creating uniformly coloured diagonal rows on the vertical axes from bottom right to top left. A geometrical arch is positioned at the top end of the centre filed creating the distinctive prayer-niche design of the prayer rug. To the left of the arch’s tip is discretely woven the date of manufacture using red knots. In Arabic letters and numbers it states “year 1253” in the Islamic calendar. The border shows a row of “bird motifs”, resembling bunches of red grapes, on an ivory background. These bird motifs are one of the key distinguishing features of Marasali carpets, and have evolved from clearly rendered abstracted birds bending to peck at the ground to the form you see on the border of this carpet, which looks more like a bunch of grapes with a leaf at its base.

35453f02-5851-5ed4-841e-211439b842c4.name: Qur’an with box
35453f02-5851-5ed4-841e-211439b842c4.short_description:
The small Qur’an belongs to a group of diminutive holy books intended as a talismanic object. Written in India in the *Turabi* calligraphy style with a single horse hair, the Qur’an represents a devotional book hard to read with the naked eye.  
  
Encased in a silver box, sometimes in textile pouches, the script becomes a pendant for a necklace. While the amulet would guard and empower the wearer, its manufacture was often reserved for sultans and their soldiers for their protection. Furthermore, the silver embellishes the protective power as a lucky metal in Islam. Carried around the neck or attached to ceremonial objects and weapons, good luck charms endure and appear throughout time and place.

35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.name: The Archangel Gabriel
35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.description: This icon depicts the Archangel Gabriel turned to the left, indicating that it comes from the Deesis tier of an iconostasis. He wears the *alb* (tunic) of a deacon and the liturgical coat of a bishop. In his right hand, he holds a sphere of light and in his left hand, a rod. The Archangel Gabriel, whose name means “man of God” in Hebrew, has been called the leader of the heavenly hosts. He is associated with numerous biblical events, including the announcements of the births of Mary and John the Baptist, and most importantly, the Annunciation, in which Gabriel proclaimed to the Virgin Mary that she would conceive and bear a son named Jesus.
35a55142-cbad-545f-9150-ff76ab018f9b.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2010. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography; Angels

35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.name: Textile with prayer niche (*mihrab*).
35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.description: The fabric, made of red, black and yellow-brown silk, is decorated with motifs embroidered with silver- and gold-plated copper wire woven into a cotton base. The basic decorative element consists of a large prayer niche (*mihrab*), at the centre of which, at the top, there hangs a mosque lamp. Above and beside it there are scrolls containing decorative epigraphic motifs. The background of the fabric, with the exclusion of the inside of the niche where there are naturalistic floral motifs, is decorated with arabesque elements consisting of intertwined palmettes of various shapes or half-palmettes surrounded by spirals.
35d28d2d-69ab-5ec0-a006-32f2135420d3.short_description: This fabric, embroidered with metal thread and decorated with a prayer niche (*mihrab*), a large mosque lamp and epigraphic motifs, is typical of late Ottoman textile production.

370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.name: *Feast of St. Anthony of Padua*
370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.description:
The subject is a relatively scarcely represented scene from the life of St. Anthony of Padua, priest, preacher and disciple of St. Francis of Assisi. The Franciscan saint sits at the table in the house of a wealthy man, blessing goblets of wine. On the left, a *putto* brings a lily, symbol of purity and one of the saint's attributes. On the right, precious tableware is displayed, as was customary at feasts from the 16th century onwards. Although the scene is illuminated at the centre, the picture features two pictorial sections: the left symbolising austerity and humbleness and the right, luxury and superiority. The artist also draws attention to the two sections by use of character types: the face of St. Anthony with his halo reflecting spiritual delight, while the gross face of the rich man shows sensual pleasure, greed and a boorish approach to the situation. The listening man on the right points out his gluttony, one of the seven deadly sins. The painter highlights the scene with a contrasting motif of deep-red drapery, which sets the colour tone for the whole picture. The painting stands out among Kracker's altarpieces and ceiling frescos because of its genre-painting atmosphere and use of chiaroscuro. It also manifests the artist's bold monogram *JK*, but not as distinctively as on some of his more sizeable compositions.  
The picture was part of the decoration of the refectory in the Franciscan Monastery in Moravská Třebová, together with *The Feast of the Holy Family* and *The Feast of St. Wenceslas*.  
Kracker was a leading exponent of the Vienna Academy style represented by Paul Troger and Michelangelo Unterberger. After studying in Vienna Kracker was active in the workshop of Josef Tadeáš Rotter in Brno, and later settled in Znojmo. His best-known works include ceiling paintings and altarpieces in the Church of St. Nicholas in Prague and in Nová Říše. His later work was associated with Hungary, where he joined the service of Bishop K. Esterházy in Jager.
370f95db-5572-52d3-b9d7-f5099026bcc9.short_description: The subject is a relatively scarcely represented scene from the life of St. Anthony of Padua. The canvas formed part of the decoration in the refectory of the Franciscan Monastery in Moravská Třebová. It is an early piece by the artist, J. L. Kracker who was active in Bohemia, Moravia and Hungary.

377425e8-db47-571b-85e2-27702d394d1d.name: Scroll with views of Mecca and Medina
377425e8-db47-571b-85e2-27702d394d1d.short_description: The text consists of Qur’anic verses, short prayers, invocations and numerous repetitions of the *basmala* and the *shahada*, the latter arranged into decorative shapes such as vases, flowers, a pagoda and *Dhu’l-faqar*, the bifurcated sword given by the Prophet to ‘Ali. In addition, there are depictions of the Masjid al-Haram at Mecca and the Prophet’s mosque at Medina (where the domed tomb is depicted on the wrong side). The last panel encloses the *hilya* of the Prophet Muhammad.

38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.name: Curtain for the *minbar* of the Meccan sanctuary, with the name of King Faruq I of Egypt
38408d83-304f-5d3b-ba1f-3b4dc4fb028b.short_description:
This is an exceptionally fine example of the high quality of embroidery produced by the craftsmen of Dar al-Kiswa in the mid 20th century. Very few curtains for the Meccan *minbar* survive, and none of the known examples predates the early 20th century. This is probably one of the last ones made, as Egypt stopped sending curtains for the Meccan *minbar* around that time.  
  
The top panel is inscribed, ‘God Almightly said in his revered book’. The three lines below have *sura al-Jumu‘a* (LXII), verse 9, which appropriately mentions the call to prayer on Fridays. The last panel states that ‘This sitara for the minbar of the sacred House of God was ordered by him who depends on God, the king of Egypt Faruq I, may God grant him succor, in the year 1365’.

38bee4ad-cee4-5177-b8e7-dff8c1f903a8.short_description: A fine floor mat, woven on the loom, with sparse decoration, self-patterned borders with interlocking lozenge pattern and pairs of brown brocaded bands. The inscriptions, written in a *kufic* script, have benedictory content with details about the work's creation, as naming *Tabariya* the place of production. Such floor coverings were made for domestic and religious interiors and were possibly used during prayers.

38c8715f-fcca-5d98-afc6-976902eb06dc.name: Coconut shell dipper
38c8715f-fcca-5d98-afc6-976902eb06dc.description:
This dipper is inscribed in Arabic with the verse:  
*"Wa ja‘alnā mina’l-mā’i kulli shay’in ḥay"* (Surah al-Anbiyā, 21:30), "And We made from water every living thing."  
  
It also bears the Basmala — *"Bismillāhi’r-Raḥmāni’r-Raḥīm"*, "In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful."

38e4904d-c574-52b6-a1e1-5202c0c6e8ba.name: Pilgrimage certificate
38e4904d-c574-52b6-a1e1-5202c0c6e8ba.short_description: This certificate was made for a pilgrim named Sayyid Yusuf bin Sayyid Shihab al-Din Mawara al-Nahri for his ‘umra, illustrating significant locations in Mecca, Medina, and other religious locations. Beside these illustrations are inscriptions from the Quran and texts written in Arabic and Persian related to pilgrimage, with the name of the pilgrim and his six witnesses featured at the end. Pilgrimage certificates are considered legal documents acquired by the pilgrim at the end of the journey.

392875c0-7574-582d-b567-f145659f7e9b.name: Prayer rug
392875c0-7574-582d-b567-f145659f7e9b.description: The oldest carpets preserved till today that were produced in Asia Minor date from the 13th century, from the time of the Seljuqs. Turkish carpets were exported to Europe from the 14th century onwards and that is when we start to find them in the paintings of the Italian masters, especially the Siena and Florentine schools. The best examples of the carpet art of Asia Minor, boasting exceptionally imaginative designs, can be found in the prayer rugs. In the centre of Kula prayer rug is a dark blue *mihrab* or prayer niche. In the middle of this field there is a stylised star-like floral design in the shape of a pillar. The inside edge of the *mihrab* has smaller flowers while the surrounding area is covered with large geometric, flower motifs. There are eight borders, of which three are missing at the narrow ends of the rug. One of the narrow borders is repeated several times, with the same geometric motif, but in contrasting colour combinations. The other borders have a floral motif. The colours used are blue, brown, red and green.
392875c0-7574-582d-b567-f145659f7e9b.method_for_datation: Ref. Stojanović, D., *Orijentalni tepisi i ćilimi* \[Summary in English\], Belgrade: Muzej primenjene umetnosti, 1971.
392875c0-7574-582d-b567-f145659f7e9b.bibliography:
Vitković-Žikić, M., "Odsek za tekstil i kostim", in I. Zorić (ed.), *55 godina Muzeja primenjene umetnosti: 1950–2005*, Belgrade: Muzej primenjene umetnosti, 2005: 97–121.  
Stojanović, D., *Orijentalni tepisi i ćilimi* \[Summary in English\], Belgrade: Muzej primenjene umetnosti, 1971.
keywords: Kula; prayer rug; wool; symmetrical knot

39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.name: Basin.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.description: A large marble fountain-basin. The basin is basically a large hemisphere supported on a short foot and topped with a 12-sided rim, one side of which is blank and another of which has a section cut out to support the channel which brought water. Eleven of the sides carry an inscription giving the name and titles of the Ayyubid governor of Hama, al-Malik al-Mansur Muhammad ibn al-Muzaffar Mahmud ibn Muhammad ibn ‘Umar ibn Shahanshah ibn ‘Ayyub (also known by his shorter title of Mansur II Muhammad), who ruled from AH 641–83 / AD 1244–84. The exterior of the basin is carved with a bold design of two interlacing arabesque designs, each repeated six times in alternation and set off against a background of smaller floral decoration. Such a fine basin would probably have been placed in a prominent public mosque to serve the needs of congregants and to proclaim the glory of the ruler.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.short_description: A large marble basin for ablutions, carved on the exterior with prominent interlacing arabesque designs. The 12-sided rim is inscribed with the name and titles of the patron, the governor of Hama. Thus the basin served both the ritual needs of the community and the governor’s public image.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.method_for_provenance: The basin is inscribed with the name and titles of the Ayyubid governor in whose honour this object was made (see description above).
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.bibliography: Ayers, J., Oriental Art in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London, 1983, p.111.
39548f51-03b2-558c-9e39-2e9427feaf5c.author: Barry Wood
keywords: floral decoration; religious objects; water; inscription

39c77b9c-54ff-5cb2-bbbc-c8a5ef99dbc2.name: Set of Icons from a Festival Tier
39c77b9c-54ff-5cb2-bbbc-c8a5ef99dbc2.description:
This set of 12 icons, the only one of its kind in the United States, is believed to be from the Pskov region of Russia. The icons were originally hung on the festival tier of an iconostasis, the partition separating the nave from the sanctuary of an Orthodox church. The festival tier highlights the major holidays of the Orthodox liturgical calendar. This set includes the following images:  
  
1\. The Meeting of Anna and Joachim  
2\. The Nativity of the Virgin Mary  
3\. The Nativity of Christ  
4\. The Presentation of Christ  
5\. The Transfiguration  
6\. The Raising of Lazarus  
7\. The Crucifixion  
8\. The Three Marys at the Sepulchre  
9\. The Descent  
10\. The Ascension of Christ  
11\. The Holy Trinity  
12\. The Feast of Pentecost
39c77b9c-54ff-5cb2-bbbc-c8a5ef99dbc2.obtention: From the De Wijenburgh Collection. Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Idonen Galerie, Germany, in 2012. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography; Life of Jesus

3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.name: Silver service.
3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.description:
A silver service consisting of identical pairs of candlesticks, incense burners and perfume sprinklers. 'Adila, the daughter of Sultan Mahmud II, presented the service as a gift to al-Aqsa Mosque. The design is heavily influenced by the European style.  
Each of the candlesticks is composed of a base, a shaft, a body, neck and the candleholder. The base of the candlestick is broad and octagonal in form, and is adorned with engraved leaf decorations. The base is connected to the body via the shaft, on top of which is a cupped ledge in the form of a leaf. The leaf-shaped ledge curves upwards, resembling the leaves engraved on the base. The body of the candlestick is composed of two globular areas: the lower one resembles a small sphere, while the one above it is a relatively large ovoid. Both are decorated with leafy engraved motifs similar to those that decorate the base. The body is connected to the neck, where there is another cupped leaf-shaped ledge, resembling that below it and of approximately the same size.  
Both the incense burners and the perfume sprinklers resemble each other, for each piece is composed of a base, body and punctured neck; the base fluted and wide, narrowing immediately. The base of one of the incense burners carries an Ottoman inscription in Arabic letters that reads: “Sultan Mahmud Han Sani hazretlerinin kerimesi, devletlü, ismetlü Adile Sultan hazretlerinin Mescid-i Aksa'ya mahsus vakfıdır.” (“Endowment of her Excellency Adile Sultan, daughter of his Excellency Sultan Mahmud Han II, to al-Aqsa Mosque.”)  
The date “1305” \[AD 1887\] is inscribed on it as well. This date was added during the reign of the Ottoman sultan, 'Abd al-Hamid II (r. AH 1293–1327 / AD 1876–1909). The body of the incenser is globular and fluted in form, slender at the bottom in order to adhere to the base, and at the top in order to cleave to the neck. The middle of the body is divided into two: the upper and the lower parts, which are connected to each other by a hinge, whereby one can open the censer and fill it. The necks of the incense burners are punctured to permit the fragrance to escape, similarly the necks of the sprinklers terminate with holes from which to sprinkle perfume and, like the incensers, they open at the apex in order to fill the inside of the sprinkler with perfume. Both the incense burners and perfume sprinklers end with a small globular section decorated with vegetal leaves, which resemble those decorating the candlesticks.
3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.short_description: This silver set is worked in the European style and is made up of six pieces that are similar in size and shape and decorated with vegetal motifs: identical pairs of candlesticks, incense burners and perfume sprinklers.  It was given to al-Aqsa Mosque by ‘Adila, the daughter of Sultan Mahmud II.
3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.initial_owner: ‘Adila, daughter of Sultan Mahmud II (r. AH 1223–55 / AD 1808–39), who gave it as part of an endowment to al-Aqsa Mosque, Jerusalem.

3b20eedf-73ef-58bb-867b-4bd1624b5b9c.method_for_datation: The service has a written inscription on the base of one of the incense burners that includes the date.

3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.name: Two mosque lamps.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.description:
Two glass mosque lamps with globular body and flared neck, decorated with enamel and gilt. Around the body is a bold inscription, while roundels exhibiting a cup emblem alternating with calligraphy surround the neck. The inscriptions around the body of both these lamps state that they were made for Sayf al-Din Shaykhu al-‘Umari, a prominent amir for Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. Shaykhu achieved the status of commander-in-chief of the palace and then Great Amir before being assassinated in AH 759 / AD 1357. The roundels around the neck and the underside of body contain a cup motif, the blazon of Shaykhu, indicating that he held the post of cup-bearer. The neck is inscribed with the Qur’anic verse 24:35, known as the ‘Light’ verse: ‘God is the Light of heavens and the earth; the likeness of His Light is a niche, wherein is a light, the light in a glass, the glass as it were a glittering star’.  
Mamluk lamps with their non-figurative decoration, and inscriptions of Qur’anic verses, were mostly intended for religious buildings, hence the term ‘mosque lamp’. However, there are some lamps of the same shape from this period that would have been used in a secular setting. These lamps are part of a group of extant lamps probably made for the mosque Shaykhu commissioned in AH 750/ AD 1349, or for the sufi hostel (*khanqa*) he had built soon after in AH 756/ AD 1355, situated at the foot of the Citadel in Cairo.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.short_description: A pair of glass mosque lamps decorated with enamel and gilt. Around the body are medallions containing the cup emblem, the heraldic symbol belonging to the patron Sayf al-Din Shaykhu al-‘Umari, who was cup-bearer for Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.dates: Hegira mid-7th century/ AD mid-14th century.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.dimensions: Height 53 cm, diameter (at base) 14 cm, diameter (at top) 26 cm.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.method_for_datation: Embellished with the blazon of Shaykhu these lamps were probably made for one of the religious buildings he commissioned; a mosque in 750/ 1349 and a *khanqa* in 756/ 1355. Shaykhu rose to prominence in the 740s / 1340s, and helped re-instate Sultan al-Nasir Hasan on the throne in 754 / 1354. Thenceforth Shaykhu effectively ruled the Mamluk Empire until he was assassinated in 758/ 1357. These mosque lamps probably date to the mid-7th / mid-14th century when he was at the height of his powers.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.method_for_provenance: The objects are embellished with the blazon of Shaykhu (amir of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad in Cairo, Egypt), and inscribed with his name, it is probable, therefore, that these lamps were made for one of the religious buildings that Shaykhu commissioned.
3c54f80b-766c-5ff6-959e-037413ba35e0.obtention: One of the lamps (OA+521) was bequeathed by Felix Slade in 1868; the other (G.497) was part of the Godman Bequest of 1983.

3fb86eda-1e8c-5fdf-9e0b-53b50204bf6c.name: Seljuq Rug
3fb86eda-1e8c-5fdf-9e0b-53b50204bf6c.description: A “Konya Group” rug found in the Konya Aladdin Mosque and acquired by the museum in 1911. The condition of this rug is poor, nevertheless it is possible to perceive the general decoration. The rug is in three pieces, the remaining parts of a large carpet. The main border is wide and light red in colour. Stylized *kufic*letters in dark red are contoured with brown and placed side by side. The main border is separated from the basic ground by a yellow band framed with a narrow brown line. The dark blue ground is a diamond pattern with hooked ends. There are small heart shapes in their middle of these diamond shapes. Seljuq rugs were commonly woven in large sizes. They were decorated in plain geometric patterns, generally with a small number of colours in various shades contrasted with a wide *kufic* border.

4110beeb-d623-5316-b3ea-13f8ecd8e3db.name: Mahmal
4110beeb-d623-5316-b3ea-13f8ecd8e3db.short_description:
This ceremonial *mahmal* consists of a tent-like cotton cloth embroidered with gold and silver threads. Placed upon a wooden frame (litter) on a camel’s back, the *mahmal* would bear the *kiswa* (Kaaba covering) and other religious items to Mecca in a pilgrimage procession.  
  
This example from Ottoman Turkey features the Mamluk yellow colour embellished with the Throne verse *(Ayat al-Kursi)*, the Muslim invocation (*Basmala*), and the declaration of faith *(Shahada)* in *thuluth* calligraphy. The signature of the Ottoman sultan is visible in *tughra* script.  
  
During the *hajj* or pilgrimage season, the caravan would parade the streets of Cairo in a festival accompanied by musicians before embarking on the journey to Saudi Arabia. The *mahmal* reminds of a wedding procession and carries feminine connotations through its familiarity with the *howdaj* used to transport women hidden away from the public eye.  
  
Muslim rulers would commission a *mahmal* in an opportunity to highlight their sovereignty, taste and piety. Although the legend of Mamluk Sultanah Fatima Shajarat al-Durr associated the ruler with the first *mahmal*, scholars debate the first appearance with earlier references recounting Zubaydah, the wife of Harum al Rashid, using a palanquin in a pilgrimage procession from Baghdad to Mecca.
4110beeb-d623-5316-b3ea-13f8ecd8e3db.owner: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani
4110beeb-d623-5316-b3ea-13f8ecd8e3db.method_for_datation: The date and origin were established in research-based comparison from an examination of material, embroidery and style.
4110beeb-d623-5316-b3ea-13f8ecd8e3db.method_for_provenance: This mahmal was used to carry the kiswa to Mecca, Saudi Arabia.

4161509c-5db0-57a2-b378-312463a1e2f2.name: Qur’an Bag
4161509c-5db0-57a2-b378-312463a1e2f2.short_description:
This Moroccan leather bag would encase a copy of a Qur’an or other religious texts to protect the manuscripts against dust, moisture and dirt. Silver thread embroiders the Islamic Star known as *Rub Al Hizb* with two overlapping squares, floral vines and Arabic calligraphy in the ancient Moroccan style. The calligraphy reads "Prophet Muhammed - Peace Be Upon Him".  
  
The silver thread and calligraphy transform the leather bag into a talismanic object, casting protection upon the Qur’an and the owner. North African Qur’an cases often embodied a twofold protective function: book cover and talisman.  
  
Furthermore, the case exemplifies the craftsmanship of Maghrebi artisans, including the traditional skills of leatherwork and metal-stitching.

4285852d-bdc9-521a-a814-ba8b902153a3.name: *Mihrab* (prayer niche)
4285852d-bdc9-521a-a814-ba8b902153a3.short_description: This mihrab, nearly 12 feet tall and dated 663/1265, is the masterpiece of the DDFIA collection. It is one of six surviving luster mihrabs made during the Ilkhanid period of rule in Iran (1256–1353) and one of only two of its type outside of Iran. Originally, it was located in the Imamzada Yahya, a tomb of a descendant of a Shi‘ite imam in Veramin, Iran. In the tomb’s prayer sanctuary, the mihrab was located on the qibla wall—the one indicating the direction of Mecca.

43f2e562-6eda-5dde-81a4-a1b3639f9c94.name: 'Transylvanian' Double Niche Rug
43f2e562-6eda-5dde-81a4-a1b3639f9c94.description:
A characteristic type of Ottoman rugs is the 'Transylvanian' double niche rug. Several variants of the type fashionable for over two centuries are known. Its common feature is the hexagonal medallion filling the central field. This is created by mirroring the original *mihrab* (prayer niche) of the traditional prayer rug across the central axis. This rug of symmetrical design was particularly popular in Transylvania where it was used as table or bed cover and wall hanging. The name "Transylvanian" refers to the place of frequent occurrence and not to the place of origin.  
  
This exquisite specimen is from the first double niche rug period and is characterized by arabesque tendrils (First Period "Transylvanian" Double Niche Rug). The dark blue field is filled with subtly designed tendrils, with flowers and leaves arranged symmetrically to both axes. This design is complemented by two mosque lamps hanging from the apexes of the *mihrabs* (prayer niches). Ochre fields above the niches with blue arabesque tendrils can be traced to Persian design prototypes. The main strip of the 'Transylvanian' border pattern contains elongated polygonal cartouches alternated with eight-pointed stars, a pattern typical of this carpet type. A similar design with an ochre central field is kept in the collection of the “Black Church” in Brassó (now Braşov, Romania).

4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.name: Prayer rug.
4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.description:
This carpet demonstrates through its design that it belongs to the group of prayer rugs. The inner area is adorned with a red-coloured arch-shaped *mihrab* (prayer niche). Placed in front of the niche is a basin, seen from above, from which emerges a small tree with green leaves, rendered in a semi-abstract design with fine lines. A small yellow jug with a handle and short spout has been incorporated into the centre of the tree. This jug may relate to Sura 5 verse 8 of the Qur’an, which mentions obligation of ablutions to be undertaken before prayer. Green-coloured, eight-pointed plaited stars can be seen in the corners of the *mihrab* arch. Above the *mihrab* is a rectangular space filled with palms and cypresses. Two borders frame the inner area. The thinner border is filled by a decorative cloud-motif band. This cloud-motif band is a common feature of Ottoman art since the AH 9th and 10th / AD 15th and 16th century, and it originated in China. On this rug, the yellow cloud-motif bands are displayed over a red background, and are positioned very close to one another. The rug’s wider border consists of a continuous tendril-like interlacing band involving plant motifs, over a light-green background.  
The rug’s symbolism derives from the connection between the *mihrab* motif and that of the garden of Paradise, which is perhaps what is being illustrated on the rug through the pool of water and the tree. Paradise, described as a wonderful garden, is promised at different points throughout the Qur’an to those who believe in the Islamic faith. Followers of Islam will one day arrive and stay in this garden full of lovely streams, wonderful plants and beautiful young virgins (*Huri*s).  
Prayer rugs from Cairo are frequently mentioned in the sources, but this particular rug is the only surviving Mamluk prayer rug. It is particularly noteworthy for its incorporation of Mamluk motifs with those derived from Ottoman art, hence the reason for dating it to around AH 900 / AD 1500 or a little later.  
Mamluk rugs can be seen in Italian paintings from the 15th and 16th century and moreover are mentioned in a great number of sources. During this period there was also a flourishing trade between Mamluk Cairo and Italy.
4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.short_description: This is the only prayer rug to have survived from the Mamluk period. It was probably made in Cairo around 1500. Its design shows a mixture of Mamluk and Ottoman features. Carpet manufacture flourished in Egypt under the Mamluk sultans and rugs were also exported to Europe.

4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.method_for_datation: The carpet exhibits both Mamluk and Ottoman elements in its style, and thus could be from around 900 / 1500 as manufacturers in Cairo were just in the process of adopting Ottoman elements into their repertoire. However, as all that remains is this single Mamluk prayer carpet, it is difficult to give an exact date.
4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.method_for_provenance: The whole host of its unique motifs, colours and characteristic asymmetric or Persian knots all collude to suggest that this carpet was made in Cairo in a Mamluk carpet workshop.

44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.name: Processional cross
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.alternate_name: Processional standard of the brotherhood of the Tears of the Virgin Mary or of the Ponte del Borgo, later del Borgo, later Company of the Holy Sacrament
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.description:
This solemn gilded cross bears a rich decoration of vine leaves and vine-shoots made with a drill. There are interspersed with cherub heads and angels carved in the round, crowned with polychrome flowers and holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ.  
The branches resemble tree trunks with bark and knots. They end with two small knobs. The dead Christ in the middle is carved in the round, polychrome with an ample gilded cloth around his hips. On the upper part of the longitudinal arm hangs a cartouche with the writing \`INRI\` held by three small angels.  
Along the lower sides, stand on shelves four small statues carved in the round. They represent the Mourning Madonna, St. Bartholomew and two angels with gilded clothes and polychrome features.  
The stylistic features are late seventeenth-century and the delicate carving is associated with a skilled use of a drill.  
After the suppressions of 1798 that affected all religious companies and brotherhoods by the confiscation of their property, many of these processional items got lost. Thanks to a decree by the viceroy of Italy Eugenio Beauharnais in 1807 which stated for each parish church the presence of just one company of the Holy sacrament many processional crosses were preserved as properties of these companies. This happened in Budrio, where even the name of the company was changed.
44cf7449-7064-5e7b-8625-27f3fafdff19.short_description:
This solemn gilded cross bears a rich decoration with vine leaves and vine-shoots made with the drill. It is interspersed with angels carved in the round holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ.  
In the middle is the dead Christ surrounded by the Mourning Madonna, St. Bartholomew and two angels.  
The elaborate design is reminiscent of the local artistic taste of the end of the seventeenth century.

44ff5030-1782-52cb-a816-7b58f2d32a22.name: The *Mass of Saint Gregory*
44ff5030-1782-52cb-a816-7b58f2d32a22.description:
References in Portuguese inventories to the carpets of “Castile” and the “Levant” became progressively more frequent in the first half of the 16th century and coincided with the period when representation of knotted carpets, in the form of Iberian and Turkish carpets, reached its peak in Portuguese painting.  
This fact is owed to the Muslim presence in the Iberian Peninsula. Pre-existing contact with Arab culture, as well as the production of knotted carpets, preceded the arrival of oriental counterparts and restricted their demand in the market. Facing an already-established network of Iberian, Turkish and North African manufacturers, carpet manufactories had to respond to the demands of a society well used to the consumption of exotic luxury goods.  
The *Mass of Saint Gregory* originally constituted one of the panels from the *predella* of an altarpiece in the church of the Convent of São Francisco. The *predella* comprised 16 paintings depicting scenes from the Eucharist. The painting seen here represents a story made popular in the Golden Legend of the moment when Christ reveals himself on the altar to Pope Gregory; Christ responds to Pope Gregory’s prayer for a sign to convince a deacon, who had earlier confronted him with doubts about the doctrine of transubstantiation. In the painting, St. Gregory kneels before the altar on a carpet of Spanish origin. The carpet’s field is filled with octagonal medallions in which stars and quatrefoils are alternately inserted; the border is filled with a pseudo-*kufic* design interwoven with stylised floral motifs.

451583b8-a3a8-528a-b5bb-8db3d1096e78.name: Ladik Prayer Carpet (*seccade*) on Red Ground
451583b8-a3a8-528a-b5bb-8db3d1096e78.short_description: A prayer carpet in which the lower part of the field has an arched prayer niche in red. Small trefoils project into the field from each side of the niche. The blue spandrels are decorated with lanceolate leaves, rosettes, triangles, ewers, and hooks in various colors. The panel above the spandrel is separated from the latter by a band with a wavy floral scroll. The panel in red encloses the characteristic Ladik pattern of five lily stalks and *vandykes* with triangles and hook motifs. The field is framed by a narrow blue stripe containing S-motifs. The border has a repeat pattern of lilies and rosettes separated by varicolored narrow bands on a blue ground. The guard bands in yellow or orange contain wavy floral scrolls. Small S-motifs form the design of the guard stripes.

45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.name: Coupled-Column Prayer Rug
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.description: A version of 17th century Ottoman Turkish prayer rugs very popular in Hungary was the "column" rug, in which the *mihrab* (prayer niche) is divided into three fields by three, four or eight columns. The most common is the six-column version, considered by many to have the most beautiful design of 17th century Turkish rugs. Their general characteristic is a *mihrab* (prayer niche) whose background colour is red or ochre (rarely ivory or blue), divided into three parts by slender columns in a 1+2+2+1 distribution. The rug’s ochre *mihrab* (prayer niche) is supported by six narrow columns, dividing it into three fields. The spandrels have a blue and red arabesque decoration on an ochre field, and the crenellated frieze above has straight-stem flowers growing out of it. The design of the peak field and the frieze are not sharply delineated. Rounded cartouches of alternating colour run along the border; the outer border has a row of leaves of alternating orientation and the inner border is decorated by leaves and flowers strung along an undulating stem. In May H. Beattie’s classification, the rug is an early, type I Coupled-Column Prayer Rug.
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.dates: First half or middle (?) of 17th century

The rug entered into the inventory of the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts in 1962 as 'Item in store, of unknown origin'.

45b19a0c-0267-54d0-a134-624669d15108.name: Qur’an Sections
45b19a0c-0267-54d0-a134-624669d15108.short_description:
'This book binds two of the thirty parts (*ajza*) of the Qur’an. Known as *juz*, it was often sold separately during medieval Islam, with delicate floral and geometric patterns decorating the brown cover of the book.  
  
The *ayah* (verses) appear in *naskh* calligraphy sectioned with golden illustrations of vegetal motifs including the lotus and other flowers incorporated from ancient Chinese and Buddhist tradition.  
  
Although most Muslims in China did not speak Arabic, a few Chinese Qur’ans existed during the Ming and Qing dynasties. Since the spread of Islam and establishment of Islamic schools during the Yuan dynasty, prayers recitation and calligraphy were performed in Arabic. Many Muslims originating from the Arab world had a merchant background where *naskh* script represented the official writing. Adapted forms of *naskh* including *Muhaqqaq* and *Rihani* thus became the predominant styles for Chinese Qur’ans decorated with the typical gold ink.

473c085f-9830-5584-affd-3362c3aff805.name: Coupled-column Prayer Rug
473c085f-9830-5584-affd-3362c3aff805.short_description: A prayer rug where the creamy-white field is decorated with a triple arch on double columns in yellow, red, blue, and green. Between each pair of columns is a row of lozenges in yellow and red. The spandrel is decorated with a diaper of geometrical scrolls in white, reserving in the ground double arrow motifs in yellow and red. Across the top of the field is a panel with stalks of lilies alternating with other plants (probably tulips) in yellow, red, light and dark blue, and green on a creamy-yellow ground. The arches or so-called *vandykes* along the bottom of the panel are in blue and yellow and enclose arabesques in white, red, blue, and green. In the border is a row of compartments in blue, yellow, or green with floral devices in yellow, red, blue, and green. The guard bands contain a repeat pattern of a flower and leaf motif in white and red on a yellow ground (inner guard band) or in yellow (or green) and red on a white ground (outer guard band).

482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.name: Chasuble
482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.description:
The background is made of red silk velvet embroidered with different silver threads. The white silver stitches blocking the metallic threads create many different surface motifs of different heights, and flat areas thanks to a light padding.  
Most likely manufactured in Bologna, this vestment has a common decorative scheme especially evident in the chasuble. It is divided in three by a central rich bush of acanthus interlaced with the instruments of the Passion of Christ forming the main decorative feature. Great inflorescences alternate with the crown of thorns, the cock and the glove. They build a sort of central axis from which depart wide branches linked by delicate nets and vine shoots. The vestment is clearly indebted to models made in Rome in the age of Pope Benedict XIV, such as the ones donated to the Cathedral of San Pietro in Bologna. This is evident in the use of the silver thread as a reflective surface. The ample motif extended on a flat surface and the symmetrical disposition of the main shoots lead to Emilian decorative schemes and patterns. The colour red of the vestment and the symbols of the Passion might suggest a use connected with the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross or the Invention of the Cross, the sacrifice of Christ might also be generally referred to martyrdom.  
The high quality of the work was recognized in 1900 when the vestment was sent to the exhibition of sacred art held in Bologna, in the church of San Francesco. In 1926 this same vestment was photographed by the local Soprintendenza in one of the first campaigns documenting church heritage.
482b2fe7-2ab8-521c-aeb6-542db13d4285.short_description: The red background of the chasuble is divided by silver lace in fields. Two leaf garlands curl against a net ground; the sides are marked with a garland pattern in front of a net ground. The central pole springs from an acanthus bush holding the instruments of the Passion of Christ in its spires. Veil, burse, stole and maniple are embroidered using the most decorative patterns from the design.

483e8679-d93d-56cd-b566-f321c598b6de.name: *Dala’il al-Khayrat* (*Guidelines to Blessings*) by Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Jazuli)
483e8679-d93d-56cd-b566-f321c598b6de.short_description: The *Dala’il al-Khairat* (The Signs of Benediction) is a compilation of prayers for the Prophet Muhammad and other faith-related information by Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Jazuli (d. ca. 1465). Popular throughout the Muslim world and particularly in Ottoman lands. It also contains descriptions of the Holy Mosque in Makkah and the Prophet’s Mosque in Madina, the two most important Islamic pilgrimage sites. Both are typically depicted in the centre of the manuscript, Here, detailed birds-eye views of both sanctuaries appear, surrounded by gold margins. On the right, at tthe heart of the Makkah mosque, the Ka’bah is dressed with its black kiswa cover, further enhanced by a golden belt (hizam) above and a golden door curtain (sitara or burqu’). On the left, within the mosque complex at Madina, a domed chamber contains the tombs of the Prophet and the first caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar, draped in golden covers – perhaps a reference to the precious, gold and silver-embroidered textiles that were spread over the tombs in Ottoman times.

4859e54f-5855-587b-935f-40a00ec2c500.name: The Mother of God Axion Estin
4859e54f-5855-587b-935f-40a00ec2c500.description:
These four icons form a set that depicts the Hymn of Axion Estin, as follows:  
  
It is truly meet and right to bless you, O Theotokos,  
Ever-blessed and most-pure mother of our God.  
More honorable than the Cherubim,  
And beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim,  
Who without corruption gave birth to God the Word,  
True Theotokos, we magnify you.  
  
According to tradition, this hymn was revealed to an elder monk and his disciple before an icon of the Mother of God in the sanctuary of the main church of Karyes on Mount Athos. During an all-night vigil, they were joined by an unknown monk who called himself Gabriel. As he chanted an unfamiliar hymn, the icon of the Mother of God began to glow. The elder asked Gabriel to write down this hymn, so he inscribed the prayer with his finger on a roof tile “as if it were made of wax”. The tablet was sent to Constantinople, while the image was venerated as miracle-working. The revelation is commemorated on June 11, and the icon is celebrated on July 13.
4859e54f-5855-587b-935f-40a00ec2c500.obtention: From the private collection of Jacques Zolotnitzky. Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2012. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.

4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.name: Prayer rug.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.description: In the AH 12th and 13th /AD 18th and 19th centuries, the small town of Milas in the southwest of Turkey was a centre for the manufacture of prayer rugs. A characteristic feature of later Milas prayer rugs is the dark red angular prayer niche. The inner side of the niche is edged all around with small flower-like ornaments. In the lower part of the niche is an octagon connected with four rosettes. The ornamentation within the arch is badly worn. Four green and red peonies with a rhomb between on a white background fill the area of the spandrels. The central rectangular field containing the prayer niche is framed several times by stripes of different geometrical patterns. The next border shows on a yellow background a design consisting of red octagons, alternating with large stylised blossoms in red, white and dark and light blue. From each of these blossoms emerge four heavily stylised carnations. The outer band shows a row of multicoloured small octagons on a white background.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.short_description: Prayer rug from Melas. Its characteristic feature is the dark red angular prayer niche surrounded by several stripes of geometrical pattern. Different kinds of flowers are spread over the whole area of the rug.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.holder: Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities (Medelhavsmuseet).
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.owner: National Museum of Fine Arts, Stockholm. In order to reorganise the expanding collections, the main part of the Islamic collection has been on permanent loan to the Museum of Mediterranean and Near Eastern Antiquities since 1982.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.method_for_datation: Milas was a centre for the manufacture of prayer rugs in the 12th–13th / 18th–19th centuries. Prayer rugs from Milas showing angular niches are ascribed to the 13th / 19th century; a Milas prayer rug showing a very similar pattern is dated to the first half of the 13th / 19th century.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.method_for_provenance: Rugs with similar designs and colour schemes are usually ascribed to the Milas group of rugs.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.obtention: Gift from the estate of Axel and Nora Lundgren, registered 29 September 1977.

4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.name: Mosque lamp.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.description:
Glass mosque lamps with enamel decoration were mainly made during the Mamluk period in Egypt or Syria. They were made on commission and were presented by Mamluk sultans as gifts to Cairo mosques.  
The most famous of the Museum of Islamic Art’s mosque lamps is made of honey-coloured glass, with a foot shaped like an inverse chalice and a belly-shaped body that turns, above an indentation, into a long conical neck. On the body there are six eyelets laid on and pressed into escutcheon-shaped spaces. Chains were attached to these in order to hang the lamp from the ceiling. An additional funnel-shaped small oil lamp, which emitted the light, was hung within this lamp.  
The decoration consists of two frieze inscriptions, and of flowers painted on a small scale that betray a Far Eastern influence through their lotus blossom motif. The frieze inscription over the body of the lamp has been done in gold over a blue background. It mentions the name of the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, who ruled at various intervals (r. AH 698–708 / AD 1299–1309 and AH 709–41 / AD 1310–41). The mosque lamp could have been commissioned for a mosque or school that contained or had an adjoining mausoleum. These kinds of building complexes were constructed in Cairo in AH 704 / AD 1304 and between AH 718 and 736 / AD 1318–35. The inscription in blue over a tendril ending in spirals and a background that was originally painted in gold is particularly apt for a mosque lamp as its subject matter is based on the ‘Light verse’ from the Qur’an (Sura 24, verse 35). Both inscriptions are written in the *thuluth* script typical of the Mamluk period.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.short_description: Glass lamps were produced for mosques, shrines and mausoleums. An inner container held the oil and wick. According to the inscription on its body, this lamp was made in the name of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad. It is also adorned by the Light verse of the Qur’an (Sura 24 v.35).
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.initial_owner: Count F. von Pourtales, St. Petersburg.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.dates: Hegira first half of the 8th century / AD first half of the 14th century.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.method_for_datation: A large number of glass mosque lamps were made during the Mamluk era. This one states the name of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, who ruled in the 8th / 14th century.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.method_for_provenance: Mosque lamps were probably made in Syria as well as in Egypt. It is not yet possible to assign a precise origin to this piece.
4b8ffd8e-ec58-5468-9e97-3c950ff7e6c9.obtention: A gift from Count F. von Pourtales in 1913.

4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.name: La Crucifixión
4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.description:
This piece was exhibited at the International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts exhibition in Paris, 1925, and won a Gran Prix Award.  
The Taller Mauméjean dates back to 1860, when Jules Pierre Mauméjean, aged 23, opened his first workshop in Pau (France). Jules Pierre Mauméjean was married to Marie Honorine Lalanne in Pau on 23rd July 1868 and they went on to have five children. All of their sons followed the same artistic career path as their father. However, although Joseph, Henri and Carl worked together, Léon remained independent in Paris, where he passed away on 1st March 1921.  
In 1890, Jules Pierre Mauméjean opened a workshop in Anglet, which he later moved to Biarritz in 1893. He passed away in San Sebastián in 1909, at age 72. Jules Mauméjean maintained permanent contact with the circles in Madrid that offered him various commissions and led to him becoming the official glass painter at the Casa Real de Alfonso XII.  
Joseph, known as José Mauméjean, the firstborn of the family, spent numerous periods in Madrid. Not only did he spend time in the city to keep an eye on his workshops, but also to capture new clients. It was here that he met Augustine Jeanne Pastora Vic, daughter of Joseph Julien Vic, from Hendaya, then general agent of Saint-Gobain Glass in the Spanish capital. Born of his marriage to Marie, Joseph opened a new Mauméjean workshop in Madrid in 1898, located on Calle Abascal, Nº39, before moving to Paseo de la Castellana, Nº24, where he created the pieces currently located in the Museum.  
Some years later, the Hermanos Mauméjean opened more branches in Barcelona, followed by San Sebastian. These workshops formed part of the S.A. Mauméjean Hermanos, with their headquarters in Madrid.  
The Hermanos Mauméjean opened a new workshop in Paris, registered in 1921. This was a Venetian Enamel-Mosaics workshop, changing its name to S.A. Mauméjean two years later, with headquarters in the same building. Shortly after, they opened a new, successful workshop in Hendaya.  
Henri led the workshop in Mauméjean and passed away in 1932, leaving the workshop to his brother José, who passed away in 1952, aged 83, followed by Carl five years later and his son Georges, in 1970.  
The Mauméjean dynasty were involved in many national and international exhibitions. The most notable international exhibitions included Madrid in 1894, Paris in 1925 and 1937, Philadelphia y Pamplona in 1926, Milan and Madrid in 1927 and Seville in 1930.  
In Spain, the Mauméjean workshops in Madrid, Barcelona and San Sebastian provided stained glass to all major Spanish cities. Depending on the buyer, the workshop created stained glass with different themes and styles. These themes were predominantly religious, heraldic, labour-related, commercial and fundamentally ornamental. All of the styles have a historicist feel, reminding us of the Gothic, Renaissance, Classicism, etc.
4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.holder: Technological Glass Museum. Royal Factory of Glass and Crystal of La Granja
4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.bibliography:

4be5a512-234f-5c97-a190-95e30c9a3d5f.author: Paloma Pastor Rey de Viñas

4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.name: Two apexes from banners of the Prophet Moses.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.description:
A pair of apexes from ceremonial banners widely used in official religious processions that took place at most of the religious sites and shrines in Palestine. Such processions formed an important part of the local cultural history of the region. The banners would carry either the name of the season, the city, village, or the family name of the household whose members were bearing it. The banner bearers would lead the procession. The banners had specific social and religious significance especially in a growing popular consciousness. In some cases, it indicated the high social standing of the family, the importance of the city, or a certain village. The raising of the banner was traditionally restricted to certain religious and social processions, limiting it to the local people, who considered it a form of social prestige.  
One of the most famous religious seasons in Palestine was that of the Prophet Moses. This celebration began in the Ayyubid period (beginning of the AH 6th / AD 12th century) and continued to widen and grow. It took place at the end of spring every year coinciding with Easter which was celebrated by the Christian communities in Palestine. Delegations would come to Jerusalem from different parts of Palestine, especially from the cities of Nablus and Hebron. Throngs of people would gather at the Haram al-Sharif with those who were participating in the celebration from Jerusalem. They would march in procession together, with a large and splendid retinue raising flags and banners that were specific to each city, village and important family as well as Sufi *tariqahs* (Sufi Orders). They would finally arrive at the Sanctuary of the Prophet Moses which was located between Jerusalem and Jericho. Here festivities would continue as well as the fulfilment of pledges, for the period of a week or more.  
The banner is typical, composed of a cylindrical pole of about 3m. The fabric flag held inscriptions that might be verses from the Qur'an, names of God, supplications, religious expressions, or the names of individuals or places. The two apexes exhibited here are similar in composition: each consisting of a cylindrical base that would fix onto the head of the pole, and a neck that bears a circular ring to support the apex. The circle of the apex includes an inscription of two lines, spaced out in copper, it reads: “God, our Lord”. On top of the circle is the crown of the apex; a spaced rhomboid shape, within which is a solid rhomboid.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.short_description: Banners were used in festivals and processions in Palestine and bore the names of the Prophets, shrines, cities and important families. The most famous shrine was the tomb of the Prophet Moses. Each of this similar pair has a copper crown that would be mounted on the head of a pole. An inscription of two spaced lines states ‘God, Our Lord’.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by means of studying its style and shape and looking at the casting technique used to produce it.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this piece was made in Jerusalem where such banners were widespread. There are still some families in Jerusalem who make similar pieces.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.obtention: The piece was transferred at an unknown date, from the Haram al-Sharif to the Islamic Museum.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.bibliography: Tamari, V., “Two Ottoman Ceremonial Banners in Jerusalem”, in S. Auld and R. Hillenbrand (eds), *Ottoman Jerusalem,* London, 2000.
4c547f09-e5de-5249-976c-d3b8e43f3370.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Banner: apex; crown; pilgrimage; Nabi Musa

4c5ec9e7-571c-57c0-a345-64717d007c10.name: *Nazareth School*
4c5ec9e7-571c-57c0-a345-64717d007c10.short_description: Pictured here is the Nazareth School, founded in 1868 by Mother Pauline de Vaux, Superior General of the Congregation of the Ladies of Nazareth. The decision to found this school was supported by the Bishop Vallegra, in Rome. It was first located in a large house in the European quarter of Beirut, nicknamed "The Blue Castle". However, with the number of students rapidly growing, the school had to relocate. In 1877 the new convent was opened for this purpose on St. George Hill, bought by the *firman* of Constantinople. The building is U-shaped and made of stone, with white cloisters and surrounded by a huge garden.
4c5ec9e7-571c-57c0-a345-64717d007c10.author: Hady El Hajj, Jennifer Harb, Cynthia Karaki
keywords: School; Education; Nazareth; Beirut

4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.name: Prayer rug with multiple prayer niches (fragment).
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.description:
This carpet fragment is the preserved part of a considerably larger prayer rug featuring multiple prayer niches. The carpet features a row of six red niches of various widths that are closed at the top by dark-blue arches. The sixth niche on the left-hand side is only a half-niche as the carpet was cut at this point and the border repaired. The niches are separated using fine green lines that run down to the bottom and which could be interpreted as substitute columns. The carpet’s narrow border consists of a double-edged, reciprocal pattern of alternating light-blue and yellow crenellations. The wider, less complete, border has a single row of crenellations, yellow alternating with blue.  
The particular clarity of the carpet’s design and its use of colour demonstrate the Ottoman understanding of the decorative arts and their practice. Unlike most of the other known multiple prayer-niche carpets, this one is very simple, in that nowhere is it overly decorated; however even in its simplicity, it still follows a systematic composition of ordered patterns covering the surface, as can be seen repeatedly within Ottoman art from as early as the AH 9th / AD 15th century. Its simplicity, vibrant colours and the combined overall impact it creates would definitely have appealed to middle European tastes. Followers of the Islamic faith would have prayed on multiple prayer-niche carpets placed parallel to the *qibla* wall in the mosque. Admittedly, the rows of niches on this carpet merely refer to its function or use, because, essentially, each clean surface acts as a pad on which to pray. The narrowness of each niche on the carpet hints that a believer would have required more space in which to pray than that afforded by the narrow niches on the carpet.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.short_description: This carpet with its pattern of multiple niches is part of a once much larger rug. It was probably made for use in a mosque. It is unique because the design does not include the usual complicated patterns but instead makes a strong impact through its plain vibrant colours.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.method_for_datation: The carpet has been dated on the grounds of its pattern, colours and knot-technique to be from the 11th / 17th century.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.method_for_provenance: The carpet belongs to a group of Ottoman carpets that are referred to as the Ushak Group.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.obtention: Obtained in 1961 from the O. Bernheimer Collection, Munich.
