4ee7fe82-e416-5820-a768-7626a3306e3b.name: Daghestan prayer rug
4ee7fe82-e416-5820-a768-7626a3306e3b.description:
With a few notable exceptions, Daghestan rug motifs are field repeats. Many of the field repeats are used under *mihrab*s in prayer rugs. White-field prayer rugs of this same design were woven with little obvious change for over a century.  
In the prayer niche, as the field repeat motif, there are “floral lattice” motifs on the white background. The bird-like figures are palmettes. In the *mihrab* arch there are small florets, half of the stepped medallion and two small square motifs. The arch is a field with a red meander on a light green background. The central field is framed with three borders. The main floral border is decorated with polychrome floral motifs. Minor borders are “floral meander” on light blue ground in the inner border and floral meander on a dark blue background in the outer border. Floral meander is a very common major and minor border in Caucasian rugs.
4ee7fe82-e416-5820-a768-7626a3306e3b.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Prayer rug; Caucasus

4ee99078-4b66-5d16-830e-595e4da0246e.name: Mosque Lamp
4ee99078-4b66-5d16-830e-595e4da0246e.short_description: This vase-shaped lamp belongs to a well-established lamp type made in the Mamluk workshops of Syria and Egypt, both great centres of glass making. The colourful palette of blue, red, green, yellow, and white with gilding remains subtle due to a considered distribution. Green and yellow, for example, are restrained, creating bright spots. The layout of calligraphy, from strong scrolls to arabesque and delicate lotus flowers, reflects precise planning in the layering clear in details such as the leaves that spread over the letters, themselves positioned over an arabesque background. The pseudo-*kufic* compositions, painted in blue and brick-red, placed prominently on the body of the lamp, are an original feature which creates a complementary visual contrast with the *thuluth* script (on the neck of the lamp), which reads: “mimma umila bi-rasm al-maqarr al-‘ali al-mawlawi al-‘amiri al-kabiri al-maliki" (What was made for his Excellency, the Elevated, the Servant of the Lord, the Great Amir, the Possessor). This lamp was commissioned by an unknown prince, likely intended to decorate the interior of his mosque or madrasa.

50b6f8e1-16d0-5432-9b45-cc0512192157.name: Double niche ‘Transylvanian’ carpet
50b6f8e1-16d0-5432-9b45-cc0512192157.description: The term “Transylvanian” rug refers to 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in large numbers in Transylvanian Saxon churches, and once considered to have been made in Transylvania, whereas in fact they were produced in western Anatolia. Certain Transylvanian rugs have a *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs; others, such as the present one, feature two opposing arches. The shape of this double niche and its undecorated beige ground are characteristic of later “Transylvanian” rugs, while the border of alternating polygonal cartouches and octagons can also be found in earlier examples. Several technical imperfections such as the inaccurate rendering of space, which accounts for the incomplete motifs in the main border, and the lack of left–right symmetry though indicative of a modest workshop, retain a certain appealing charm.

51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.name: Monstrance from Kopřivná
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.description:
The pedestal of this monstrance, with its relief and shell-like ornamentation, is decorated with angels’ heads, their eyes turned to heaven. The stem is a simply rendered figure of the Virgin Mary standing on a crescent moon and globe, encircled by a serpent. The spiral kinesis is enhanced by the modelling of clouds, corn stalks and grapes on a casket crowned with the figure of God the Father and an angel adoring a cross decorated with red glass.  
The uniquely shaped monstrance with the Virgin Mary Immaculata was designed by Franz Ignaz Günther as part of his decoration of the Church of the Holy Trinity in Kopřivná. The church was built by Jan Ludvík of Žerotín-Lilgenau on the border between north Moravia and Silesia as a memorial pilgrimage site. The monstrance was made to fit the high altar tabernacle, below Günther’s statue of the Immaculata.  
The composition drew on Günther’s design of a copper monstrance for Munich, as well as on Egid Quirin Asam’s design of a monstrance for the Church of St. John of Nepomuk, also in Munich. All of these were preceded by a diamond monstrance in the Loretto, Prague, which was made in Vienna and designed by Johann Bernard Fischer of Erlach.  
The silversmith who executed the design participated in the creation of the Holy Trinity Column, Olomouc and the tomb of Olomouc Bishop Schrattenbach (Kroměříž, Church of St. Mauritz). Günther arrived in Olomouc after journeyman service in Augsburg, Nuremberg, Frankfurt, Linz and Vienna and worked for the Count of Žerotín. In 1757 he studied at the Vienna Academy in Munich, where he settled, becoming one of the most influential Bavarian sculptors of the 18th century.  
During the Baroque period, the monstrance became a decorative object worthy of adoration, apart from its practical use of carrying the Holy Communion.
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.short_description: A uniquely shaped monstrance with the Virgin Mary Immaculata it was created in an Olomouc metal workshop to the design of later famous Munich sculptor, Franz Ignaz Günther. It was part of his overall decoration for the Church of the Holy Trinity in Kopřivná, on the border between north Moravia and Silesia.

51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.method_for_datation: The monstrance is marked with three hallmarks one of which is the master’s mark of Simon Forstner.
51e979e1-5041-52d1-b9e1-0d200f1af77f.obtention: The monstrance is on long-term loan to the Archdiocesan Museum, Olomouc from the parish office administering the Kopřivná Church.

529e4353-d9fb-5895-a243-1a19e6cb982c.name: Kula prayer rug
529e4353-d9fb-5895-a243-1a19e6cb982c.description:
The rug-weaving areas of Anatolia are conventionally divided into western, central and eastern regions. Western Anatolian centres such as Uşak, Ghiordes, Kula and their vicinity have a long tradition of carpet and rug production. Carpets from these centres were very popular in Europe. The town of Kula lies southeast of Ghiordes. The most notable of its varied weaves is a type of prayer rug formerly considered as among the most successful Anatolian town and village weaves. Characteristic of Kula rugs are mellow and subdued colours of yellow and brown, and more solemn shades of red, blue and green. The cross panel is usually found only above the arch.  
In the central field there is a *mihrab* (prayer niche) with field repeat motifs organized in three rows. An interesting fact is that all motifs are faced in the opposite direction from the *mihrab* arch. Motifs in the central row resemble motifs on the so-called cemetery carpets. This motif has its origin in pictorial landscapes of the Turkish Baroque period beginning in the second half of the 18th century. The other two rows have vase with stylized flower motifs. Such a large repeating hanging floral ornaments are typical for mid-nineteenth century Kula carpets. Above the spandrel there is oblong field with a dragon and phoenix motif. The central field is framed with six rows of *sobokli* border and two minor borders with a dragon motif. The *sobokli* border is common in prayer rugs. It is made up of narrow stripes, usually seven, which symbolize seven steps of paradise.
529e4353-d9fb-5895-a243-1a19e6cb982c.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: prayer rug; Kula; Anatolia; Ghiordes

53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.name: Seal of the Dome of the Rock.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.description:
A circular seal made of copper with incised lines that demarcate a square, the corners of which are cut along the circumference of the piece. In the middle of the seal there is a horizontal depiction of the Dome of the Rock, octagonal in form, and in the middle of which is a circle. Portrayed within the circle is what is considered to be the footprint of the Prophet Muhammad, and inscribed below it the words: “Foot of the Prophet”.On top of the carving designated as the footprint of the Prophet, is the Dome of the Rock crowned by a crescent. Within the circle on each side of the Dome building, there is a tree resembling a palm. It is not known whether the two palms have symbolic meaning, perhaps they were drawn simply to fill empty space. Between the middle circle and the octagon there are eight arched niches, designating the interior octagon of the Dome of the Rock. Above the upper side of the octagonal is the façade of the Dome of the Rock, composed of the drum and the dome, and topped by a relatively large crescent. The horizontal depiction of the Dome of the Rock and the Dome's façade is surrounded on three sides by buildings; three portrayals of arcades appear, again surrounding the Dome of the Rock. These are likely to be depictions of: the southern arcade, which opens out in the direction of al-Aqsa Mosque; the south-western arcade, which opens out in the direction of the Bab al-Silsila (Gate of Chains) and the eastern arcade, which opens out in the direction of Bab al-Rahma (Gate of Mercy). The northern arcade, however, hidden by the portrayal of the Dome and its crescent, does not appear. The names of the buildings appear beside the illustrations of them, including the Dome of the Rock and the names of its four gates: Bab al-Janna (The Gate of Heaven), Bab al-Salaam (The Gate of Peace), Bab al-Sakhra (Dome of the Rock Gate), and Bab al-Mizan (the Balance Gate). Similar captions appear beside the illustrations of the Dome of the Mi'raj, the Minbar al-Sharif (Minbar of Burhan al-Din), Qubbat al-Arwah (Dome of the Spirits) and Qubbat al-Silsila (Dome of the Chain). Depicted on the eastern side of the Dome of the Rock is an illustration of a plant that resembles a flower, which is not present to the east of the Dome of the Rock. Historically, there was a dearth of plants in the surrounding environs of the building.  
It is possible that the seal was used as authorisation to enter the Dome of the Rock. Or perhaps, it was used to seal the papers of visitors who hoped to be blessed by such an image, or to commemorate their visit to the Dome of the Rock. It might also have been used as some form of shorthand guidebook for the visit.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.short_description: This is a circular copper panel in the middle of which is a layout of the Dome of the Rock. It also shows the surrounding buildings and the staircases which lead to the plaza of the Dome.  It might have been used as authorisation to enter the Dome or perhaps to seal papers of visitors to take home as a blessing or as a souvenir of their visit.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.method_for_datation: The piece was dated based on a comparison with another seal which bears the names of holy places in Palestine and the date of which has been narrowed down to the 13th / 19th century.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production for the seal; the images on it were probably implemented in the area.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.obtention: The piece was transferred at an unknown date from the Haram al-Sharif to the Islamic Museum.
53de341b-560c-5d23-b886-5d480f725f2c.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Seal; copper; engraving

556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.name: Ablutions basin.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.description:
This parallelepipedic tank marked with plain striations on the inside, the short sides and the corners, was beautifully adorned on the outside, and almost all of the decoration has survived on two sides. The design on the decorated face, whose inscription has been destroyed, is divided into two styles. The first one, rising from the base, consists of a large frieze of grooved foliage, dotted with buds and rosettes and wide-veined plain palms with calyxes, and double ones with acanthus leaves and buds. The second comprises a strip in relief with two lines of grooved intersecting knotwork, one curved and the other straight, bearing fleurons and veined palms. It is framed by an edge, set back, formed by vegetal knotwork accentuated with small stylised palm leaves in the shape of six-pointed stars.  
The short side is occupied by two identical animal scenes, sculpted on two vertical panels separated by an empty space. On each panel, there is an eagle spreading its tail, carrying two quadrupeds on its wings and two gazelles from its claws. Two winged ibex confronting each other on either side of a fleuron finish the scene in the lower part.  
Most of the ornamentation on the other two sides has been destroyed, leaving only the text in *kufic* characters sculpted in relief on the rim and the decoration of the framing ribbon on the large side, which consists of a frieze of aquatic birds and fish alternating on a plant background.  
The surviving elements of the inscription that crowned the entire rim of the tank include the last digit of the hegira date (300), and the name of the patron, 'Abd al-Malik, *hajib* (chamberlain) of Hisham II.  
The design and animal scenes of this beautiful example of Caliphate artwork are reminiscent of the tank at al-Mansur and would appear to be from the same Madinat al-Zahira marble workshop in Córdoba.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.short_description: This basin is the work of a marble workshop in Madinat al-Zahira, Córdoba, the princely city built by al-Mansur. It was brought to Marrakesh by 'Ali ibn Yusuf and placed in the ablutions room of the Great Mosque.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.dimensions: Height 70 cm, length 155 cm, width 82 cm, depth 50 cm, thickness of sides 10 cm, thickness of base 20 cm.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_datation:
1\. The inscription, partially destroyed, sculpted on the upper rim of the tank reads '(the year) three hundred, in the name of God! God's blessing. Victory and divine assistance to the Hajib \[followed with his honours\] Abu Marwan 'Abd al-Malik ibn Amir (…), this is part of what he commissioned (…)'.  
2\. We know that 'Abd al-Malik was appointed *hajib* of Hisham II between 381 and 398 / 991 and 1008) by his father al-Mansur.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_provenance: Although it was discovered in the Ibn Yusuf Madrasa in Marrakesh, which belongs to the Sa'did period (10th / 16th century), the name of the patron and the comparative study with the al-Mansur basin in the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid suggest that it was originally from Madinat al-Zahira in Córdoba.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.obtention: As state property from a historical monument.

55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.name: A bronze Greek cross.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.description:
The Christian cross is a familiar religious symbol. Its significance lies in the belief that the governor of Judea executed Jesus Christ on a large wooden cross. The cross was the first of the instruments of the passion that came to be venerated in the form of a relic.  
  
This bronze cross is of Greek form, decorated with concentric incised circles on each arm and on both faces of the cross. Two of three iron nails are still preserved on the vertical arm while the third, at the bottom, is missing.  
  
It seems that this cross was nailed to a wooden box as a reliquary in the Church of St Stephen at Umm al-Rasas. The upper part of the vertical arm is broken into two pieces and has been mended recently.  
  
The importance of this cross is linked to its discovery at the Church of St Stephen, which was paved with mosaic floors in AH 138 / AD 756, according to the dedicatory inscriptions on either side of the altar. The inscription is significant because it indicates that there was an active Christian community present at Umm al-Rasas six years after the end of the Umayyad period and after more than a century of Islamic rule in the region.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.short_description: A bronze cross of Greek form from the Church of St Stephen at Umm al-Rasas, decorated on both faces. This cross was probably nailed to a wooden box by three iron nails, two of which are still preserved on the vertical arm.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.dates: Hegira, first third of the 2nd century / AD first half of the 8th century.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.method_for_datation: The cross was dated by a dedicatory inscription discovered at the Church of St Stephen.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.method_for_provenance: The cross was discovered at Umm al-Rasas during archaeological excavations but where it was originally manufactured is uncertain.
55ec1f26-ba55-52bc-a1b6-556c48ff41e4.obtention: The cross was acquired by the Museum as a result of an archaeological excavation carried out at Umm al-Rasas by the Studium Biblicum Franciscanum, on-going since 1986.

5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.name: Ablutions font.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.description: Ablutions font with a circular bowl, formed with eight lobes in the style of a flower. It has a unique decoration on the outside of the rim, a band in relief bearing an epigraph. Water has worn this away, obliterating the letters on the outer curves, with just a few remaining on the corners where the lobes meet. On one of them it is possible to read the beginning of the *Basmala* (first verse of the Qur'an) and everything leads us to suppose that this was completed with a quotation from the Qur'an, as was common on facilities of this kind related to ritual ablutions at the entrances to mosques. Another specimen of similar characteristics and probably from the same period is known in the Lisbon area.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.short_description: Almohad ablutions font decorated on the outside of the rim with a band inscribed in relief with the beginning of the *basmala*, which suggests that it also included a Qur’anic inscription. This piece was probably related to the ablutions ritual practised when entering a mosque.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.method_for_datation: The style of lettering dates it to the Almohad period.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.method_for_provenance: Dr José Leite de Vasconcelos left notes in the National Museum of Archaeology to the effect that it belonged to the collection of Estácio da Veiga and that it probably came from Cacela.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.obtention: It was probably taken to the National Museum of Archaeology by Dr José Leite de Vasconcelos.

56ae89a4-e69e-5467-915e-b99f5b5f752d.name: Panorama: al-hujjaj bi-mina yawn al-‘id al-akbar (‘The pilgrims at Mina on the day of the big feast’)
56ae89a4-e69e-5467-915e-b99f5b5f752d.description: Muhammad Sadiq Bey was the first person to take photographs of Mecca, Medina and the Hajj. An Egyptian army engineer and surveyor, he was also the treasurer of the Egyptian Hajj caravan, travelling numerous times to the Hijaz. Using a technique first invented in the 1850s, Sadiq Bey took his first photographs in 1861 using glass plate negatives, especially useful for large-format frames. His most important photographs, of both the buildings and interiors of the sanctuaries at Mecca and Medina, as well as sites at Arafat and Mina, were taken in 1861, 1880 and 1881. For the first time, the pilgrimage and the holy cities were precisely and realistically documented.
56ae89a4-e69e-5467-915e-b99f5b5f752d.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
keywords: Pilgrimage; Mina; Ottoman; Documentation; Photography;

56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.name: Prayer carpet '*sajada*'
56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.short_description: A highlight of the Khanenko Museum's Islamic collection is an Ottoman carpet dating to AD late 17th–first half of the 18th century. The carpet belongs to the traditional type of "*sajada*", or prayer, carpets, with composition based on a stylized picture of *mihrab* - a prayer niche in a mosque indicating the direction where Muslims turn during the prayer. The composition and motifs of the carpet, particularly the central niche coloured in plain dark blue and crowned with arch of an acute stepped shape as well as a peculiar geometrized carnation pattern above and below the niche, suggest that the item was manufactured in workshops of Giordes or Kula, two leading centres of Turkish carpet-making in the 17th–18th centuries. Numerous narrow ornamental borders that fringe the central arch add a specific elegance to the piece of art.
56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by Yu Miller (examination, 1961,  date, origin), Hanna Rudyk and Antonina Makarevych (examination based on B. Biedronska-Slotowa publication, 2019, date and origin specified).
56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).
56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.obtention: Purchased by Bohdan and Varvara Khanenko. Donated by Varvara Khanenko in 1918, nationalized by Bolshevik regime in 1919.

56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.name: Lamp.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.description:
Bronze lamp consisting of various elements supported by a central rod. First, four spherical parts arranged in ascending order of size with a central fretwork border and *naskhi* inscription. Next, an eight-sided prismatic element with vegetal fretwork decoration. The lamp is completed by a truncated pyramid in the shape of a four-sided bell, decorated with plant motifs and two inscribed cartouches, one at the top and one at the bottom, with the emblem of Muhammad III: 'There is no conqueror but God. The Most Exalted'. There is another inscription in the bronze on the border, with a series and blessings and titles, as well as the date of manufacture.  
There is a convincing hypothesis as to the placement of the holders for the lights: the lamp arrived at the Museum with its hinged arms badly damaged; these arms would open out around the truncated pyramid section into a circle, some of which has survived. There were two arms per side, making a total of 16 arms and between 48 and 64 glasses that produced light without being obscured by the body of the object.  
We know that the Royal Alhambra Mosque was constructed at the behest of Muhammad III, and therefore the lamp would have hung in the central nave before the *mihrab* (prayer niche), the appropriate place for an object bearing the sovereign's emblem. It is logical to assume that the founding sovereign would have also provided the fixtures.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.short_description: A masterpiece of Andalusian metalwork for the exquisite fretwork decoration on the body, this lamp was commissioned by Muhammad III for the mosque in the Alhambra, according to its inscription. The body still bears the hooks for the arms that would have held the glass bowls for the lights.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.initial_owner: Following the conquest of Granada in AH 898 / AD 1492, the lamp was removed from its fixing and taken to Oran. Eventually it became part of the collection of Cardinal Cisneros, who deposited it with San Ildefonso College in Alcala de Henares, from where it passed to the University.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.dimensions: Total height 230 cm, height of truncated pyramid 54 cm, diameter 79 cm.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.method_for_datation: The lower edge of the lamp bears a *naskhi* inscription with the year 705 / 1305.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.method_for_provenance: Despite the damage to the lower part of the lamp, the titles that appear in the inscription around the edge allow us to attribute it to Muhammad III (r. 702–9 / 1302–9), who would have commissioned it for the Alhambra mosque.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.provenance: Mosque of the Alhambra, Granada, Spain.
56be57e8-2f07-5969-a236-a5ddc30a31cd.obtention: The piece was assigned to the National Archaeological Museum as part of the organisation of the State collection on 20 March 1868.

5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.name: Crescent from the Dome of the Rock.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.description:
A large copper crescent moon that once crowned the dome on the Dome of the Rock, removed in AH 1317 / AD 1899. The crescent consists of five parts: the first is the fluted base that takes the form of an inverted cup, and which was affixed to the apex of the dome. The base is connected by means of a small cylindrical neck to a second part, which consists of a large undecorated mass resembling a sphere. Next is a small cylindrical neck, on top of which is a ring, which transfers it to the third section consisting of a fluted and elongated ovoid form. This part ends with a ring, similar to the former. Adjacent to it is a cylindrical neck that is connected to the fourth part. This consists of a small spherical mass reminiscent of the sphere (the second part). On top of this section is a cylindrical neck, which forms the zone of transition to the fifth and final part of the section, the crescent.  
The crescent consists of a circle whose diameter measures 90 cm, and which takes a principal position. It is thickest at its lowest part, tapering in along the two sides to reach, at its height, its thinnest form. This crescent is considered one of the largest used on any building in the Islamic world, and on account of what we know about the singularity of its size, it may be the largest acquired by any museum. The Islamic Museum in Jerusalem acquired two other great crescents, which were brought from the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque respectively. The crescent shown here is in good condition and is undecorated as the crescent was placed at such lofty heights that no eye could possibly discern or distinguish any decorative detail.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.short_description: This large copper crescent crowned the apex of the Dome of the Rock. It has a circular ribbed base in the form of an inverted cup and continues in a number of forms to end with a large circle whose diameter measures 90 cm. This crescent is considered one of the largest in the Islamic World, and is probably the largest housed in a museum.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.method_for_datation: The crescent was dated based on a comparison with similar pieces whose dates are agreed.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.method_for_provenance: Jerusalem was narrowed down as the place of production because such a large object as this would probably have been made on site.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.obtention: The piece was transferred following its removal from the Dome of the Rock to storage facilities at the Agency of Islamic Awqaf in the Haram al-Sharif; it was transferred to the Islamic Museum in around 1923.
5830662b-6f93-5e08-826b-c8179eb39b3c.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Copper; crescent

58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.name: Large pitcher
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.description:
This pitcher is inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the following text:  
  
*"Bu güğümden su içene şifalar olsun; eğer dahi kâfir içerse İslamla müşerref olsun. Tarih 1266’dır, cümle hakkında hayr olsun."*: “May those who drink water from this ewer be granted healing; and if an unbeliever drinks, may he be honored with Islam. The date is \[AH\] 1266; may it bring goodness to all.")  
  
It also reads *"Fet oğlu Hüseyin Ağa, tûl-i ömrü ile muammer olsun."*: "May Hüseyin Ağa, son of Fet, live a long and prosperous life."
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.method_for_datation: Its date was determined by Islamic metal artefacts expert Güner Liman.
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.method_for_provenance: Its date was determined by Islamic metal artefacts expert Güner Liman.

5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.name: *Angel I*
5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.description: This monumental figure of an angel is part of the sculpted decoration of the Minorite Church in Znojmo, only fragments of which have survived. The sculpture with its preserved polychromy, gilded robe and wings has retained its expressive air despite the loss of its former link with the architecture of the altar retable. Despite its larger-than-life size it features precise carving, full volume and a reduced means of expression: an elegant gesture of the hand and decoratively sculpted locks. The face has Heinz’s original trademark modelling of the nose, arches above the eyes and, in particular the chin. The figure testifies to the sculptor’s sense of monumentality. Heinz was among only a few sculptors in Moravia whose starting point was the Czech Radical Baroque style. His first experience as a sculptor was under the tutorage of Jan Sturmer in Olomouc and then in the circle of Matyáš Bernard Braun; he also collaborated with Severin Tischler. The decoration of the garden and funeral chapel in Velké Losiny Chateau exhibits the influence of Baltasar Permoser. Heinz first lived in Olomouc and travelled in Moravia. In 1755 he joined the Dominican Monastery in Znojmo. Whilst there he produced statues for the grounds and decorated altars predominantly in the Znojmo area (Lechovice, Louka, Šatov).
5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.short_description: The *Angel* figure testifies to the sculptor's sense of monumentality for retable compositions. Heinz was among only a few sculptors in Moravia whose starting point was the Czech Radical Baroque style. The sculpture features precise carving, full volume and a reduced means of expression.
5a261785-3c23-5c9b-b6cc-bbab118fe4a4.obtention: The sculpture comes from the decoration of a Franciscan (originally Minorite) Monastery. Around 1843 part of the interior was transferred to the Church of St. Anne, Znojmo, from whence it passed to the Museum of South Moravia, located on the premises of the former Minorite Monastery.

5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.name: Printing block (stamp) listing holy places in the region of Palestine.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.description:
A printing block (stamp) composed of a simple copper panel that is rectangular in shape. It is devoid of decoration except for the inscribed record on its surface. A frame encompasses the list on all four sides, composed of straight lines engraved into the copper with the exception of the lower line, which takes the form of an undulating wave. There are two curved forms on both edges of the last line. The block holds an engraved Ottoman Turkish inscription that names the principal holy places in Palestine, such as al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, as well as al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil). The block also includes the names of the tombs of some of the prophets, including that of Moses located on the road leading to Jericho; the tomb of David, located outside the walls of the Old City of Jerusalem and the tombs of Ibrahim (Abraham) and Isaac as well as Jacob, and their wives, in al-Haram al-Ibrahimi and the tomb of al-Khadir. In addition, the block records the names of a series of sites and shrines that include: the Mihrab of Zakariya in the Haram al-Sharif;the site of Abu 'Ubaida 'Amar bin al-Jirrah in 'Amwas (Nicopolis); the Tomb of Mary at the foot of the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem;the Qubbat al-Mi'raj (Dome of the Mi'raj); Qubbat al-Arwah (Dome of the Spirits); al-Buraq al-Sharif (Sanctuary of al-Buraq) in the Haram al-Sharif; the Qubbat Rahil (Rachel's Tomb) in Bethlehem; the tomb of Joseph in Halhul and al-'Ais in Sa'ir. The block also contains the names of the great saints of the Sufi paths, among whom are Muhammad al-Khalili (d. AH 1146 / AD 1734), who was one of the *'ulama of the Bait al-Maqdis* (scholar of the Bait al Maqdis) and Muhammad al-Budairi (d. AH 1220 / AD 1805) who was another scholar of the *Bait al-Maqdis*. The inscription ends with the word “Opening”.  
It is possible that the printing block gave authorisation to enter the holy places named, or perhaps it was meant to be a list of places a Sufi should visit in the region of Palestine. It is likely that it was used to print on paper and then distributed to an interested public.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.short_description: A rectangular copper panel devoid of decoration. It is inscribed with a list of the most important sites and shrines in Palestine. It might have been authorisation to enter these places, or a list of places that one should visit, or merely places where one could be blessed. It was probably stamped on paper to be distributed to interested parties.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.method_for_datation: The piece was dated by ascertaining the life-spans of the pious men who are mentioned (Sheikh Muhammad al-Khalili and Sheikh Muhammad al-Budayri).
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this printing block was made in Palestine, as there were a number of copper workshops producing a variety of copper objects In Jerusalem. In addition, the names of the sites detailed on the printing block are all in Palestine, which strengthens the hypothesis that it was made locally.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.obtention: The printing block was transferred on an unknown date from the Haram al-Sharif to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem.
5b39f275-54df-59e1-af9d-1758c033e5d5.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Entrance authorisation; printing block; copper; list of holy places; list of shrines; engraving; inscription

5c13ad64-b549-5470-8c28-60447c1829ab.name: Christ in Majesty
5c13ad64-b549-5470-8c28-60447c1829ab.description: This icon, known as Christ in Majesty, was once part of the Deesis tier as well as the centerpiece of an iconostasis, a wall of icons separating the nave from the sanctuary in an Orthodox church. An icon of the Mother of God would have hung to the right and an icon of John the Baptist to the left. The Deesis tier usually extends outward on either side with Archangels Michael and Gabriel and the apostles facing Christ. This image represents Christ’s Second Coming and Last Judgment. He is seated on a throne surrounded by seraphim and cherubim angels in a scene of glory based on visions of the Old Testament prophets. Christ’s radiance illuminates the whole scene. The corners depict the symbols of the four evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. Christ bestows a blessing with his right hand and in his left holds the Bible open to the passage, “Come to me all ye that labor and are heavy laden and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28-29). The Greek letters in three sections of Christ’s halo represent the oneness of the three-part Trinity. At the very top of this icon are the letters IC and XC, representing the first and last initials of the Greek name for Jesus Christ.
5c13ad64-b549-5470-8c28-60447c1829ab.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from the Temple Gallery, London, in 2009. Gifted by Gordon Lankton to the Museum of Russian Icons in 2013.
keywords: Jesus Christ; Religious iconography; Allegorical and symbolical figures; Angels

5cdd4963-ab03-5834-84db-f850572ca208.name: Maronite Benevolent Catholic Society of New York rule book
5cdd4963-ab03-5834-84db-f850572ca208.short_description: A copy of the book of regulations for the Maronite Benevolent Catholic Society of New York, a charitable society aimed at helping the needy within the Maronite community. It provided financial support for the poor and free medication for the sick, and financially supported burial of the deceased. The book outlines the objectives, rules and structure of the association.

keywords: Society; Social institution; Association; Immigrants

5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.name: Reliquary of St-George Chiopolites from Aivali
5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.short_description: The reliquary contained the head of George Chiopolites, who was martyred in Aïvali / Kydonies in 1807. The container made for the head has intricate rococo decoration with ribbons, bows, roses, blank heraldic shields and St George holding the attributes of a neomartyr under the imposing two-headed eagle of ecclesiastical authority. From the mid-eighteenth century, thanks to special administrative treatment or privileges, the inhabitants of Aïvali transformed what had been a small fishing village into a flourishing commercial centre on the Aeolian coast. The inscription on the reliquary refers to the goldsmith and to the Guild of Soap-Makers, which was one of the biggest trade associations in the town. It also refers to Sophronios, who oversaw the commissioning, and has been identified to the parish priest and a close relative of Theophilos Kaïris, a teacher at the Academy of Kydonies who was later expelled from the Church under the free Greek state for his revolutionary ideas and was to die in prison, the last ideologue of the Enlightenment.
5cf8b622-bc23-5c90-a393-46a79bb0514b.author: Ballian 1992, 84, no. 44
keywords: relic; rococo

5d100163-7783-5d0b-b8a8-5ee5feece0df.name: Candlestick
5d100163-7783-5d0b-b8a8-5ee5feece0df.short_description: The candlestick was dedicated by the Mamluk sultan Qaytbay to the shrine at Medina in 1482. Monumental inscriptions whose letter-ends curve to form tongs enclosing small palmettes, occupy almost the entire height of the base. The sultan Qaytbay had the mosque of the Prophet restored in 1480 and offered to it at least five candlesticks, of which another two have survived and are now in Cairo.
keywords: Candlestick; Sultan Qaytbay; Metalwork
materials: Brass inlaid with black organic material

5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.name: Brass head of flagpole
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.short_description: A crescent shape made of casted brass fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.
5d377e78-b054-59b0-820b-7328307c7e77.holder: Jordan Museum for Costumes and Jewellery, Department of Antiquities

5d81f529-0519-5b10-ba1c-6c8d92b01735.name: The Battle between the Novgorodians and the Suzdalians
5d81f529-0519-5b10-ba1c-6c8d92b01735.description: This icon type, among the first to depict an event from Russian history, illustrates the 1169 battle in which the Suzdalians besieged the city of Novgorod. During the siege, Archbishop Ilya of Novgorod ordered that an icon of the Mother of God be brought out from the Church of the Transfiguration to give the Novgorodians courage. According to legend, the icon was displayed on the city walls where it was struck by a Suzdalian arrow. The icon miraculously began to weep, and through the intercession of the Mother of God, the Novgorodians defeated the Suzdalians. This image is particularly rich in its narrative and compositional details.
5d81f529-0519-5b10-ba1c-6c8d92b01735.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 1995. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography

5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.name: Mihrab
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.short_description: A mihrab is a characteristic architectural element in mosques and other places where Muslims worship. It serves to emphasize the direction of Mecca, toward which all prayer is oriented. Shaped like a niche, the mihrab is usually concave, but flat examples also occur, as here. This mihrab, which represents only the upper central panel of what was undoubtedly a larger ensemble, is inscribed with a passage from the Qur'an (15:45–47) that refers to Paradise, suggesting that it may have once graced a funerary monument.
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.dates: Hegira early 8th century / AD early 14th century
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.method_for_datation: This mihrab relates to several dated luster mihrabs, including one from the shrine at Qom from Hegira 734 / AD 1334 now in the Iran Bastan Museum in Tehran (3270). Such tile mihrabs and related tile ensembles were likely produced in Kashan rather than in situ. Luster tile production in Kashan seems to have come to an end around 1340, providing an approximate terminus ante quem.
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.method_for_provenance: Kashan was a major site of ceramics production in the 12th- 14th centuries (with a break during the Mongol invasions).
5d9bc47e-05b8-5889-945e-09b9078e013b.obtention: Kevorkian Collection (sale, Parke-Bernet, New York, December 18, 1970). Collection of Nasli M. Heeramaneck (1902-1971), New York, until 1973 (sold to); LACMA, The Nasli M. Heeramaneck collection, gift of Joan Palevsky.

5d9fc24f-9c51-56b2-a925-33389c038005.name: Paper crown for *Maulid an-Nabi*
5d9fc24f-9c51-56b2-a925-33389c038005.short_description: In Egypt, houses are festively decorated for the Prophet's birthday, the *Maulid an-Nabi*, and the mosques are brightly lit. Jugglers, fire-swallowers and dancing Sufis fill the streets and squares of Cairo. Processions snake through the streets. Children are treated to carousel rides. Merchants appear and sell a variety of figures made out of sugar, wrapped with coloured paper; that are particularly popular with children. Another hit amongst the children is a birthday crown, made out of cardboard, printed tissue paper and wire, on the forehead of which is displayed a paper image, cut out of a newspaper, of an *ʿud* (lute) player, or a famous star from film and television. Gifts given at the festival of *Maulid* are made of ephemeral, perishable materials such as paper. These are small works of art full of poetry and definite meaning. *Ephemera* are intended for shortterm use as they are unsuitable for prolonged use in daily life.
5d9fc24f-9c51-56b2-a925-33389c038005.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.

5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.name: Small magic cup
5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.description: Religious formulas or numbers written on magic bowls are used to compensate for medicine’s limitations. Liquid that comes into contact with these formulas acquires their curative property. The centre is decorated with a representation of the *Ka'ba* on top and a six-pointed star on the reverse.
5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
5dd25402-aa83-5544-9e46-d6ccfe8b2a79.obtention: Purchased at auction on advice of François de Ricqlès, 2001.

60db83b0-e090-5ad3-b467-090f3263e0b9.name: Single Niche 'Transylvanian' Prayer Rug
60db83b0-e090-5ad3-b467-090f3263e0b9.description: A characteristic type of Ottoman rugs is the "Transylvanian" double niche rug. Several variants of the type fashionable for over two centuries are known. Its common feature is the hexagonal medallion filling the central field created by mirroring the original *mihrab* (prayer niche) of the traditional prayer rug across the central axis. The carpet is a fine example of the rare single niche version of "Transylvanian" rugs. Its red *mihrab* (prayer niche) is filled with a floral-foliate scroll symmetric about the long axis, and a mosque lamp hangs from the peak of the *mihrab*. The spandrels are decorated by a large rosette and serrated leaves on a dark blue field. In the border, "Transylvanian" cartouches alternate with eight-pointed stars.

6131fb50-04d3-542e-b078-c6c43dfd4c0a.name: Chasuble (Mass vestment for the Catholic liturgy) made of decorative velvet and silk weave
6131fb50-04d3-542e-b078-c6c43dfd4c0a.short_description: The chasuble is a *pasticcio* consisting of an older Italian decorative velvet and a chasuble cross of Ottoman silk. The latter silk has a pattern of large lancet ovals filled with tulips, pinks and floral scrolls, a decoration typical of Ottoman silk weaving of the time. This combination of textiles for a chasuble demonstrates that there were no reservations about using a textile from Islamic regions for the Christian liturgy on account of its impressive appearance.

618bc97a-0543-5e59-aeff-839fc23ec12e.name: *Sitara* for the *rawda* of the Prophet’s mosque in Medina
618bc97a-0543-5e59-aeff-839fc23ec12e.short_description:
That this curtain was intended for the *rawda* is suggested by the text in the large medallion at the top. It consists of a *hadith* of the Prophet, *ma bayna qabri wa minbari rawda min riyad al-janna* (‘Between my tomb and my minbar is one of the gardens of Paradise’). The same text appears above the *mihrab* in the *rawda*.  
Sultan Mahmud II is known to have practised the art of calligraphy and a number of *sitara*s commissioned by him for the Prophet’s mosque bear his pear-shaped signature cartouche which reads, *katabahu al-‘abd Mahmud bin ‘Abdulhamid khan* (‘written by the servant \[of God\] Mahmud, the son of ‘Abdulhamid Khan’).

61f8f6ec-92d5-556e-b7d6-2e874ba81191.name: Hanging
61f8f6ec-92d5-556e-b7d6-2e874ba81191.short_description: This prayer rug is woven with a triple arcade, hanging lamps, vases with bunches of flowers and large flower scrolls. The pastel pinkish colours and the band woven with a flower scroll are typical of Chian silks. A famous one dated 1742 is kept in the monastery of Nea Mone on Chios. The export of Chian silks is recorded from the 15th century when the island was under Genoese rule and continued when the island passed into Ottoman hands in 1566.

63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.name: Pair of *mihrab* candlesticks.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.description: Each candlestick has a round base, a bell-shaped body, a cylindrical neck with a ring, and a wide candleholder. At the top and bottom of the body is a band of heart-shaped motifs with palmettes at their centres, a border repeated at the bottom of the neck. On the ring of the neck are large leaf motifs in relief. The neck itself is decorated with wavy lozenges featuring *hatayi*\-style (peony) motifs shown both frontally and in profile. The candleholder is decorated with interlacing cartouches with inscriptions. The main part of the body is decorated with a wide inscription band on a background of peonies and spiralling tendrils. The inscription in Persian is a poem praising the light of the candlestick; the Arabic inscription reads: 'May Sultan Bayezid be preserved from calamities'; the inscription in Ottoman Turkish informs us that the candlesticks were made for the mosque of Sultan Bayezid II in Edirne. Both candlesticks are entirely gilded. The forms of these candlesticks recall Mamluk candlesticks.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.short_description: When Ottoman sultans commissioned the construction of their mosques, they also ordered the production of candlesticks to be placed on both sides of the *mihrab*. These candlesticks were made for the Mosque of Bayezid II in Edirne and the inscriptions offer good wishes for the sultan.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.method_for_datation: The mosque of Bayezid II in Edirne, named on the inscriptions of the candlesticks, was completed in 894 / 1488. Thus the candlesticks must have been produced at about the same time.
63d7eb6d-8326-5395-9279-d48a47c2abba.obtention: The candlesticks were transferred to the Museum in 1911 from the Selimiye Mosque in Edirne.

65786a69-ccf0-52e9-acec-40d5ded53000.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
65786a69-ccf0-52e9-acec-40d5ded53000.description: Before the celebrations of Mawlid al-Nabawi (Feast of the Birth of the Prophet), shops in the historic Buzuriyya market in Damascus are filled with many types of sweets and chocolates. The most important sweet for Aid al-Mawlid is the *Mulabbas*, which consists of roasted almonds coated with a thin layer of sugar mixed with rose water. The shopkeepers arrange the various sweets inside the shops, while they place large bags of *Mulabbas* at the entrance to attract customers. The mosques organise the Mawlid celebrations, which take place between the Maghrib and Isha prayers in the evening, and a number of women like to host a Mawlid party in their homes. During the celebration of Mawlid, *Mulabbas* are distributed to all celebrants. Damascenes believe it is important to cook white food or serve white sweets on religious occasions, in order to greet the coming days with optimism symbolised by the colour white.

665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.name: Piece of the *kiswa* (cover) of the Ka’ba.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.description:
A piece of the Ka'ba *kiswa* (cover) which was probably produced in Syria, and was sent as part of the *Shami mahmal* (the Syrian Caravan carrying gifts for the Ka'ba) to Mecca to re-adorn the Ka'ba. Such a ritual occurred every year before the season of the Hajj, and included a venerated ceremony at which the commencement of the Hajj season was officially announced. It was and still is the case that the Ka'ba is washed, perfumed and purified every year and is then covered with a new *kiswa*. The fragmentexhibited here is made from red silk and embroidered with silver silken thread. The design includes two undulating bands which assume the form of a continuous chain made up of number “7”s. Both bands run from the beginning to the end of the cloth. Small, dispersed decorative elements are scattered between the two borders, as well as between the two undulating bands. Written inscriptions appear, the most prominent being: “There is no God but God and Muhammad is his Prophet”, repeating in the middle of the *kiswa* between the two zigzag bands. The two expressions, “Ya Mannan” (“Oh Merciful”) and “Ya Hannan” (“Oh Compassionate”) are also repeated, and consist of flowery forms running along both edges. On the upper undulating band, there is a verse from the Qur'an, “al-Baqara” (“the Cow”, 2: 144). The lower undulating band holds another chapter from the Qur'an: Surat Al 'Imran “the Family of Imran” (3:96). At the top and the bottom of the piece there are two expressions: “Dhu al-Jalal” (“Possessor of Majesty”) and “Dhu al-Ikram” (“Possessor of Honour”). One can conceptualise the size of the complete *kiswa* by bringing to mind the enormous scale of the Ka'ba. It is likely that the forms and inscriptions on this piece were repeated on the *kiswa* in its entirety. The name of the donor, the date of production and the emporium where it was produced is not recorded; the evidence has probably been cut off.  
It is worth mentioning that once used to cover the Ka'ba, the *kiswa* was cut into small pieces and sent as gifts to different capitals and cities in the Islamic world to bestow blessing on them. Ruling palaces and councils contained pieces of the *kiswa*, which were used to confer legality and sanctity.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.short_description: Every year the Ka’ba is washed and covered with a *kiswa* (cover) marking the beginning of the Hajj season. This piece is of red silk and embroidered with silver silk forming fragmented zigzags that repeat from the beginning of the piece to its end. Small forms are scattered in different places within inscription bands.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.method_for_datation: This fragment was dated based on comparison with similar pieces in the museums of Istanbul, whose dates had been narrowed down to around the 13th / 19th century.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this piece was made in Syria, since it is reminiscent of other pieces in the museums of Istanbul known to have been produced in the region.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.obtention: Al-Sayyid Tahir Sayf al-Din, about whom nothing is known, donated the *kiswa* fragment to the Islamic Museum in 1937.
665aed9d-195b-51b5-8961-06a52dfd6aab.author: Nazmi Al-Ju'beh
keywords: Embroidery; silk; cloth; kiswa of the Ka’ba; textile; silk textile

694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.name: Great lantern of al-Mu‘izz.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.description: The lantern is made up of a bronze hook supporting a shallow-domed hemispherical basin with an outwardly inclined upper rim. Attached to the six-faceted outer sides of the basin are three perforated chains with geometric and stylised floral decoration in the form of tracery and tri-lobed leaves. This is a common type of decoration in Middle-Age Kairouan. The chains support the large hammered-brass basin, which is shaped like a circular vase and allows light to shine through the myriad perforations. At the lowest point of the basin a six-point star has been punched out. This is surrounded by three inscriptions, one around the collar; another between the ring supports and a third circling the star. On the first strip, *kufic* calligraphy proclaims: 'Praise be to God … May he bestow blessings, good fortune, happiness, success, prosperity, health and glory on all who embrace Him.' On the circumference of the base is inscribed: 'The work of Muhammad son of Ali al-Qaysi al-Saffar \[the metalworker\] for al-Mu'izz.' This lantern closely resembles a mosque lamp kept at the Chicago Art Institute and a lantern of Persian origin belonging to the David collection in Copenhagen (Denmark). Both date from the AH 4th or 5th centuries (AD 11th century). All the evidence suggests that the lantern of al-Mu'izz, which lit up the Great Mosque of Kairouan, is an example of Byzantine–inspired craftsmanship, which was in vogue throughout the Arabic-Islamic world during the AH 4th and 5th centuries (AD 10th and 11th).
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.short_description: Used to light the Great Mosque of Kairouan, this lantern is an example of Byzantine-inspired craftsmanship fashionable in Arab-Islamic society in the AH 4th–5th / AD 10th–11th centuries. A bronze hook supports a shallow basin from which three chains suspend a large circular brass basin perforated with holes for light.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.method_for_datation: The last inscription states that the lantern was a gift from the Zirid prince, al-Mu'izz ibn Badis (r. 406–54 / 1016–62) to the Great Mosque of Kairouan. This donation could be contemporaneous with the legacy of the *Mudawwana* volumes, the work of the great Sunni legal expert Sahnun ibn Said (160–240 / 777–855), from the same prince to the Great Mosque of Kairouan in 424 / 1032. It was certainly before the Hilalian invasions of 443 / 1051.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.method_for_provenance: This lantern was part of the furniture of the Great Mosque of Kairouan. It was specially made by a lamp-maker for the reigning Zirid prince, so it was probably fabricated in a Kairouanese workshop.
694dde47-bada-58b2-bcc0-6d5bd86a4ac0.obtention: After the founding of the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada in 1986 it was decided to return this lantern, which was on display at the Bardo Museum, to its original location.

6952044c-cc8b-5648-b20d-435ae6281ac3.name: Niche or prayer carpet
6952044c-cc8b-5648-b20d-435ae6281ac3.description: This is the first carpet purchased by the MAK after its founding. Together with numerous embroideries, it was bought in 1868 from the Mechitarist congregation based in Vienna and formed the start of the MAK’s internationally notable carpet collection. It supposedly came via Iran to Vienna. If one compares it with the pictorial carpets containing landscapes and pairs of birds, one clearly recognises the further development of the Mughal style: away from the naturalistic depictions towards the detailed *mille-fleur* design of the centre field and the integration of vegetal elements into the architecture, such as the flanking cypresses. The carpet displays a flora made of fine Pashmina wool, which allowed especially detailed lines.

696eb90a-0ce9-5dba-973b-b54eeda3a5ad.name: Miniature Folding Iconostasis
696eb90a-0ce9-5dba-973b-b54eeda3a5ad.description: Miniature and folding iconostases were used starting in the 16th century, both by priests who traveled to rural areas and domestically by the Russian people. These icons, which vary in size and composition, are scaled-down versions of the partitions found in an Orthodox church and were largely used as a way to bring faith into the home. This icon consists of 15 parts and depicts the Deesis, festival and prophet tiers. The Mother of God is pictured in the center of the top row, flanked by unidentified saints.
696eb90a-0ce9-5dba-973b-b54eeda3a5ad.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Simon Morsink, Amsterdam, in 2008. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.name: Anatolian prayer rug
69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.description:
Anatolian prayer rugs with two columns in the central field can be found in the west (Ghiordes and Kula rugs) and central (Ladik rugs) parts of the region. The spread of common design features makes it at times difficult to determine just which pieces are from which part of the region. It is very difficult, e.g. to determine the exact origin of this particular rug. The two column *mihrab* (prayer niche) resembles, with its geometrical decorated columns, some 19th century Kula prayer rugs. Palmettes in the border resemble some Caucasian palmette designs. The colours of the carpet are vibrant shades of red and blue that can be seen on Ladik rugs. The *mihrab* arch consists of a series of step-like progressions towards the top, which is also a characteristic of Ladik rugs.  
This Anatolian prayer rug was a gift to Izidor Kršnjavi, former director of the Museum of Arts and Crafts, from Ćiro Truhelka, former director of the National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. In the central field, on red background, there are two columns of geometric blue and white motifs. The border is decorated with rosettes, palmettes and octagons on the blue background. In the upper left corner there are two medallions with an inscription. In the upper medallion there is the Hegira 1190 /AD 1776. In the lower medallion there is the name of the weaver: Insuf.
69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and inscripted year
69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: prayer rug; Anatolia, inscription band; Ghiordes

6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.name: Hanging (*sitara*) for the Mosque of the Prophet, Medina al-Munawwarah
6c834b03-f120-537f-ad07-f35c0f191253.short_description: The interior walls of the Shrine of the Prophet in the Madina were traditionally honoured with elaborate hangings. During the Ottoman period, it was customary for the Sultan to send hangings for the shrine  on the occasion of his ascension to the throne or when wear and tear demanded them to be replaced. The old  hangings were returned to Istanbul.Judging by their inscriptions, it has been suggested that  black-grounded Ottoman textiles like this one may have been commissioned specifically to cover the tomb of the Prophet (pbuh). In addition to qur'anic inscriptions, the calligraphic panels include a large green medallion with a hadith of the Prophet: ‘ (For) whosoever may visit my grave, my intercession will become an obligation’. Below, elaborate arabesque scrolling surrounds the emblem or tughra of the sultan Abd al-Hamid II (1293 H/1876 AD – 1327 H/1909 AD), who commissioned this hanging.

6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.name: Qur’an Cabinet
6d56bfde-b2d7-5b3d-b418-0b9d3e98d0e8.short_description:
This Qur’an cabinet from Istanbul would embellish rooms in private homes, mosques, *madrasas* (Islamic education centres), and mausoleums. Crafted in the Ottoman style, the box stands on four legs, mother-of-pearl inlaying, geometric patterns and calligraphy.  
  
This rare type of Qur’an cabinet (called *sunduq* or *kursi*) attracts with an unusual form several compartments for religious items and scripts, and the dome-shaped cover. The calligraphy in *Diwani* style reads *Al Fatiha* (the opening chapter of the Qur’an) and *Al Zalzalah* (the 99th chapter).  
  
In the 19th century, the mother-of-pearl style called Damascene became increasingly popular in Ottoman Turkey. Artisans arranged precious materials including mother-of-pearl, tortoiseshell, metals and ivory into interlocking asterisks, octagons and hexagons.

6da483f8-19ce-5f70-9bd8-3d093b8b1250.name: Carpet
6da483f8-19ce-5f70-9bd8-3d093b8b1250.description: The field of this knotted-wool carpet is decorated with a prayer niche (*mihrab*) whose centre features a willow flanked by two pear trees upon which birds are perched. Snakes coil themselves around the branches, while two lions lie at the foot of the trees. Deer on fields of red adorn the upper corners. The cartouches on the side-borders show birds in pear trees, while those on the horizontal borders depict doves or rabbits. The warp and weft yarns are in cotton. The three-millimetre-high wool knots – the rug has 4,030 of them per square decimetre – are asymmetrical. The motifs are in a wide array of colours: pink, red, yellow, green, orange, blue and brown.

6ef65cc3-4c33-56d6-9397-2ea841e48bc8.name: Carpet
6ef65cc3-4c33-56d6-9397-2ea841e48bc8.description: Carpets had a number of functions in Central Asia, dictated by the specific way of life in this part of the world. The nomadic tribes wove smaller carpets, while the population in large settlements mostly used larger carpets. These carpets retained a great number of traditional patterns since they were less exposed to foreign influences. A strictly geometric pattern is always used in composing the design and flowers are skillfully stylised into geometric shapes. In prayer rugs, the top of *mihrab* or prayer niche is slightly emphasised. The central field is most often filled with geometric shapes – octagons, rhombi or stars. The rhombi are sometimes graduated and sometimes filled with hook motifs. Motifs taken from nature most often take on an octagonal shape. We also encounter dogs and camels, faithful companions of the nomads. Carpets belonging to this group are always distinguished by a central field and borders, usually three borders of which the middle border is most accentuated. The so-called *ensi* rugs have a central field within a frame or cross, which are filled with decorative patterns. The colours are mainly dark, mostly different shades of red, from brown to purple. The borders and central field are always the same colour, which may vary in tone. The individual patterns are blue, green, yellow and white. The warp is traditionally wool, and the weft and pile material fine sheep’s or goat’s wool, sometimes even camel hair. The carpets are usually made by knotting and the asymmetrical knot is almost always used. The central field of this carpet is divided into patterned strips with four mini-fields and at the centre of each of them is the *tree of life*. The main field has six borders of which two narrow ones are repeated, while the other four are different. The third border from the edge is the widest and is filled with geometric shapes in the form of squares. The overriding colours are dark red, blue, white and brown.

6f7fa000-1d38-5400-8b90-6b15054dd8a3.name: Inscription recording the presentation of a new rain spout for the Ka‘ba
6f7fa000-1d38-5400-8b90-6b15054dd8a3.short_description:
The inscription, which is written out at full size, is the first of three lines inscribed on the Mizab al-Rahma – the rain spout on the Ka‘ba – which was commissioned by the Ottoman sultan ‘Abdulmajid I in 1856 and installed in 1859.  
The present inscription, with its masterly interweaving of the letter forms, testifies to the skill of the master calligrapher, ‘Abdallah Zuhdi, who was known as katib al-haramayn (‘the calligrapher of the two Holy Sanctuaries’). Sultan Abdülmecid also commissioned ‘Abdallah Zuhdi in to re-design the inscriptions in the Prophet’s Mosque in Medina. He began his work there in 1856 and the task took him seven years to complete. Zuhdi spent the latter part of his life in Cairo, where he re-designed the inscriptions on the various embroidered textiles sent from Cairo to Mecca with the *kiswa*.

6fa63cbf-0340-5e3e-8071-e07e6642fc87.name: Bib for the camel of the Egyptian *mahmal*
6fa63cbf-0340-5e3e-8071-e07e6642fc87.short_description:
The camel destined to carry the Egyptian *mahmal* was specially chosen for its appearance as much as for its strength. It was looked after by a special employee in Dar al-Kiswa, and was caparisoned in richly embroidered textiles while being paraded through the streets of Cairo and major cities on its way to Mecca and back.  
  
The Qur’anic inscription, *sura al-Nahl*, verse 7, is apposite. It reads, ‘And they carry your heavy loads to lands that you could not otherwise reach except with souls distressed. Truly, your Lord is full of Kindness, Most Merciful.’  
  
The cotton lining bears a stamped trade mark of a firm in Manchester, England, consisting of an open hand bearing a name, possibly Abraham Harawi, in Arabic.

70e81fc7-992c-56d9-a3b4-5af8b1052c23.name: Prayer pulpit (*minbar*).
70e81fc7-992c-56d9-a3b4-5af8b1052c23.description:
This *minbar* features seven steps that are held up by two pentagonal sides, decorated with triangular, square and trapezium-shaped panels that have been joined through tenons and mortises. An interrupted horseshoe arch is positioned at the foot of the steps on two supports that are ornamented with vegetal decoration. This structure is linked at its sides by two lateral arches of the same height, which are likewise resting on two supports, their upper parts interlinked by a banister. The upper section of this entrance is adorned with candleholders.  
The panels are sculpted in bas-relief, embellished with floral or geometric decoration; the frontal arch features floral decoration, and, embracing the shape of the arch, a *kufic* inscription reads, rising from the right-hand side, 'In the name of Allah, the Merciful Benefactor. This pulpit was created'; sideways: 'The first of the month of Rajab; and rising from the left, 'of the year 490 \[AD 1097\]. The work of Muhammad'.

718b2755-b86b-5577-8fe4-dae39544ddbd.name: Scenes from the Life of John the Baptist
718b2755-b86b-5577-8fe4-dae39544ddbd.description:
John the Baptist was the cousin of Jesus Christ and preached in the Judean desert. He lived a life of self-denial by wearing camel hair clothing and eating only locusts and wild honey. The people of the region came to him to be baptized in the Jordan River. When Jesus asked to be baptized, John proclaimed that he was not worthy of such a task and that Christ should baptize him. Christ insisted, however, and during the baptism the Holy Spirit descended and a voice from heaven proclaimed, “This is my beloved Son in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). John got into trouble when he criticized King Herod’s marriage to Herodias, who had a child from her previous marriage to Herod’s brother. Herod’s stepdaughter, Salome, convinced him to arrest John and demanded his head on a silver platter. Granting her wish, Herod ordered John beheaded.  
This icon shows several scenes from John the Baptist’s life in a single frame. At the top left, John is depicted in the wilderness, surrounded by animals. He receives inspiration from God in the form of flames. At the bottom, John is seen baptizing followers in the Jordan River while more followers prepare for baptism or don the white clothes of the newly baptized. In the top right corner of the icon, people stream out from the city while members of the aristocracy look on from above. The three figures in the central arch could be King Herod, his wife and stepdaughter, all of whom were responsible for John’s martyrdom.
718b2755-b86b-5577-8fe4-dae39544ddbd.obtention: Purchased by the Museum of Russian Icons from a private collection in 2010.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

71d27a74-72e5-584a-a669-aeffec6787d6.name: Prayer rug (fragment)
71d27a74-72e5-584a-a669-aeffec6787d6.description: Although less than half the size of the original rug, the fragment is still one of the most remarkable textiles of the Islamic art collection in the Museum. Following the latest research, the original rug was reconstructed based on several well-preserved details (see the virtual reconstruction of the original design, ill. 1a). The *mihrab*, an essential element of the mosque architecture represented on prayer rugs, has been replaced here with a triple arch reminiscent rather of a gateway or the cross section through a mosque; the dome over the centre arch in the original design supports this hypothesis. The coupled-column motif could be traced back to the architecture of Muslim Spain, and was apparently disseminated by Sephardic Jews. Similar columns, whose bases are rendered in linear perspective, feature on 16th-century Ottoman prayer rugs some of which were imperial court commissions produced in Istanbul; others, as is the case here, were made in Cairo, where the tradition of Mamluk workshops continued long after the Ottoman conquest (1517). The asymmetrical knot is characteristic of Mamluk carpets, whereas the decorative repertoire is typical of Ottoman art. The original rug may have served as a prototype for “Transylvanian” coupled-column carpets dating back to the 17th and 18th centuries, which only comes to highlight the historical significance of this fragment.

72ba3bfe-0cc8-514d-9707-7a480f54966b.name: Prayer rug
72ba3bfe-0cc8-514d-9707-7a480f54966b.short_description:
This is one of approximately 90 prayer or niche rugs often known as a ‘Salting’ group which are now generally accepted as having been woven in Iran sometime in the 16th or 17th century. Many are believed to have come from the Topkapi Palace Museum (which still holds some 35 examples), sold off during the economic crisis resulting from the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–8. It is very likely that they were a diplomatic gift and that they entered the Topkapi Palace sometime before 1680, as a treasury ledger of that year mentions Persian prayer rugs with embroidered inscriptions in metal thread. It has been suggested that they may have remained unused in the Palace stores due to the presence of inscriptions integral to Shi‘i daily prayers on some of them, which may account for the bright colours and often remarkable condition of many examples, including this one.  
  
The inscriptions on this carpet consist of the *Ayat al-Kursi* (‘Throne verse’), *sura* *al-Baqara*, (II), verse 255, in the outer border and *sura* *al-Ahzab* (XXXIII), verse 56, in the inner one. The corner medallions enclise the phrase, ‘Glory to my most high Lord, and to His praise’. A pair to this carpet, previously known as the ‘Perez’ prayer rug, is in a private collection in Italy.

73c04230-63e1-510e-98c5-207e053e23cf.name: Chaplet of an Ottoman dervish
73c04230-63e1-510e-98c5-207e053e23cf.short_description: The Austro-Hungarian troops who joined the Ottoman forces in 1915 performed their service very close to the Allies, but were never put under the administrative control of the Ottoman Empire, as the German soldiers were. Souvenirs of this very exotic mission during World War I were in high demand and were brought back to Austria after the end of the war.

keywords: Sufi; Bosnia; Sufi Hadschi Loja; religious object; souvenirs; war; warfare

74a9ac30-d924-5b63-8349-21d424570c93.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
74a9ac30-d924-5b63-8349-21d424570c93.description: During the Prophet’s birthday, the historic Buzuriyya Market in Damascus is crowded with people buying the necessities for the occasion, such as sweets and chocolate. The celebration usually takes place in the evening after Maghrib prayers in many mosques. The Mawlid opens with a short recitation of the Holy Qur’an, then comes the “Mawlid Recitation”, which is a narration of the Prophet’s biography recited in a special style. After that, specialised chanting groups perform religious songs and praise of the Prophet, and the Mawlawiyya dance to their music. The ceremony concludes with the Isha prayer and the distribution of sweets.

75647d49-efe8-541c-828b-b58acf35195a.name: God Rested on the Seventh Day
75647d49-efe8-541c-828b-b58acf35195a.description: In this icon, God reclines on a bed, illustrating the part of the creation story that reads, “On the seventh day He rested” (Genesis 2:2). Angels hold his bed and the temporarily vacant throne aloft while the Holy Spirit, represented by a dove, flies above them. All this takes place within a circle featuring the archangels, the evangelists, Christ and the Mother of God. Meanwhile, scenes from the rest of the creation story take place below. Labels on the back of this icon reveal that it was sold by Gimbels department store in the late 1930s, suggesting that it once belonged to William Randolph Hearst. Hearst was a newspaper entrepreneur who famously sold off large parts of his immense art collection during the Depression.
75647d49-efe8-541c-828b-b58acf35195a.obtention: Sold at "Exhibition of Russian Icons Arranged by Hammer Galleries", New York City, in 1937. Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2013. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography; Biblical stories; Jesus Christ; Angels

757957ce-46d4-5799-8792-5f05be3e1e3f.name: Hanging (*sitara*) for the Mosque of the Prophet, Medina al-Munawwarah
757957ce-46d4-5799-8792-5f05be3e1e3f.short_description: This green and black silk textile is richly embroidered with silver and gilt metal threads. The centre displays six cartouches with thuluth inscriptions, followed below by a black niche with a central lamp motif. A border with trefoil scrolling surrounds the central panel. The inscriptions used on this textile clearly indicate that this textile was intended for the Prophet’s Mosque in Madina. The four main cartouches contain verse 56 from chapter 33 (Al-Ahzab) of the Holy Qur’an: ‘Allah sends His Salat (merciful blessings) on the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), and also His angels. O you who believe! Send your Salat on him and greet him with the Islamic way of greeting’. The inscriptions in the two cartouches below state that this curtain was ordered by the Ottoman sultan Abd al-Hamid II (1293 H/1876 AD – 1327 H/1909 AD) and renewed by Efendi Abbas Hilmi, the last Khedive Pasha of Ottoman Egypt (1291 H/ 1874 AD – 1350 H/ 1931 AD) in 1321 H/ 1903 AD.
757957ce-46d4-5799-8792-5f05be3e1e3f.holder: Sharjah Museum of Islamic Civilisation /Sharjah Museums Authority
