keywords: thuluth; Khedive; sitara
materials: Silk, cotton, silver and silver gilt metal thread

7b36747d-dca7-598b-b985-ad4799a191fe.name: The Mother of God of the Burning Bush
7b36747d-dca7-598b-b985-ad4799a191fe.description:
The Mother of God is shown in the center of this icon surrounded by rays of light that extend outward to form an eight-pointed star. Angels, archangels and symbols of the evangelists are pictured both in and around the star. This icon is a reference to a passage from the book of Exodus in which Moses saw the burning bush unconsumed by fire. Moses and other prophets are often interpreted as foretelling the coming of Christ while the unburnt bush serves as a symbolic representation of the Virgin Mary.  
In this icon, the four evangelists are represented by four winged figures. The angel represents Saint Matthew, the lion stands for Saint John, the ox symbolizes Saint Luke and the eagle is associated with Saint Mark. These symbols are based on the biblical interpretations of Saint Irenaeus (130-202).
7b36747d-dca7-598b-b985-ad4799a191fe.obtention: Purchased by the Museum of Russian Icons from ArtVKG, New York City, in 2012.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography; Angels

7bcc1f68-b1fc-5f4e-9ba9-572b00e46c54.name: Qur’anic Manuscript
7bcc1f68-b1fc-5f4e-9ba9-572b00e46c54.short_description: Interlocking circles, often punctuated by circles or dots, are used in conjunction with squares, rectangles, diamonds or triangles to form the basis of intricate geometric patterns. Interlocking circles grace doors and windows, prayer niches and arches as an architectural ornament. Silver and gold jewellery and musical instruments also incorporate patterns based on interlocking circles. With such a broad range of applications, the scale of the patterns varies dramatically. For example, a pattern stamped in gold leaf for the decoration of a Qur’an case necklace can measure as little as few millimetres in diameter, while an identical pattern used in stucco or plaster that serve to adorn the interior of a prayer hall can be exponentially larger.
7bcc1f68-b1fc-5f4e-9ba9-572b00e46c54.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
keywords: Qur'an; Manuscript

7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.name: Mosque lamp.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.description:
An enameled glass and gilt mosque lamp with a wide flaring mouth and a squat globular body, a steeply sloping shoulder and flattened base. The body rests on a tall pedestal foot. Six applied loop handles are placed around the shoulder at regular intervals. The lamp holds extensive enamelled decoration on the mouth, body and foot, enhanced by gilding; the mouth having a large Qur’anic inscription in *thuluth* script executed in blue enamel and outlined in red. The inscription is interrupted by three roundels containing a *fleur-de-lys* blazon in red against a white background. The base of the mouth shows a delicately drawn scroll-band interrupted by cusped floral cartouches.  
The top of the shoulder displays a narrow band with cusped floral medallions, while the main part of the body has a wide inscription band in *thuluth* script that reads, translated: ‘This is one of the objects made for his most noble and high Excellency, the learned, the just, the administrator, the councilor, the regent, the vizier Najm al-Din Mahmud ibn Ali ibn Shirwin, the officer of al-Malik al-Muzaffar (Hajji), regent of the noble Islamic provinces, may Allah the Exalted make his victories glorious’. The inscription, set against a blue background, is interrupted by six lozenge-shaped areas that hold the trailed suspension loops.  
The underside of the body has further *fleur-de-lys* roundels and floral detailing. The foot (half of which is a replacement) holds a succession of five horizontal bands filled with abstract scrolling that alternates, linearly, with thickly drawn detailing. The horizontal bands are interrupted by three lozenge-shaped medallions that hold abstract vegetal motifs.  
The lamp dates exactly to AH 746–7 / AD 1346–7, during the short reign of al-Malik al-Muzaffar Hajji. Interestingly, the donor Najm al-Din Mahmud ibn Ali ibn Shirwin, did not begin his career as a slave contrary to usual practice. It is known that he arrived in Cairo in AH 737 / AD 1337, having been a vizier (a minister) in Baghdad. The red *fleur-de-lys* on his lamp is his heraldic device. Najm al-Din’s lamp is especially important because it appears to be the earliest example of a *fleur-de-lys* used as the badge of an official, a motif previously reserved only for sultans.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.short_description: Glass mosque lamps with enamelled decoration were commissioned in large numbers by the Mamluk elite in Egypt and Syria. Decorated with Qur’anic inscriptions and the titles of the patron, they were destined for the numerous mosques and *madrasas* endowed by the Mamluks throughout Cairo and the empire.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.initial_owner: Najm al-Din Mahmud ibn Ali ibn Shirwin.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.method_for_datation: The lamp was commissioned by an officer of al-Malik al-Muzaffar Hajji, who reigned for less than two years between 746–47 / 1346–7.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.method_for_provenance: Mamluk mosque lamps of this type are generally ascribed to Syria, where they were made for export to Mamluk Egypt.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.provenance: Syria; made for export to Egypt.
7f0081a0-67a5-56a0-9212-f80fe70cbeec.obtention: Purchased by the NMS from the Major W. J. Myers Collection in 1900.

80275793-c91b-5334-93ac-d4126f4e645c.name: Prayer rug
80275793-c91b-5334-93ac-d4126f4e645c.description: Gördes prayer rugs of the 18th and 19th centuries were much appreciated in Western Europe as well as in Romania, where they have been preserved in large numbers. Here, the stepped arch of the niche is featured on a white ground; the floral and geometric motifs of the *mihrab* field are reminiscent of a mosque lamp. A tiny brown mosque lamp appears as such in the centre of the composition, hardly discernible amid stylised flowers and stars. The elaborate decoration, with a wealth of floral motifs on the inner edges of the niche, is a recurrent feature of 19th-century Ottoman carpets at a time when architectural motifs derived from courtly art were gradually losing their original shape and meaning. The cross panels featured above and below the niche are decorated with Chinese cloudbands. The main border is made up of seven narrow bands on white and red ground, sometimes associated with the seven heavens, while the secondary borders contain flowers connected by wave scrolls.

81099b4c-753f-53ba-9785-217e53613a49.name: Madonna and Child
81099b4c-753f-53ba-9785-217e53613a49.description: It was not roses that guarded the sleep of the enthroned Madonna with the Child, but human bones. And her sleep lasted not for a hundred years, but for several centuries. The sculpture was piously buried in the charnel house of the church of Raron according to a custom prevalent in Europe at the time, and gradually vanished beneath the skulls and bones of the dead. The reason for burying the wooden figure was provided by the rebuilding of the parish church between 1510 and 1515. The Romanesque Madonna had fallen out of fashion and was no longer needed. The person who finally kissed her awake again was not Prince Charming, but a tradesman from the canton of Valais. During restoration work on the charnel house of Raron in 1924, he was told to clear out the bones – and so he stumbled upon several sculptures, including the most significant example of Romanesque art in Switzerland.
keywords: Madonna; Child; Sculpture; Raron; Vallais
materials: Carved in the round, limewood, polychromy

825bbc31-2ea9-5983-a4b5-235679be04cb.name: Niche of al-Uweyna Mosque
825bbc31-2ea9-5983-a4b5-235679be04cb.short_description:
The 10th century AH/16th century AD is considered the richest period for production of *mihrabs* (mosque niches), known for the work of masters like Abdullah bin Qasim al-Manahi and the family of Mushmil al-Manahi who lived during this time. Talib bin Mushmil al-Manahi, who built the niches of the Grand Mosque in Nakhl and as-Saruj Mosque in Samail, also made the niche of al-Uweyna Mosque in 970 AH/1562 AD. The niche on display is covered with geometrical decorations, fine inscriptions, quotes from the Holy Qur'an and inscriptions documenting the names of the builder, designer and the patron.  
  
The Islamic *ash-shahadatan* (Declaration of Faith) is written in *kufic* inscription at the upper part of the niche and the outer rectangular frame contains 30 seals with floral decoration. The niche itself sits in the cove of the inner frame with a rectangular shape above it baring inscriptions in two triangles and three plates of glazed Chinese pottery in the centre.
keywords: Mihrab; Niche; Declaration of Faith; kufic; Geometric

82850beb-2fc7-5463-8d56-45c22b84b71b.name: Carpet with triple-arch design
82850beb-2fc7-5463-8d56-45c22b84b71b.short_description: This carefully drawn, subtly coloured carpet is among the finest of all Ottoman weavings. One of the earliest carpets to include a triple-arched gateway, its design probably originated in the Ottoman imperial workshop. The hanging lamp in the centre arch recalls verses from the Qur’an that liken God to the light of a lamp placed within a niche. The combination of this carpet’s imagery, high quality, and relatively small size suggest that it was used as a prayer rug by a member of the Ottoman courtly elite.

8483f56d-4097-5e63-a47a-8a53aa99f289.name: *Hilye*
8483f56d-4097-5e63-a47a-8a53aa99f289.short_description: Despite the steady advance of western-style artworks, traditional Ottoman arts and crafts did not disappear entirely. This hilye or word portrait of the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) has been rendered on tripartite, foldable cardboard, decorated on the outside with elaborate ebru paper marbling. Its composition follows a layout current since the 11th/17th century when it was devised by the famous Ottoman calligrapher Hafiz Osman (1052-1110 H/1642-1698CE). Traditionally, the hilye presents Hadith recounting the noble physical and spiritual attributes of the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), often embellished with rich illumination. A large oval cartouche, with the hadith in black naskhi, appears in the centre, surrounded by four roundels naming the four rightly-guided caliphs Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. Above the cartouche, the Bismillah is written in thuluth style. Below, a verse from the Holy Qur'an (68:4) is followed by the last lines of the hadith, a prayer, the names of the artist and two individuals certifying his work, and the date. All calligraphic elements are set against a stippled gold background enhanced with European-style floral elements.

8485bf89-aab8-53ff-a59e-03b0ed9c4935.name: The Last Judgment
8485bf89-aab8-53ff-a59e-03b0ed9c4935.description: The Last Judgment is a common topic in Christian art. It combines biblical and apocryphal stories into a unified account of the end of times, of Christ coming to judge the world and of the afterlife. Typically, Russian Orthodox icons that depict the Last Judgment show Christ enthroned with a scale and an open Gospel. He is often flanked by the Virgin and Saint John the Baptist, who intercede for humankind. Adam and Eve are frequently seen kneeling at Christ’s feet. In Russian Orthodox iconography, the “serpent of suffering” is often depicted as well. Originally, the serpent was viewed as the instigator of original sin, seducer of Adam and Eve and the embodiment of evil. In this icon, 20 sins are depicted along the body of the snake in order of severity. They are as follows: (1) lying, (2) greed, (3) tale-telling, (4) idle talk, (5) anger, (6) blasphemy, (7) gluttony, (8) drunkenness, (9) slander, (10) foul language, (11) adultery, (12) fornication, (13) rape, (14) vanity, (15) money-mongering, (16) self-love, (17) despair, (18) murder, (19) self-glorification and (20) pride.
8485bf89-aab8-53ff-a59e-03b0ed9c4935.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2006. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Religious iconography; Biblical stories; Jesus Christ; Angels

84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.name: Three choir stalls.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.description:
Three surviving seats from the choir stall. The arms, elaborately carved, mimic smooth timber columns with finely worked capital and base. The separators between the seats have been hollowed out and outlined to form mixtilinear arches with a strong Almohad influence. There are wheels in relief on the spandrels. There is now practically no colour left, with the exception of the persistent red and a few other traces from which a painted lion can be made out, already quite deteriorated when the piece was acquired. The dominant decorative elements are plant arabesques and the polychromy of the heraldic motifs relating to the kingdom of León.  
This piece is noteworthy not just for its intrinsic quality, but also because it demonstrates the importance of León in the emergence of Mudéjar carpentry. This low stall, along with the Astudillo stall also held at the National Archaeological Museum, is one of the most exceptional examples of this type of carpentry in this Mudéjar style.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.short_description: Mudéjar craftsmen were sometimes used to work on choir stalls in churches and monasteries, and they brought their own techniques and decorative motifs. These stalls from the Monastery of Santa María de Gradefes in León are particularly noteworthy for the excellence of the joinery and their rich decoration of plant arabesques.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.method_for_datation: From its typical characteristics. The earliest document on the monastery dates from 1140.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.method_for_provenance: From existing documentation. It remained in the monastery until its sale in 1874.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.provenance: Monastery of Santa María de Gradefes, León, Spain.
84dd3553-46ec-5600-8a2a-e99eb0f50285.obtention: The piece was purchased for the National Archaeological Museum from José Gil Dorregaray on 13 March 1874.

87cd43a9-2f34-5603-8fcc-c5f26dd19789.name: Noble Qur'an Manuscript
87cd43a9-2f34-5603-8fcc-c5f26dd19789.short_description:
Literally meaning "the recitation", the Noble Qur’an is the central religious text of Islam. It was revealed to the Prophet Muhammed (Peace be upon him) from Allah verbally through archangel Jibril (Gabriel) over a period of twenty-three years (609–632 AD).  
  
The Qur’an is comprised of 114 *surah*s (chapters) classified into two types, *Makki* and *Madani*, depending on whether their *avat* (verses) were revealed before or after the Hijrah (the Prophet’s migration from Makkah to Madinah). The Qur’an is arranged in 30 *juz* (parts).  
  
Muslims regard the Qur'an as proof of Muhammed’s prophethood and the culmination of a series of divine revelations from Adam, the first prophet, and continuing with the Scrolls of Suhuf Ibrahim (Abraham), the Torah or *Tawrat* (Pentateuch) of Moses, the Book of Zabūr (Psalms of David, and the *Injil* (Gospel) of Jesus.
87cd43a9-2f34-5603-8fcc-c5f26dd19789.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
keywords: Noble Qur'an; Manuscript
materials: Ink, gold leaf and opaque watercolour on paper

88a1a2c9-da3a-59b6-88ec-2a538e5b82e2.name: *Flügelaltar (Winged Altar)*
88a1a2c9-da3a-59b6-88ec-2a538e5b82e2.description: The creator of this triptych, which was intended as a small travel altar for private prayer, was Jan van Eyck, the most important representative of Old Netherlandish painting. Characteristic features of his new artistic style are the miniature-like, extremely realistic rendering of details and the use of brilliant colours. Enthroned in the centre of the Basilica is the Madonna with her son, the infant Christ. Stretched out at her feet is a precious woven carpet. It has a rhombic pattern featuring eight-pointed stars set in circles. Its intense colours contrast with the muted hues of the ingeniously patterned floor tiles.

8965ef4e-0491-5348-8ff0-02681f79580f.name: Woman’s court robe (*conteş*)
8965ef4e-0491-5348-8ff0-02681f79580f.short_description: This *seraser* silk was discovered in the latter half of the nineteenth century in a monastery located in the historical region of Oltenia (southwestern Romania), probably at Bistriţa, where it was preserved as an ecclesiastical cope. A hundred years later, following ample restoration undertaken at the Museum, it regained its original form, namely that of a woman’s court robe. It can be assumed that the robe had been donated to the monastery by a boyar’s family, which testifies to the wealth and refinement of the Romanian aristocracy in the sixteenth century, given the fact that *seraser* silk was by far the most precious Ottoman textile, covered ‘from end to end’ with silver and silver-gilt thread. The robe features a design of large palmette garlands, outlined with green silk, each of which encloses a circular motif and a crescent. Between the garlands, circular motifs surrounding a star.

89b49f74-0b20-58b1-a4a0-9699eb76d737.name: Caucasian prayer rug
89b49f74-0b20-58b1-a4a0-9699eb76d737.description:
In Caucasus there is a great variety of motifs due to artistic exchange among ethnic groups. Different classifications of carpets are based on the weaver's ethnicity and the geographic origin of the carpet or the carpet structure. No system of classification is based on design or motifs. Therefore it is difficult to establish the origins of this peculiar rug.  
In the prayer niche there is a diagonally placed polychrome (white, yellow, blue and green) of small hooked medallions on a red background. These medallions resemble an *aina kochak* motif. In the upper part of the *mihrab* (prayer niche) there are two larger medallions which resemble hooked diamond medallions. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border is a “floral vine” border in red, blue and green blossoms (possibly carnation) on a white background. This type of border can be found in Kuba, Seishour and other rugs of the Caucasus. It may be used as either the main or a minor border. Two minor borders are *laleh abbasi* (abbasi tulip).

keywords: prayer rug; Caucasus; medahil

89f81d78-7886-5bf1-850f-f11ee861c1ae.name: Qur’an Pages with Case
89f81d78-7886-5bf1-850f-f11ee861c1ae.short_description:
Single pages of the Qur’an from Granada remain inside this box stitched of brown, black, red and white leather. Two leather covers without a spine mantle 1,172 loose paper sheets.  
  
Floral and geometric patterns in red and yellow ink surround the *ayah* (verses) in Arabic calligraphy. The Mudejar and Morisco read and wrote scriptures in Arabic as well as Spanish as distinct interpretations of the Qur’an.  
  
Since the forced expulsion of Muslims in the 15th century, very few complete samples of Qur’ans from Andalusia still exist. While Arabic calligraphy expresses a religious devotion as the worldly form of God's word, a gradual disappearance of Islamic schools in the Iberian Peninsula limited access for Muslims to study the Arabic language.

8a101d28-6d11-5832-8d73-47c11308f989.name: Letter from Father Joseph Yazbek to the Maronite Patriarch Yuhanna el-Hajj
8a101d28-6d11-5832-8d73-47c11308f989.short_description: A small but growing Maronite community settled in the Chinatown area of Boston in the 1890s. In 1893, the Archbishop of Boston, John Williams, assigned F. Gabriel Korkemaz as the first Maronite priest. He was succeeded by his cousin, F. Stephan Korkemaz, two years later, and shortly afterwards by F. Joseph Yazbek. At the time, the hundred-or-so families that formed Boston's Maronite community worshiped at the St. James' Church on Harrison Avenue. Father Yazbek later bought a four-storey building on Tyler Street, which he remodelled to include a chapel, social hall, and priest's residence. This letter is a copy of a letter sent by Father Yazbek to the Maronite Patriarch Yuhanna el-Hajj, inviting him to the ceremony dedicating the Syro-Maronite chapel to Our Lady of the Cedars of Lebanon.

8b569dc5-e1b2-50a0-b4d0-c169fc260f13.name: Engraved rock
8b569dc5-e1b2-50a0-b4d0-c169fc260f13.description:
This engraved rock bears an inscription of a poem consisting of 12 verses composed by Khalfan bin Rashid. The prose documents the completion of a well in the Wilayat of al-Hamra for the Governor Saif bin Muhammad ibn Sayyar in AH 1177 / AD 1763, during the reign of Imam Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi, the founder of the al-Busaid Household.  
  
The poem reads as follows:  
  
The Almighty granted the efforts with success  
The well has been built with mold and rocks.  
Its omens were like a magic,  
The area around seems heavenly, a garden full of trees bearing fruits.  
What a garden that burying sadness, with its flourishing beauty  
Blessed be its owner, the builder and those who dwelled in it.  
  
He , who had been freehanded to build the well, is Saif, son of Mohammad ibn Sayyar,  
And is the wise Wali of Oman, and the best leader.  
( )  
May the Almighty Allah protect him from the enviers, and those who are disloyal  
The best we conclude is by prayers upon the prophet Mohammad (Peace be Upon Him) as much of rainy clouds and more.  
In AH 20 Safar 1177, was written by (), Khalfan bin Rashid, ().
8b569dc5-e1b2-50a0-b4d0-c169fc260f13.provenance: Local acquisition – Purchased 2020 from Badar bin Mohammed bin Hamed al-Sinani

8c4c25d1-c138-5454-9937-8a71723f3492.name: Prayer rug
8c4c25d1-c138-5454-9937-8a71723f3492.description: The singular shape of the *mihrab* on Milas prayer rugs with its two side indentations can be traced back to 17th- and 18th-century Ottoman carpets. Here, a triangular indentation has been added at the bottom of the niche. The red ground of the *mihrab* is decorated with parallel rows of small red or white floral motifs. The inner side of the niche is edged all around with tiny blossoms. Different coloured stylised flowers identical in shape cover the white area of the spandrels. The rather unusual decoration of the wide border includes eight-pointed stars separated by red octagons. The warm colour scheme dominated by a strong red is typical of 19th-century Milas carpets.

8de9b633-bd8a-5dc3-8bc1-cea21fc40ec5.name: Seljuq Rug
8de9b633-bd8a-5dc3-8bc1-cea21fc40ec5.description: This is an outstanding example of the “Konya Group”. It is considered one of the earliest Turkish rugs found in the Konya Aladdin Mosque in Anatolia. The main border bears large stylized green *kufic* letters which are contoured with white on a dark blue background. This design gives a monumental image to the rug. Such monumental *kufic*script borders are characteristic of Seljuq rugs. The thin border framing the main border inside and out has eight‒cornered dark blue crosses. The stylized double diamond infinity motifs are a dark red on a light red background. One end of the double diamond motif is open and looks like tongs. The motifs have blue dots in the middle.

8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.name: Hanging lamp.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.description: A ceramic lamp with bulbous body and flaring neck, painted blue-and-white. The neck bears an inscription in angular *kufic* script between friezes of geometric knotted designs. Small split-palmette tendrils emanate from some of the letters. The words are illegible but may derive from the phrase 'wa-asu Sahwan' ('and they grieved distractedly'). Around the main body is a scroll of lotus blossoms with the distinctive 'tadpole' leaf common to a number of blue-and-white ceramics of this period. The row of elongated pointed panels around the shoulder of the lamp is a design that is also found on Ottoman silverware, and a motif that recalls Balkan silverware. This presents an interesting example of the innovative exchange both artistically and culturally that saw shapes, designs and patterns shift between different materials and between the cultures of Europe and Asia.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.short_description: Around the neck of this blue-and-white ceramic lamp is a *kufic* inscription of illegible words. Although modelled on a glass prototype, this ceramic lamp would clearly give little light. Its function must have been more symbolic or decorative than functional.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.method_for_datation: It is thought that this lamp came from the Turbe of Bayezid II (d. 917 / 1512), because of its close resemblance to a group of four lamps made for this building.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the main centre of production for ceramics of this quality in Ottoman Turkey.
8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.obtention: Bequeathed to the British Museum by John Henderson 1878.

8fd8864e-24a3-584e-8096-e0df273d81e1.author: Emily Shovelton
keywords: Blue-and-white; Mosque interior decoration

90125812-6d25-5c71-907f-5f0277cdf7b9.name: Mosque Lamp
90125812-6d25-5c71-907f-5f0277cdf7b9.short_description: Enamelled and gilded mosque lamps are a well-established type of glass vessel made in workshops of Syria and Egypt, both important centres of glass making during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods. This Mamluk mosque lamp has a globular body, a long-flared neck and a splayed foot. Six small loop handles are applied around its body. On the neck, two narrow horizontal bands with sketchy vegetal motifs outlined in red frame a broad register with red and white enamelled floral decoration on a blue background accented by three circular medallions with a badge that usually would refer to the donor. The body of the lamp shows another wide register containing a red outlined inscription on a blue background. The *thuluth* inscription reads: “izzli-mawlana al-sultan, al-malik, al- alim, al’adil" (Glory to our Lord, the Sultan, the King, the Wise, the Wise, the Just). The underside of the body shows the same floral pattern as the broad band on the neck. This mosque lamp probably belonged to a Cairene mosque as a donation from an unknown ruler, sultan or high officer. The floral decoration of the mosque lamp, however, is very similar to other mosque lamps belonging to the Complex of Sultan Hassan (r. 748-752 and 756-762 AH / 1347-1351 and 1355-1361 AD).
90125812-6d25-5c71-907f-5f0277cdf7b9.bibliography: Carboni, Stefano, *Mamluk Enamelled and Gilded Glass in the Museum of Islamic Art*, Qatar: The Islamic Art Society of London, 2003: 40-43, 5.
keywords: Glass; Mosque Lamp; Free-blown; Enamelled; Gilded; Mamluk
materials: Glass; free-blown with tooled, enamelled and gilded decoration

90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.name: *The Kiss of Judas*
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.description:
The sculpture represents a scene from the Gospel of St. Matthew (26:49) when Judas, one of the apostles, marks Christ with a kiss as the man who should be arrested and tried. As in the sculptures featuring Christ parting with Mary in the Heiligenkreuz Monastery Museum, Austria, and in the Bratislava City Museum, Slovakia, in *The Kiss of Judas* Giuliani concentrates – in the encounter of two figures – on the motif of instant motion typical of the work of Giovanni Bernini, a key baroque sculptor. The dramatic subject of Judas's treason is conveyed by means of the medium as a contrast in the approach to both figures: the figure of Christ is self-absorbed, resigned to his fate, characterised by calm gestures and static drapery flowing in large forms, while Judas approaches Christ in an expressively captured haste which the sculptor has portrayed, aside from Judas's step forward, by a dramatic gesture extended into space, as well as by Judas's clothes floating around the body as if blowing in a wind.  
The sculpture is unique, in that no associates or assistants participated in its creation, as was the case with Giuliani's sizeable works.  
Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice, and later in Munich under Andreas II Faistenberger. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy, in Moravia for the Kounics (Slavkov) and many times for the Liechtensteins (Lednice).
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.short_description: The sculpture depicting a dramatic scene of treason from the Gospel of St. Matthew exemplifies a typical baroque motif of instant motion. Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice and later in Munich. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy in Austria and Moravia.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.method_for_datation: The overall approach to shape in the figures is classic Giuliani. His authorship is confirmed by the execution of the faces as well as by the softly modelled and finely executed drapery of both figures, which complement not only the form but also become major interpretational elements of the content.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.obtention: The sculpture became part of the museum’s collections before 1962; its provenance is unknown.

91edb81f-fd53-5ef4-97f9-e53eac5c04c2.name: Saint Nicholas of Mozhaisk with Scenes from His Life
91edb81f-fd53-5ef4-97f9-e53eac5c04c2.description: Saint Nicholas, a 4th-century bishop from modern-day Turkey, is one of the most venerated saints in Russia. Stories of Saint Nicholas giving gifts to the needy and protecting children spread far and wide as people traveled or emigrated from Russia to other countries. In this icon, a full-length statue of Saint Nicholas is set in a *kiot* (wooden box). Painted panels with images of Christ and the Mother of God were once affixed to either side. In the center panel, Saint Nicholas originally held a sword in his right hand and a church in his left hand; both are now missing. The doors are illustrated with important scenes from the saint’s life.
91edb81f-fd53-5ef4-97f9-e53eac5c04c2.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Sotheby's Auction in 2005. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

9245b827-e2b3-5d39-ad6f-d1f2358eaffb.name: Fatwa on water management
9245b827-e2b3-5d39-ad6f-d1f2358eaffb.alternate_name: Legal opinion on water rights; Islamic jurisprudence manuscript
9245b827-e2b3-5d39-ad6f-d1f2358eaffb.description: This manuscript presents a fatwa—an Islamic legal opinion—concerning the management and distribution of water in Moroccan society. Issued by a religious jurist (*faqih*) in Marrakech during the AH mid-14th / AD mid-20th century, it reflects the pivotal role of Islamic law (*fiqh*) in regulating access to water as both a natural resource and a sacred trust. The fatwa provides guidance on conflicts between water users, allocation of irrigation turns, and the religious duty of ensuring fairness and equity in distribution. Written in Arabic script in clear, formal calligraphy, the text embodies the enduring connection among law, faith, and environmental stewardship in Morocco. Such documents illustrate how water, a scarce and precious resource, was historically governed through ethical and religious frameworks, complementing customary practices and communal agreements. Today this manuscript serves as a testimony to the moral and spiritual dimensions of water management, highlighting how Islamic scholarship reinforced the idea of water as a collective right entrusted by God. The manuscript’s presence in the museum underscores the continuity of faith-based governance and its influence on Moroccan hydraulic traditions.

92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.name: Key for the Ka’ba.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.description:
A single key that was used for the *Ka'ba* (meaning literally cube in Arabic). It consists of a ring (the diameter 3.6 cm) that is attached to a moveable cube-like shape with bevelled edges, and which is linked to the handle of the key. The handle consists of three small cuboids that alternate with two baluster-shaped separators. The body of the key itself assumes the form of an elongated cuboid whose cross-section is small in relation to its length, measuring 13 cm. The body of the key terminates with four protrusions.  
A number of inscriptions with religious, political and documentary significance ornament the key including a series of inscriptions written in *naskhi* script that appear on all three of the handle cuboids. The inscriptions, carved on four planes of the first, read as follows: 'It is He who has sent His messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to prevail it over all religion' (Qur'an: 'The Victory'; 48:28). The inscriptions written on the second are: 'By order of Allah, no God but Allah – Sha'ban ibn Husayn – in the year 765'; while the inscriptions on the third cuboid read: 'One of the things made for Bayt al-Haram (the Sacred House, the *Ka'ba*) during the reign of our lord the Sultan al-Malik al-Ashraf'. Thus, the inscriptions clearly indicate that the owner of the key was the Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Sha'ban ibn Husayn who began his reign on a Tuesday, the 15th day of the month of Sha'ban, in the year AH 764 (AD 1362), when he was 12 years old, and that he ruled Egypt and the Levant until his death in AH 778 / AD 1376. The key bears the date of manufacture, AH 765 (AD 1363).  
On the shaft of the key there are a number of inscriptions in Mamluk *naskhi* script, distributed over its four surfaces. These consist of the following Qur'anic verses: 'Verily We have granted thee a manifest victory: That Allah may forgive thee the faults of the past and those to follow; Fulfil his favour to thee and guide thee on the straight way. And that Allah may help thee with powerful help. It is He who sent down tranquillity in to the hearts of the believers to increase their faith'. ('The Victory'; 48:1–4). 'The first house \[of worship\] appointed for men was that at *Bakka* full of blessing and of guidance for all kinds of beings. In it our signs manifest; (for example), the Station \[*maqam*\] of Abraham; whoever enters it attains security; Pilgrimage thereto is a duty men owe to Allah – those who can afford the journey; but if any deny faith, Allah stands not in need of any of his creatures.' ('Al-Imran'; 3:96–7).  
It may be observed that the Qur'anic verses recorded on the body of the key complement the key's objective, and affirm the religious obligation of the *Hajj* (pilgrimage) on Muslims. In addition, the verses allude to the city of Mecca by the name 'Bakka' which is one of a number of names given to the city including, 'Umm al-Qur'a', 'al-Balad al-Amin' and 'al-Bayt al-Haram'. Likewise, the verses also point out the Station of the Prophet Abraham. According to Imam al-Bukhari, the intended meaning of the Station of Abraham is a rock, upon which Abraham is believed to have stood when he raised the building of the *Ka'ba*. The rock is located in proximity to the *Ka'ba* and is covered by a wooden dome, the interior of which is decorated with gilded ornamentation. The structure rests on stone supports, between which there are four iron windows.  
Egypt used to send the keys of the *Ka'ba* with the *kiswa* (cover) every year to Mecca. Despite the fact that the keys were presented every year, those housed in museums today number very few, and date back to the Mamluk and Ottoman periods. The Topkapi Palace Museum in Istanbul has acquired most of the *Ka'ba* keys, while the Islamic Art Museum in Cairo houses only this one *Ka'ba* key.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.short_description: Sultans and amirs sent gifts to the holy sites in Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem. This key was a gift from Sultan Sha'ban to the Ka'ba. It is decorated with verses from the Qur'an, ornamentation and inscriptions. A *kiswa* (covering) for the Ka'ba was sent with the key every year in the pilgrimage season.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.method_for_datation: The key is accurately dated by the inscription recorded on it.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.method_for_provenance: It is likely that this key was made in Egypt since it carries the name of the sultan of Egypt at the time and the year of production. That this piece was made in Egypt is further supported by the fact that Egypt was responsible for despatching the *kiswa* along with the key each year to Mecca.
92b6403f-d36a-550d-b953-dceb45d22cf5.obtention: This object was purchased in 1945 from a dealer of antiquities, Ralph Harari.

934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.name: Mosque lamp.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.description:
A large ceramic mosque lamp with a high flaring neck and a bulbous, almost pear-shaped body on a low foot. The lamp is divided into three registers by thin white bands. In the top register, around the neck, a Qur'anic inscription features part of the famous Light Verse (24: 35), which, because it likens the light of God to a lamp, was often used on mosque lamps. The lower two registers are decorated with floral motifs on the body which are painted under the glaze in turquoise, cobalt-blue, black, and red. Curiously, the floral motifs, most noticeably the large bisected quatrefoil motifs in red, do not line up between the middle and lower registers; perhaps the painter was working from a design not originally meant for an object of this shape. Around the middle of the lamp are large bosses alternating with handles, one of which is now missing. The loss of one handle may be the reason that the suspension chains have been riveted directly to the lamp's body.  
  
This 'lamp' – which would have shed no light, being made of ceramic, and is thus clearly meant to be symbolic – is reputed to have been made for the mosque complex in Istanbul built by Sultan Süleyman 'the Magnificent'. This complex was an important act of architectural patronage which provided a major stimulus to the Ottoman ceramic industry, centred at Iznik. One result was the addition of a brilliant red to the colour range of Ottoman ceramics. The clearly tentative quality of the red on this lamp, the thin and uneven application of the pigment, indicates that it comes from the early phases of the Ottoman potters' experimentation with the colour.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.short_description: A ceramic ‘lamp’ with a bulbous body and flaring neck. Although clearly meant to hang from a ceiling like a regular lamp, it would have shed no light, and is thus clearly meant to be symbolic. It is reputed to have been made for the Süleymaniye mosque complex, which was completed in AH 963 / AD 1557.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.method_for_datation: The lamp is supposed to have been made for the mosque complex built by Sultan Süleyman in around 963 / 1557.
934df7dd-8577-516b-8cc1-6742a0d27a2d.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.name: Incantation bowl
93ee1091-8763-5b6d-885f-d833bd95f55d.description: The bowl is inscribed in Mandean script, in Aramaic Mandean dialect. The text spirals from the bottom of the bowl about fifteen times around. The beginning of the text is unreadable because of a crystal deposits and blackening. The name of the sponsor, the beneficiary of these incantations, which is typically stated at the beginning of the text, remains unknown here. The remaining lines consist essentially of a repetition of names of demons exorcised by linked formulas, including the female demon Lilith, her ancestors (“all her families and lineages”), and her offspring. The Aramaic communities of Mesopotamia are heirs to ancient beliefs dating back to the Akkadian and even Sumerian texts, according to which demons were of an inexhaustible variety. The Mandean, because of his dualistic faith, believes in evil spirits whose harmful actions he dreads. Magic is therefore an essential aspect of his religious life. This practice, consisting in burying the cups thus inscribed at the four corners of the house, was widely diffused among the various religious communities of Mesopotamia until the Muslim conquest and beyond.

940aec1c-3a64-5908-99a0-bb3d302b70cd.name: The Noble Qur’an (single volume)
940aec1c-3a64-5908-99a0-bb3d302b70cd.short_description: The circle is an Islamic symbol of wholeness and unity and a quintessential element of Omani design. This is a recurrent theme throughout Islam culture as demonstrated by this example of the Noble Qur'an. Circular motifs and families of patterns are based on the mathematical division of circles into smaller geometric components. Hexagons, octagons, squares and triangles are used in combination with smaller circles and other geometric elements to form elaborate medallion-like designs known as 'roundels'. Roundels are featured in wood, plaster, copper and silver work and serve as a central motif on the *al-kummah* (men’s traditional embroidered cap). Contained entirely within a single circle, the roundel exemplifies the mathematical lucidity that characterises all Islamic art and architecture.
940aec1c-3a64-5908-99a0-bb3d302b70cd.obtention: Ministry of Heritage and Culture Collection
940aec1c-3a64-5908-99a0-bb3d302b70cd.scriber: Umar bin Salim bin Said al-Mahruqi
keywords: Noble Qur'an; Manuscript

94a5375c-0f26-51bb-b2ed-85c5c6b0cf18.name: Portière (*kapı perdesi*)
94a5375c-0f26-51bb-b2ed-85c5c6b0cf18.short_description: Used mostly to embellish garments, furnishings or household items, Islamic embroidery is also present on large textiles. The most important is *kiswa*, the cover enclosing the Ka'ba, which is sent every year to Mecca at the time of the pilgrimage. Over the door of the Ka'ba hangs an embroidery called *sitara*, decorated with inscriptions in different calligraphic styles. The present embroidery was probably destined to cover a mosque door. The rounded arch in the centre recalls the shape of the *mihrab* and its representation on prayer rugs. The entire surface of the cover, made from yellow, red, black, and turquoise pieces of silk, is decorated with cartouches and rosettes filled with vegetal and epigraphic motifs embroidered in the *dival* technique, i.e. over a base of paper or wool. The inscriptions, some of which were written in mirror-image, are illegible.
94a5375c-0f26-51bb-b2ed-85c5c6b0cf18.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania
94a5375c-0f26-51bb-b2ed-85c5c6b0cf18.obtention: Transferred in 1949 from the Toma Stelian Museum in Bucharest.

95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.name: *Minbar*.
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.description:
The *minbar*, a raised wooden pulpit used for delivering the weekly oration, or *khutba*, during Friday communal prayers, is one of the earliest types of Islamic liturgical furnishings, introduced in the time of the Prophet himself. When Nur al-Din (d. AH 569 / AD 1174) came to rule Syria and al-Jazira, he commissioned several important *minbars* as part of his propagation of piety and *jihad*. He assigned the execution of these wooden *minbars* to the renowned carpenters of Aleppo.  
This *minbar*, now located in the Museum of Hama, was commissioned by Nur al-Din as part of a new mosque he constructed in Hama in AH 558 / AD 1163. It consists of a narrow staircase attached to a raised chair with a covered top. Although it has lost its original stairs and flanking walls, the upper structure is entirely original. The raised chair is square with three arched openings and a back rest. A richly engraved and domed entablature crowns the top. Vegetal and geometric arabesques demonstrate a high level of wood carving. It also contains two historical inscriptions along the friezes on either side of the balustrades. The left inscription, which has been removed and hung above the mosque's entrance, speaks of Holy War and Justice. The right inscription, still *in situ*, emphasises Piety and Humility. The cornice also bears a Qur'anic inscription describing the wonder of God's Creation and the Heavens, while the back of the chair is inscribed with the *Shahada*, or declaration of faith, written in two lines of large *thuluth* script within a cartouche.  
Clearly, the *minbar* re-affirms Nur al-Din's political and religious position, a stance which is reiterated on the inscriptions of the mosque as well. The importance of the *minbar* lies in its symbolism of authority. The inscriptions carved upon it and the speeches delivered from its platform are visible and aural manifestations of the community's leadership and vision. In Nur al-Din's case, historical records show that he was meticulous in organising what was said on his behalf in the many mosques built in his name. The image he projected was one of piety as opposed to magnificence, humility as opposed to wealth, and always dedication to Holy War.  
Nur al-Din's dream of liberating Jerusalem is expressed by a similar but more richly ornamented *minbar* he commissioned for the Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, prior to its reconquest from the Franks by Saladin. Sadly, this *minbar* was destroyed by fire in recent history (1969).
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.short_description: Nur al-Din's *minbar* of Hama is an important example of Syrian woodcarving. Nur al-Din is known to have employed the most talented Aleppine carpenters to create a number of *minbars* which he distributed throughout the mosques of Syria in order to preach Holy War when the Crusaders took Jerusalem.
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.initial_owner: Nur al-Din Mahmud bin al-Zangi (r. AH 541–69 / AD 1146–74).

95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.method_for_datation: The inscription on the back of the chair reads “559” (1164).
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.method_for_provenance: The pulpit was originally in the Nur al-Din Mosque in Hama which was constructed by Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi in 558 / 1164.
95f0e5c9-0936-55b5-ae88-631dafd406d1.obtention: Although it was originally located in the Nur al-Din Mosque in Hama, the *minbar* is now in the Hama Museum.

9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.name: Carpet
9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.description:
The rug’s red-background, three-part prayer niche (*mihrab*) is supported by slender columns set on footings and arranged in a 1+2+2+1 formation. A carnation representing a lamp hangs from the peak of the central, higher arch and from each of the two outer, three-peak arches. The blue spandrels above the arches are decorated on each side by two arabesque-like curved leaves leaning towards each other and one serrated rosette; in the middle, the palmette growing out of the peak of the *mihrab* is surrounded by serrated leaves. The horizontal band, the frieze above the arch is filled with arabesque-like motives alternating with each other on a red ground.  
The main border contains undyed and red serrated rosettes sting along an undulating stem on ochre ground. The inner secondary border consists of small flowers of alternating orientation and colours. The outer secondary border is a succession of rosettes alternating with tree-of-life on a red ground.  
  
The provenance of the rugs is still uncertain, and so they are found referred to under a variety of names in the literature. Ernst Kühlbrandt, and later Emil Schmutzler mentioned this group of rugs as Säulenteppich (Kühlbrandt 1911, Schmutzler 1933), but later scholars, identifying their place of manufacture as the town of Ladik, designated them Ladik prayer rugs. In a 1968 publication, May H. Beattie called the Ladik origin into doubt and traced the six column type to 16th century Ottoman Court rugs, naming them, after the double column supporting the three-span vault, coupled column prayer rugs (Beattie 1968). Beattie classifies six column prayer rugs by the decoration in the spandrels above the arches. Ferenc Batári also considered there were insufficient grounds for asserting that the rugs came from the town of Ladik, he used the title ‘Ladik type prayer rugs’ (Batári 1994). Stefano Ionescu adopts the Beattie classification and maintains that the technical execution of the rugs is close to the other types found in Transylvania. He classifies column rugs by the number of columns, i.e. two, three, four, five and six column “Transylvanian” rugs (Ionescu 2007, p. 67–68). (Pásztor 2007, 137.).
9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.owner: Eszterháza Kulturális, Kutató- és Fesztiválközpont, Fertőd-Eszterháza

9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.method_for_datation: The six-column prayer rug, a version of Ottoman Turkish prayer rugs was very popular during the 17th century. Their general characteristic is a prayer niche (*mihrab*) whose background colour is red or ochre (and rarely ivory or blue), divided into three parts by slender columns in a 1+2+2+1 distribution.
9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.method_for_provenance: The carpet was exhibited at the 1914 Turkish Carpets from Transylvania exhibition in the Museum of Applied Arts in Budapest, it appeared under catalogue number 284. (Csányi 1914, 81). The carpet was published by Végh 1925, 24. Since then until xxxxxx the carpet's whereabouts were unknown. This carpet was the prototype of many  copies or forgeries made at  the Tuduc worshop in Rumania between 1925-1940. (Ionescu 2012, 94.)

96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.name: Mosque lamp.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.description: Lamp in the form of a jar with six rings for suspending it and a tall truncated cone-shaped foot. It has an inscription in duplicate on the neck and on the rounded part with the following text: 'This is one of the objects made for the mausoleum of Amir Alan al-Din Ali, son of his Excellency Sayf al-Din Baktamur, *al-hajib* (chancellor), may God grant him mercy.' Three blazons divide the inscription on the neck into equal parts, while another three blazons alternate with stylised arabesques around the lower section of the rounded part. The tall foot has three medallions with simple trefoil motifs. The circular blazon is divided into three fields: the upper and lower areas are white, while the central field contains the image of a horse with a structure in the form of a cupola on its back.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.short_description: The lamp’s inscription dates it to c. AH 721 / AD 1321: ‘This is one of the items made for the mausoleum of Amir Alan al-Din Ali, son of his Excellency Sayf al-Din Baktamur, *al-hajib* (the chancellor), may God grant him mercy’. The shape and decoration of the lamp are typical of the Mamluks.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.dates: Later than Hegira 23 Muharram 721 / AD 21 February 1321.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.dimensions: Height 31 cm, diameter (of rim) 21 cm, diameter (max.) 20.5 cm, diameter (of base) 13.5 cm.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.method_for_datation: Dated, according to the inscription, a short time after the death of the Amir Ali ibn Baktamur, on 21 February 1329.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.method_for_provenance: By expert examination, stylistic and comparative analysis and published catalogues.
96998c67-dbae-5a23-8da5-21ca0231218d.obtention: It came from the collection of Baron Gustave de Rothschild, purchased from Philip Sassoon through Joseph Duveen, in London, on 8 November 1919.

96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.name: Mosque lamp.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.description: An enamelled glass mosque lamp with a flaring mouth and squat body standing on a low foot. The glass is brownish, with decoration in blue and white enamelling, and highlights in red, green, yellow and gold. The decoration consists almost exclusively of an inscription in majestic *thuluth* script, with additional bands of exuberant floral decoration around the neck and just above the foot. The inscription includes verses from the Qur'an (83:22, 24–5) and the phrase 'Glory to our lord, the Sultan, al-Malik al-Muzaffar, the learned, the just, Rukn al-Dunya wa'l-Din, may God grant him victory'. This refers to the Mamluk Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II, who ruled only for a short period, from AH 708–9 / AD 1309–10, before being overthrown and killed. He did, however, govern with a fellow officer as co-regents for the captive al-Nasir Muhammad Ibn Qala'un, beginning in AH 698 / AD 1299. He also built a fine complex in Cairo, containing his tomb as well as a lodge for Sufis, between AH 704–8 / AD 1306–9. Inscriptions in the building – immediately erased by his successor – referred to him even then as Sultan. Since the Qur'anic inscriptions on this lamp refer to the afterlife, it may have been intended to hang in the tomb chamber. The lamp's decoration is also similar to that found in a large Qur'an that Baybars had commissioned for the same complex, suggesting that there may have been a team of designers consciously working to give a unified look to the decorative programme there.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.short_description: An enamelled glass lamp of typical Mamluk form, whose decoration is almost exclusively calligraphic. It includes Qur’anic verses and praise of the short-lived Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II. The verses refer to the afterlife, implying that the lamp may have been intended for the sultan’s tomb.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.method_for_datation: The lamp dates from the brief reign (708–9 / 1309–10) of the Mamluk Sultan Rukn al-Din Baybars II, to whom the phrase in the inscription, 'Glory to our lord, the Sultan, al-Malik al-Muzaffar, the learned, the just, Rukn al-Dunya wa'l-Din, may God grant him victory', refers.
96b73ca3-92f9-5650-8a53-7c417d5387ad.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that glass lamps like this were made in Cairo, as it would have been easier and safer than making them elsewhere and then transporting them.

97c84e4d-b5db-513a-8e7d-cfa06d0b62ff.name: In Thee Rejoiceth
97c84e4d-b5db-513a-8e7d-cfa06d0b62ff.description:
This icon is based on a famous hymn written by 7th-century saint and theologian, John of Damascus, to the Mother of God. The hymn includes the following text:  
  
All of Creation rejoices in thee, O full of grace:  
the angels in heaven and the race of men,  
O sanctified temple and spiritual paradise,  
the glory of virgins, of whom God was incarnate  
and became a child, our God before the ages.  
He made thy body into a throne,  
and thy womb more spacious than the heavens.  
All of creation rejoices in thee, O full of grace:  
Glory be to thee  
  
In this icon, the images of the Mother of God and Christ are serene while the choir of saints and people depicted at the lower part of this icon are animated and immersed in song. The landscape, with green trees on a white background, is symbolic of paradise. The crowd at the bottom of the image represents humankind, and the domes signify the church.
97c84e4d-b5db-513a-8e7d-cfa06d0b62ff.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2013. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Allegorical and symbolical figures; Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography; Angels

99095f8b-3eac-55bd-8d83-8bd6a4a69678.name: Qur’an
99095f8b-3eac-55bd-8d83-8bd6a4a69678.short_description: This *juz'* is the final section of a 30-volume Qur’an from Morocco, written in brown ink using *maghribi* script, developed in AH 4th century / AD 10th century North Africa. Sura headings are in Kufic script, the word Allah is highlighted in gold through the text. Verses are marked by polylobed gold markers, while groups of verses are separated by teardrop and circular shapes. Copied by Ahmad ibn ‘Ali, it was dedicated to Abu Muhammad Sayyid ‘Abdallah al-Ghazwani, a Sufi saints of Marrakesh.

998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.name: Prayer rug.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.description: A rug produced by peasant weavers in Ghiordes, Anatolia, famous for their tightly woven work with a short, silky wool pile. Ghiordes was one of the major carpet-making centres during the AH 13th / AD 19th century and both the design and colour scheme of this rug, a deep-blue niche framed with elaborate spandrels and borders, is typical of Ghiordes rugs. The niche confirms that this is a prayer rug, used to provide a ritually clean place for the five daily prayers. The niche reflects the *mihrab* or prayer niche in an Islamic mosque, indicating the direction to Mecca, towards which Muslims turn in prayer. It may also symbolise the gateway to Paradise. The ornament suspended in its apex may have a spiritual meaning.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.short_description: Every household in Ghiordes, Anatolia, had a handloom for the womenfolk and girls to weave small carpets and prayer rugs on. This prayer rug is decorated with an elaborate central niche reminiscent of the architectural prayer niche found in Anatolian mosques.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.holder: St. Mungo Museum for Religious Life and Art, Glasgow Museums.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: both the layout and weave of this rug resemble several other 13th- / 19th-century prayer rugs of this type, attributed to Ghiordes in Anatolian Turkey in particular.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

998d3461-0770-50eb-a5de-123b9ad0c56d.name: Healing basin
998d3461-0770-50eb-a5de-123b9ad0c56d.description: The base is low, and the body is hemispherical. Both the bottom and the rim are flat, while the centre is slightly convex. The interior and exterior are inscribed. The inside of the healing bowl is divided into thirteen mihrab-shaped sections. The base bears the inscription "Sahip Ali" in Ottoman Turkish.

9a411d81-270a-514a-a9ac-3f661d8e4f3e.name: Mosque lamp
9a411d81-270a-514a-a9ac-3f661d8e4f3e.short_description: This hammered brass lamp is decorated with openwork pattern inlaid with silver and a black compound. It was commissioned for the mausoleum of Mamluk ruler al-Malik al-Zahir Baybars (AH 620-675 / AD 1223–1277), constructed in Damascus in AH 675 AH / AD 1277. The inscription carries the words that plead God to sanctify the sultan's spirit and illumine his tomb. A tray would have accompanied this lamp, which when filled with oil and suspended, would have projected the inscriptions across the mausoleum.

9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.name: Processional cross.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.description:
A cross with *fleur-de-lys* outlines, with the upright and two arms intersecting inside a square, a flattened spherical node, and fitted into a tubular pole. The decoration of the field of the cross is formed by a continuous band which runs round the edge of the entire piece and contains lozenges and triangles inside it, filled with geometric and floral motifs. In the corners of the square into which the centre of the cross is inscribed there are four eight-leaved shapes. The reverse is similarly outlined by a band, with the branches and upright filled with plant-inspired geometric interlacing. A large circumference is formed in the centre, decorated with rather complex geometric interlacing, forming multiple centres, which are the most typical Islamic element of the decoration of the cross. The decoration and the strong likelihood that the metal was extracted from a North African mine suggest that this is the work of a craftsman of the Islamic peninsular communities, Christianised or otherwise, but obviously working for the Christian kingdoms of the Iberian peninsula.  
This type of cross had a twofold function: it served as a cross to be held aloft in processions and funerals, but was also able to be fixed to a base and used as part of the liturgical instruments on the altar.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.short_description: This cross of unknown origin would have been produced in the AH 8th / AD 14th century. The interlacing patterns, typical of Islamic art, at the centre of one side of the cross are particularly noteworthy. This piece would have been made by a Muslim artist working for a Christian patron.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.dimensions: Height 63 cm, width 37 cm, weight 1814.2 gr.
9adcd1ba-69fc-5d1e-b977-f72226d33bb1.method_for_datation: For stylistic reasons relating to the shape of the cross.

9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.name: *Antependium with the Tribute of Continents and Imperial Countries to the Holy Family*
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.description: This colourful embroidery was executed as a “needle painting” and is set within an original gilded frame. An eventful scene opens out with a central motif of columned architecture with staircases and balustrades, and adoring female figures. At the bottom left, four girls kneel, with the coats of arms of the imperial Electors of the clergy who facilitated the foundation of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno. The Archbishops of Treves, Cologne and Mainz are represented by the coats of arms of Karel Kaspar von der Leyen (1652–1676), Maximilian Heinrich von Bayern (1650–1688) and Johann Philipp von Schönborn (1647–1673). Opposite, four girls kneel with the coats of arms of the imperial countries: Bavaria, Saxony, Brandenburg and Pfalz. In the centre are four female personifications of the continents, Asia, America, Africa and Europe, in precious attire. The women and a host of lay people of both sexes pay tribute to the Holy Family. The Virgin Mary is supervising the education of Jesus, while St. Joseph hands to the Pope – a personification of the Church – a sheet with the text *Ecclesiae Petenti Satisfiat*. The scene is crowned with the dove of the Holy Spirit. At the sides are monumental summerhouses with decorative vases and cartouches with the inscription *Ite ad Joseph* (Go to Joseph), while the Old Testament quotation (Gen 41:55) relates to the figure of St. Joseph of Nazareth. In combination with the text on the donated sheet, it elucidates the subject of the embroidered antependium emphasising the role of St. Joseph, patron saint of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno, as a righteous protector of the church and promoter of Divine will. Towards the horizon, various landscapes alternate on the antependium, valleys and hills dotted with dominant castles. The intricate layout of the embroidery may refer to a major event in the history of the Franciscan convent or it could commemorate the establishment and construction of the Convent Church of St. Joseph in 1651–1653.
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.short_description: The subject of the technically and artistically remarkable antependium is derived from the legends of St. Joseph, a popular saint of the Baroque period. It is one of only a few examples of the use of figurative embroidery in sacred art during the first half of the 18th century, and a specimen of monastery art.
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.type: Embroidery and painting in original gilded frame
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.owner: Czech-Moravian Province of the Roman Union of the Order of St. Ursula, Prague (OSU Prague)

9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.name: Brass head of flagpole
9b0fa536-0fe5-5f95-ba19-41b4f81e9fd4.short_description: This mast, made of casted brass, bears an Arabic calligraphic decoration with the inscription "Oh God, Oh Muhammad". It is fixed on a pointed piece of copper with a hole at the bottom to install on a long wooden staff. In religious festivities such as a pilgrimage, various activities were organized. They would normally include festivals and rallies under flags and standards. The heads of flagstaffs were decorated with metallic items usually with Arabic calligraphy and some cosmic signs such as the crescent and the star.

9b960e40-8e8e-58fe-bdb1-3947c5bce14d.name: Textile fragment with white ground with the Virgin Mary and the Christ Child, surrounded by angels, tulips, roses and honeysuckle
9b960e40-8e8e-58fe-bdb1-3947c5bce14d.short_description: The image on the textile is of Our Lady of Victories (*Nikopoia*); she is holding the Christ Child, who has his arms outstretched in a gesture of the Crucifixion. Fabrics with Christian motifs were woven in the Ottoman Empire for liturgical vestments of the Orthodox liturgy and exported, Russia being an example. The Christian motif is framed by plants of Ottoman origin, such s the tulip and the honeysuckle.

9d51960b-dfb8-57bd-aa72-d264926dc7d8.name: The Presentation of the Virgin Mary into the Temple
9d51960b-dfb8-57bd-aa72-d264926dc7d8.description: This icon shows the presentation, or entrance, of the Virgin Mary into the temple. The story derives from the apocryphal book of James and is one of the 12 major feasts of the liturgical year, celebrated on November 21. This icon shows the child Mary before the priest Zacharias, father of John the Baptist. Mary’s parents, Anna and Joachim, stand with a group of maidens who also serve in the temple. Mary is seen again in the sacristy being approached by an angel.
9d51960b-dfb8-57bd-aa72-d264926dc7d8.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2007. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.

9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.name: *Pontifical Ceremonial Jug and Basin*
9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.description:
This oval basin, incised on its perimeter, is decorated with a strip of wrought ornamentation with festoons, grids, roses and a pair of *putti* heads. Its perimeter features a half-figure of St. John of Nepomuk, the patron saint of the person who commissioned the work. Opposite is a wrought oval label with a winged column representing the emblem of the Nová Říše Abbey, and engraved initials of the person who commissioned the piece, *N.A /W./P.N./C.G.* (*Nobilis Abbas \[Johannes Nepomucenus\] Wyminko, Praepositus Neureuschensis /C.G.*). Provost Jan Nepomuk Wyminko/Vejminko (c. 1683–1755) graduated from Hradisko, near Olomouc. He was provost of the Premonstratensian Abbey in Nová Říše from 1725 to 1732; in 1733 he was appointed the monastery's first abbot.  
The jug and basin are part of a luxurious set that included ceremonial cruets and a chalice (not preserved). The works, both in their shape and decoration, are derived from Augsburg models (for example, those created by masters of the Biller and Drentwett families). The jug serves for purification at the mass: the priest uses it to wash his hands before taking the blood and body of the Lord. Any spilt water is caught in the basin.  
Josef František Rossmayer probably took his apprenticeship in Prague and after journeyman's service abroad was appointed master in Olomouc in 1730. He made, among other things, candlesticks “in the Augsburg manner” for the main altar of the Sv. Kopeček Church, near Olomouc, a chalice with enamel figures of Christ's relatives for Brno cathedral and bindings for missals for the cathedral in Olomouc, in which he combined Augsburg and French models known from prints.
9f677e6f-1913-5ba1-b196-5a3e7d1c4fc7.short_description: The jug and basin are part of a luxurious set that included ceremonial cruets and a chalice. The pieces, from an Olomouc workshop, are derived from Augsburg models both in shape and decoration (compare, for example, those created by masters of the Biller and Drentwett families).

9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.name: Ship’s commode/oratory
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.description:
Oratories commonly belonged within a domestic context but an oratory desk was used either as a portable piece of furniture for religious purposes or as a cabinet-on-a-stand for reading. This particular oratory was used on board a ship and is the result of a cumulative commercial exchange among merchants who travelled via existing Portuguese trade routes to overseas colonies and ports or to north or north-western Europe. This is why it is probable that the ship's commode would have been influenced by several artistic styles: from Coromandel (the south-eastern coast of the Indian Peninsula), Chinese folding screens (*Henan*), or English Japanned furniture.  
Designed by Gaspar Ferreira and Manuel Silva, the commode was built to enable sailors and passengers to practice their religious routines on board ship. Probably commissioned by King D. João V, it is composed of two parts: the inferior part consists of three drawers and a desk with an oblique lid; while the superior section is shaped like a cupboard with a gabled segmental arch topped by the royal coat of arms.  
Carved and sculpted urns with flares decorate the top edges. Painted in bright red lacquer it has black decorative tablets and gilded iconographic motifs or *chinoiseries* – Chinese scenes. Both the design and ornamentation are characteristic of the so-called D. João V style. On the inside of the cupboard is an oratory with the following figures: St. Anthony of Lisbon on the right and St. Barbara on the left flanking Christ Crucified. The inside of the doors are painted with scenes of the Passion of Christ (Christ with the Cross; Lord of Cana Verde on the right; Christ tied to the Column and the Resurrection of Christ on the left).
9f83d7a3-3fef-5717-a3ed-b729ae98a77b.short_description: A large commode/oratory with a cupboard, for use on board ship. The black decorative tablets are decorated with vegetal elements, while Chinese scenery – known as *chinoiserie* – decorates the larger panels.

9ff5077e-cf93-5273-8105-87762d317700.name: *Ihram* belt
9ff5077e-cf93-5273-8105-87762d317700.short_description:
This *ihram* belt would have been worn by a male pilgrim, and used for carrying valuables while performing the Hajj rites. The *ihram* garment for men consists of two pieces of unstitched white cloth. One cloth (the *rida’*) is worn around the upper body while the other (the *izar*) would be worn wrapped around the lower body. This belt would have been worn around the waist on top of the *izar*. The inscription upon the belt wishes the wearer good health.  
As well as referring to ritual clothing, *ihram* also donates a state of mind in which a Muslim must enter in order to embark on Hajj. During this period, pilgrims must adhere to certain rules, for instance men and women are both forbidden from killing animals, uprooting trees, or cutting their nails or hair.

9ffa2249-250d-57c6-aa02-12cdbaa08791.name: Covered al-Buzuriyya Market
9ffa2249-250d-57c6-aa02-12cdbaa08791.description: The historic Buzuriyya Market is located south of the Great Umayyad Mosque in Damascus. This photo shows the very crowded market during Mawlid an-Nabawi (Prophet Muhammad’s Birthday). The Buzuriyya Market dates back to the Ayyubid era (AD 12th century). In the 18th century, the Ottoman government and several khans developed it together. In 1893, the Ottoman governor of Damascus, Hussein Nazim Pasha, replaced the Buzuriyya Market’s wooden roof with a metal roof. During Mawlid the market is decorated with colourful flags, especially green ones, and banners bearing the name of the Prophet Muhammad. Shops are filled with sweets, especially *Mulabbas*, which is associated with Mawlid and distributed in mosques and homes to all.

a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.name: *Presentation of the Child in the Temple*
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.description:
The production of knotted carpets in Portugal has been documented since the 14th century, mostly in association with the Moorish community. With the expulsion of the Muslims and Jews in 1496 by King Manuel I (1469‒1521; r.1495‒1521), the Portuguese carpet workshops were inevitably abandoned and the manufacturing tradition was lost. Aside from local production, Portuguese consumers imported high-quality items as well. This ensured the supply of luxury goods to the wealthier clientele. Despite that Spanish carpets were esteemed throughout the 15th century, according to representations in paintings, by the second quarter of the 16th century, they were replaced by Ottoman carpets produced in the regions of Anatolia and Uşak.  
Although, surprisingly, there are no surviving examples of this type of carpet in Portugal, its presence in paintings, as well as in other documentary sources such as in inventories, confirms their presence in Portuguese interiors, thus enabling us to identify the patterns and original colours of the imported carpets. This is the case with this painting, where a Turkish carpet, placed on the floor near the altar, displays most probably a “small-pattern Holbein” design: it comprises a repeated pattern of alternating quatrefoils and octagonal medallions, with *kufic* script motifs represented in detail on the red border.
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by José Alberto Seabra de Carvalho

a06054cf-1305-5f2c-b722-f5e5f3586c49.name: Sivas Prayer Rug
a06054cf-1305-5f2c-b722-f5e5f3586c49.description: Less well known than other regions, Sivas was an important centre for rug production. Sivas rugs are famous for their detail, an intricate design is created with a high number of knots per inch. This prayer rug is a beautiful example of a Sivas rug. Niche corners are decorated with stylized clove motifs and the *mihrab* niche is framed with four borders, from inside to outside. Very detailed plant motifs, including leaves and flowers are used to decorate the four borders.
a06054cf-1305-5f2c-b722-f5e5f3586c49.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

a319402b-f899-522c-a00d-0966b699e425.name: Cloth
a319402b-f899-522c-a00d-0966b699e425.short_description:
This devotional textile would hang from the ceiling or walls inside the Kaaba, the Muslim house of God in Mecca. Qur’anic verses in different calligraphy styles appear printed on red silk. Sultans would drape the Kaaba’s interior walls in silk from China or India as a religious offering since the Mamluk sultan al-Nassir Hassan in 1359.  
  
In medallions, *Tughra* calligraphy illustrates prayers and God’s names “the Merciful” and “the Generous”. The opening chapter of the Qur’an *al-Fatiha* and the *shahada* or declaration of faith rest between serrated lines in *thuluth* calligraphy.  
  
Protected from environmental factors inside the Kaaba, Muslim rulers would not change the interior silks annually but wash them twice a year. As a form of worship, the bestowal of this cloth would simultaneously achieve closeness to the shrine for blessings, reinforce the sanctity of the Kaaba and remind of the sultan’s power and prestige.

a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.name: Floor mat
a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.description: An almost complete mat has perimetrical bands with lozenge designs and triangular motifs. It combines brocaded decoration with self-patterned elements such as the beaded medallions in the centre. Two parallel lines of inscriptions are included in the composition and repeat the same word *baraka* (blessing) in a poorly executed *kufic* script. Geniza records describe how such reed mats were used to cover the floor surface and how detailed descriptions might be given to weavers in order to fill every available space. Based on this information, this small mat could be part of a larger commission, used to fill specific recesses or the entrance of a room.

a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.name: ‘Transylvanian’ rug
a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.description:
The term “Transylvanian” rug does not relate to the area of production but to the geographical region where many such rugs were preserved, that is, Transylvania. Rugs belonging to this group could be found mainly in Transylvanian churches. They were made in the villages of Anatolia during the 17th and 18th centuries.  
Size wise, Transylvanian rugs are rather small. Their most distinctive feature is a border filled with elongated, polygonal cartouches; however, sometimes, these are substituted by a row of simplified rosettes. The majority of so-called Transylvanian rugs are decorated with the double prayer niche, created from two *mihrab* niches in mirror image. They are mainly red, but some white-ground examples are known. “Transylvanian” rugs were very popular in Poland and many of them form part of Polish collections.  
The Kraków rug was probably made in Uşak. On the red field of the double niche, an indigo-blue cartouche of Uşak type joins with the pointed tops of the niches with flowering stems. The presence of such a medallion also suggests the place of origin of the rug. The lozenge-shape cartouche is decorated with a four-lobed motif inscribed within a double diamond, two palmettes situated on the vertical axis, and motifs of carnations and tulips as well. Placed along the edges of the cartouche are rows of graceful, small white flowers. The spandrels are decorated with lanceolate leaves and roses. The main border is filled with a row of rosettes and the outside borders with trefoil motifs.
a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis of the rather geometrised ornament suggests this rug dates to the end of the 17th century
a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.method_for_provenance: The “Uşak-style” central medallion allows us to presume that the prayer rug was made in Uşak, Anatolia

a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.name: Two Chinese blue-and-white porcelain sealed ‘Zamzam’ water bottles
a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.short_description:
Prophet was known to drink from the well and use the water for significant purposes. The most famous *hadith* (Prophetic saying) regarding Zamzam states that the water is good for whatever purpose it is intended. Thus, over time, the water has been used for many purposes: in graves, to prevent harm, to cure and in ceremonies to obtain blessings.  
Similar examples to these bottles are in the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul and were used during ceremonies involving the mantle of the Prophet. During these ceremonies the mantle was dipped in Zamzam water and what dripped from the cloth was then collected in bottles similar to these. Other comparable types were simply sent from Mecca to Istanbul containing Zamzam water and closed with leather, string and sealed with wax.  
The well is believed to have been discovered by Hagar and Ismael, after being abandoned by Abraham in Mecca. It was later rediscovered by ‘Abd al-Muttalib, Prophet Muhammad’s grandfather, who is credited with having dug several wells, most importantly that of Zamzam. From then on the responsibility of giving water to pilgrims was to remain in the lineage of one of his sons.  
Water from the well of Zamzam was previously collected in buckets by a rope pulley mechanism and then transferred to earthenware vessels. Now the well is entirely managed subterraneously by electric pumps and the King Abdullah Zamzam Water Factory produces approximately 200,000 bottles of water a day.
a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Hajj and the Arts of Pilgrimage Collection
a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.method_for_datation: Date and provenance based stylistic grounds and by comparison with similar items in the Topkapi Palace Museum.
