a878caed-2598-567c-80a3-7ec37561865b.name: Seljuq Rug
a878caed-2598-567c-80a3-7ec37561865b.description: Carpets from the 13th century Aladdin Mosque in Konya are known as the “Konya Group”. They were identified in 1906 as the first finds from this period. These carpets are of key importance in the history of World Carpet Art. This example was specially woven to be used in a mosque. It is decorated with religious motifs and*kufic*writing. A light blue eight‒pointed star design on a dark blue background covers the entire central field. The main border is divided into square sections with stylised*kufic* characters arranged back‒to‒back in light red on a dark red ground. On the small borders, bird motifs are stylized to form leaves on branches.

a96d02ab-fea4-5e29-9dc5-16c7773c9331.name: Ewer for Zamzam water
a96d02ab-fea4-5e29-9dc5-16c7773c9331.short_description: The ewer is unsual in that the cover for the mouth and the stopper for the spout are both screw-threaded, which allows them to be securely sealed in place. This implies that their purpose was more than keeping insects and the like away form the contents; rather, they were meant to minimize evaporation, a factor which has lead to the designation of such vessels as containers for Zamzam water. The somewhat flattened sides also allowed the ewer to be carried suspended from a saddle during the journey back from hajj. An almost identical ewer in the Louvre, Paris, which was on display at the Louvre Abu Dhabi in March 2018, still retains the chain which allowed the ewer to be suspended from the two loops on its sides, and which is now missing from the Khalili ewer.

a98d0e50-3029-5377-a2cf-b09ed33dce7b.name: *Hirz* (Necklace) with Qur’an case
a98d0e50-3029-5377-a2cf-b09ed33dce7b.short_description: The iconic *hirz* (necklace) with Qur’an case is imbued with religious significance, having as its central feature a rectangular or cylindrical box in which protective verses from the Noble Qur’an are kept. Qur’an cases may be simply strung on a silver chain or rope or featured as part of a much larger necklace as seen here with silver beads, coins and amuletic pendants. Smaller cases are also used as hair ornaments and incorporated in headdresses.

aa631f7f-3808-586d-b316-c8c2c17e2045.name: The Royal Doors
aa631f7f-3808-586d-b316-c8c2c17e2045.description:
In Russian Orthodox churches, the sanctuary, which contains the altar, is separated from the nave by a wall or screen called an iconostasis. A typical iconostasis has three doors. The “angel doors” are located on the right and left sides and sometimes depict the Archangels Michael and Gabriel. The “royal doors” are located in the center of the iconostasis and can only be entered at certain points during liturgical services by ordained clergy members. The use of the royal doors varies by local tradition, but they are typically opened during the reading of the Gospel and distribution of the Eucharist. The royal doors typically depict the Annunciation while the four evangelists are shown on four separate panels.  
This set includes the symbol for each evangelist: Saint John is shown with a lion, Saint Luke with an ox, Saint Matthew with a man and Saint Mark with an eagle, following the famous interpretation of Saint Irenaeus (c.120-202). The symbol for Saint Mark is different than the one depicted in The Mother of God of the Burning Bush icon in this collection, reflecting a difference in the interpretation of biblical texts by the iconographers for each image.
aa631f7f-3808-586d-b316-c8c2c17e2045.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2013. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Virgin Mary; Religious iconography; Angels; Allegorical and symbolical figures

ab4e426c-8d5c-55f7-aabf-1a580562cf9b.name: Prayer hanging
ab4e426c-8d5c-55f7-aabf-1a580562cf9b.short_description: Pieced together from numerous embroidered fabric scraps, this cotton hanging is suggestive of a mihrab, or prayer niche. The arched "niche" form at center is formed by juxtaposing light fabrics against dark reds. In the Qur'an, God (Allah) is likened to the presence of a lustrous lamp in a niche. Hence, lamps are often placed in niches in mosques and, similarly, they are depicted in niches on tile panels and textiles. In this textile, two stylized lamps extend outward from the top of the arch.

ab4e426c-8d5c-55f7-aabf-1a580562cf9b.holder: Shangri La, Doris Duke Foundation for Islamic Art
keywords: Carpet; rug; North Africa; cotton; mihrab; floral decoration; geometric motifs

ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.name: Qibla directional plate.
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.description:
Muslims must face the *qibla*, the direction of the Ka'ba in the city of Mecca, while praying. They therefore often need instruments to help pinpoint the direction of the Ka'ba. This plate is one such instrument. Its base is a round and flat area that has a circle of semi-vertical columns on it. Recorded around the centre of the circle is the name of the craftsperson and the place in which it was made (“made by Sayyid Thabit in Damascus”). Emanating from the centre towards the rim are tables in the form of a sequence of rings. These rings contain the names of a number of cities in three bands (Damascus, Baghdad, Constantinople, Jerusalem, Tehran, Kabul …), in addition to alphabets corresponding to numbers that indicate degrees of angles. The inner circumference of the plate's rim is marked by units, each of which is equivalent to five degrees and also the four cardinal directions (east, west, north, south), which are set in half circles.  
The exterior surface of the rim contains a two-line explanation in Arabic on how to use the instrument. In between these two lines are four medallions in which it is indicated that the plate was made by order of Sultan Salim I "the triumphant champion of justice and supreme ruler \[khaqan\] who is the son of the supreme ruler, king of the two lands and the two seas, and servant of the two sanctuaries, may God immortalise his rule". All this information is registered in black *kufic* script on a white background, and is covered with a transparent glaze.
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.short_description: The scientific diagram inscribed on this ceramic dish served an important function. A schematic arrangement of city names and trigonometric data help the user to establish the orientation of the Ka'ba in Mecca and thus the direction of prayer. It was especially useful when travelling.
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.initial_owner: Sultan Salim I (also Selim, r. AH 918–26 / AD 1512–20).
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.method_for_datation: The inscription on the plate indicates that it was made by order of Sultan Salim I, (r. 918–26 / 1512–20).
ab91307f-d3d5-5f2a-88d0-9f2eb6934a29.method_for_provenance: The inscription on the plate indicates that it was made in Damascus.

ac82d495-0ecf-5ced-bc7a-791a0ede9ca4.name: Milas Prayer Rug
ac82d495-0ecf-5ced-bc7a-791a0ede9ca4.description: This prayer rug was woven in the Milas region, one of the most important rug producing centres of Anatolia. It differs from typical Milas prayer rugs because it is without a *mihrab*. Rather, the design uses a central rectangle in place of the *mihrab*. The rug borders are decorated with rosettes, dragons and stylized clove strings arranged from outside to inside. The same motifs are repeated in the main ground.

ad7466a2-5fe7-545f-9873-cd226f645d31.name: Mosque lamp
ad7466a2-5fe7-545f-9873-cd226f645d31.description: Among the many forms of art present and flourishing on the territory of Syria, glassmaking was of particular importance. Syrian artisans seem to have been masters of the art, practicing various techniques from the earliest of times, for much of the best Roman glass was made in this area. The early development of glassmaking in Syria is primarily attributed to the Phoenicians, who previously inhabited the coastal belt. The mastery of techniques has continued into the Muslim period, since blown, moulded, and cut glass were made for the Muslim patrons. An essential aspect of the complete practice was the one of enamelled glass – a technique familiar to us from Roman times, but one that truly flourished and completely evolved under the Islamic rulers. A particular characteristic of this fruitful period is the decoration of a very distinctive form of lamp, with a large bulging base and upper section and narrow waist in between. Earlier examples are usually assigned to the 13th century AD, but the majority belongs to the 14th century AD or maybe even later. *Kufic* or *naksh* script were frequently the central element of decoration, whereas in Egypt, there was presence of motifs with heraldic significance. This magnificent example is decorated with gold, blue, red and green enamel, which create floral and organic forms, as well as arabesques.

ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.name: Sanctuary and Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard
ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.description:
The Cistercian Monastery of Alcobaça was founded as a gift to St. Bernard of Clairvaux shortly before his death on an estate granted by King Afonso Henriques (the first King of Portugal) in 1153. Having just conquered the Arabs, Afonso Henriques wanted to commemorate his victory, and foundation of the monastery was part of his strategy to consolidate his authority in the new kingdom. The Monastery is considered to be one of the best preserved medieval monastery complexes in Europe besides being a bastion of the Portuguese nationality.  
Sanctuary: as part of the New Sacristy, this Chapel was called the “Mirror of Heaven” by the eminent Portuguese art historian, Reinaldo dos Santos, due to its supreme beauty and spirituality. Building began in 1670 when Frei Constantino Sampaio was Abbot of the Monastery (1669–1672).  
With an octagonal plan, the interior is fully covered with gilded wood and is lit by a ceiling lantern. This light, filtered and diffused, enhances the theatrical atmosphere of the gilded and polychrome Baroque octagonal structure, which includes six horizontal niches filled by 89 reliquary sculptures.  
Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard: the sculptural ensemble in terracotta represents the Transit of St. Bernard. It was built when Frei Sebastião de Sottomayor was the Abbot of the Monastery (1675–1678). The ensemble can be divided into two groups: at the lower level is a group of free-standing sculptures and another of high-relief figures inserted at the back of the altar. St. Bernard is shown in agony at the centre of the scene, while close to his feet Cistercian monks mourn his death. Close to St. Bernard’s head, the kneeling General Abbot and a group of musician angles glorify his death. At the top, surrounded by two musician-angels and cherubs, the Virgin welcomes the soul of St. Bernard with opened arms. The life-size sculptures are built in overlapping horizontal blocks.
ae331064-372e-59a2-9ad1-641a18b7d070.short_description: The Monastery of Alcobaça was founded as a gift to St. Bernard of Clairvaux shortly before his death on an estate granted by King Afonso Henriques in 1153. The monastery became powerful due to donations throughout the centuries and contains several treasures, namely the Baroque reliquary Sanctuary and the Altarpiece of the Transit of St. Bernard.

ae7c39ba-6ec7-52c7-ab26-aa458671c2ad.name: Chasuble (Mass vestment for the Catholic liturgy) of Ottoman silk fabric with European woven borders
ae7c39ba-6ec7-52c7-ab26-aa458671c2ad.short_description: Bursa was an important hub of trade for Iranian silk and developed into a leading centre for the production of silk fabrics. As such, it did not only purvey to the Ottoman Court; silks from Bursa were coveted export goods for Europe, as is shown by this chasuble. At the same time, Italian silks were very much in demand in the Ottoman Empire. One consequence of this intensive exchange is seen in a reciprocal influencing of motifs, so that frequently technical details are the only characteristics that tell us where the silk fabric was woven, in Italy or in the Ottoman Empire.

ae7c4ab2-69d3-5454-816e-13b25357dc86.name: Multiple-niche prayer kilim (*saf*)
ae7c4ab2-69d3-5454-816e-13b25357dc86.description: The multiple-niche prayer carpets, called *saf* (from the Arabic word for “row”), are sometimes improperly referred to as “family” prayer rugs. They were used in mosques, their particular design allowing several people to pray one next to the other. Here, the uneven colour areas in the *mihrab* field, the somewhat irregular shape of the arches, and the stylised vegetal motifs are indicative of its tribal, probably Kurdish, provenance. Unlike most large Anatolian kilims, made of two narrow bands, this one is made of only one piece. The Arabic inscriptions and the fact that the carpet was dated make it all the more valuable.

af522df8-2bb6-5764-b5cf-7a2ae9be0f31.name: Kaaba Key
af522df8-2bb6-5764-b5cf-7a2ae9be0f31.short_description:
Silver-inlaid inscriptions embellish this bronze key attached to a moon-shaped ring. Its unique profile safeguards the house of God in Islam.  
  
The inscriptions bear religious and political messages, including Qur’anic verses and the name of Sultan Abd Al-Aziz, commissioner of this key in the 19th century.  
  
Prophet Ibrahim and his son Ismail are believed to have raised the sanctuary’s foundations, carrying a sacred tradition of guardianship. Today, the Shayba family preserves the key in a bag made of silk, gold and silver. As authorized keykeepers entrusted by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH), twice a year, they unlock the Kaaba for purification with rosewater and holy water.

aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.name: *Hajj Day*
aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.description:
Abdulhalim Radwi often evoked his hometown of Mecca, emphasising the importance of the Ka’ba as a source of universal energy and a religious symbol.  
In Hajj Day, the Ka’ba is surrounded by a central circle around which various elements of the composition revolve. The artist manipulates perspective so that near and far elements converge and intersect around the Ka’ba. Facial features are absent, and the artist has stripped the city of Mecca of all detail except for the main elements - the Ka’ba, the overlapping mountains and the pilgrims coming for the Hajj.  
  
In contrast to his colourful scenes, Radwi removes the vibrant colours in this work, opting for a monochrome palette to emphasise the unity of the elements under this universal energy. In his series depicting Mecca, the artist emphasises the importance of Mecca as a place of peace, where there is no difference between people, who are all there for the same reason regardless of their cultures or social status.  
  
Radwi often uses Arabic words and letterforms in his artwork, including religious expressions such as Allah; *bismillah*, or 'in the name of God'; *and la illah ila Allah*, or 'there is no god but God'), as well as other Arabic expressions. This demonstrates Radwi's commitment to incorporating an Arab and Muslim identity into his work. In addition, his continued use of visual symbols such as crescents and other motifs underlines the importance of these symbols as signs of cultural heritage.
aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art
keywords: Hajj; day; Mecca; Zam Zam; Zamzam

b1a4a767-03a6-5102-a4ba-95f407ea3166.name: Cope of Metropolitan Neophytos of Nicomedia
b1a4a767-03a6-5102-a4ba-95f407ea3166.short_description: This is a rare example of an ecclesiastical vestment made of *seraser* silk, the most opulent type of Ottoman silk entirely covered with silver and gilt thread. The loom-width design contains Chinese cloud scroll bands surrounding a large rosette reminiscent of a solar disc. A document of 1629 in the monastery of Saint John the Forerunner in Serres records the presentation of a “seraser cope” by the Metropolitan Neophytos.

b219c708-5c5d-5d57-9001-066f44ad30a5.name: Pen Case
b219c708-5c5d-5d57-9001-066f44ad30a5.short_description:
Intertwining geometric shapes, interlaced six-pointed stars and Qur’anic verses embellish the pipe-shaped pen cases. A pen or *qalam* is encased by the box called qalamdan which reveals another opening to fill with ink. In *kufic* calligraphy, the 35th verse from the Surat al-Nour stretches across the cylindrical body with the words “Allah is the light of the heavens and the earth”.  
  
Originating from Ottoman Syria during the 19th century, the pen box represents a group of religious objects belonging to Mamluk Revival metalwork. Taking inspiration from the bronze hammered objects inlaid with silver and copper, the revival ware is most often cast into the desired shape. The interlaced hexagram and calligraphy style are recognizable traits of Mamluk art.  
  
The art of writing the Qur’an reflects a significant form of worship, as the earthly materialization of God’s word. Writing tools, therefore, received exceptional attention, crafted from precious materials with Qur’anic verses as decorations. While the oldest qalamdan is dated 1148, Mamluk revival cases had a far-reaching influence in Europe and Asia.

b2648886-b553-5399-8946-93cb4e8f1c49.name: ‘Transylvanian’ prayer rug
b2648886-b553-5399-8946-93cb4e8f1c49.description: The term “Transylvanian” rug is used to designate 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in large numbers in the Saxon churches of Transylvania, whose provenance, considered once to be Transylvanian, is, in fact, western Anatolian. Some of these rugs feature the *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs; in most cases though, the prayer niche becomes a purely decorative element devoid of its original meaning, a fashionable motif popular with carpet buyers outside the Islamic world. Here, the plain red field of the *mihrab* contrasts with the main border richly decorated with alternating rosettes and palmettes encircled by lancet-shaped leaves – a simplified version of the classical court rug border. The flower on the pointed top of the *mihrab* symmetrically divides the composition with highly stylised carnations and serrated leaves represented in the yellow and blue spandrels; as such, different coloured spandrels are rather unusual.

b29465cd-3c48-54c4-8f56-a91ebfdc4e87.name: Mosque Lamp
b29465cd-3c48-54c4-8f56-a91ebfdc4e87.short_description:
Floral and geometric patterns adorn this bronze lamp to be illuminated a mosque in Jerusalem. Since the emergence of the first mosques, lamps made of ceramic, glass and metal lit religious buildings modestly; however, metal lamps endured as the most popular in Palestine.  
  
In the Palestinian territory, smiths crafted Christian and Muslim lamps in similar engraving styles and shapes from the Mamluk period, feeding their wicks with olive and other local oils. During Ramadan, the *muezzin* often suspended lamps in the minaret to light and blow out as an indication of fasting times.  
  
With its large bell-shaped body, Arabic inscriptions in *thuluth* script, and the six-pointed star of Prophet Sulayman (Solomon) for good luck, the lamp represents a typical example of Mamluk metalware to cast light in devotional buildings in the Levant until today.

b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.name: Monstrance of the Bemposta
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.alternate_name: Monstrance of the Chapel of the Palace of Bemposta or Palace of the Queen
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.description:
This magnificent monstrance in gilded silver and gold with a triangular base, sits on three volutes ornamented with floral motifs, ribbons and cartouches. On the three inferior angles of the base there are cherubs and three figures that symbolise Faith, Hope and Charity. On the top corners there are three full-bodied angels conveying Eucharistic motifs, while six cherubs and seraphs, overlap, ascending along the stem.  
On the three faces of the base oval bas-reliefs represent themes from the Eucharist: The Supper at Emmaus and the giant bunch of grapes, Fruit from the Promised Land and Christ at Calvary.  
The monstrance' sunburst is encircled by clouds. It has a radiant splendor with irregular rays, covered with precious stones. The monstrance's surface is entirely adorned with precious stones, some of them large and of excellent quality, creating a spectacular decorative and chromatic effect.  
The theatrical splendor of the Baroque is well illustrated through the use of jewels and quality chiselling, admirably assembled in a dazzling combination of metal and gemstones.  
It is likely the monstrance was commissioned by King Pedro III, husband of Queen Maria I. In Pedro III's Will of 1786 he foresees that his son, the future King João VI, should have the country house in Queluz, and urges him to care for the divine cult traditionally associated with the Bemposta Chapel, where he wished the precious monstrance to be kept.  
Attribution of this piece is controversial. Traditionally, researchers attributed it to J. F. Ludovice, the goldsmith and architect of the Convent of Mafra. Their theories were based on an existing drawing of the monstrance at the Museum, which also came from the Bemposta Palace.
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.short_description: A majestic monstrance in gilded silver with precious stones that creates a spectacular chromatic effect. The theatrical splendor of the Baroque is well illustrated through the use of jewels and quality chiselling, admirably assembled in a dazzling combination of metals and gemstones.
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.method_for_datation: Vassalo e Silva (2000) proposed that Adão Gottlieb Pollet both designed and made the monstrance. This is based on a specific analysis of the application of the gemstones. Although initially the  monstrance was dated to 1740–1750 the date is now thought to be later, 1775–1780.

b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.name: Pashmina Niche Rug
b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.description:
The new carpet style in the time of Mughal ruler Shah Jahan (1628-1647) was the flower style, featuring the naturalistic depiction of flowering plants. The refined elegance of the decorations, the use of expensive silk and pashmina and the high knot count are characteristic of the luxury carpets of this period. The silk warp was frequently dyed in bands. The flower style lived on in the works of the post-Shah Jahan workshops.  
  
In the field, the ivory-coloured *mihrab* (prayer niche) with lobed arch is adorned on both sides by a crimson half cypress growing from a finely delineated column base. From the apex of the *mihrab* hangs a trapezoidal lamp; in the centre below, a three-branched floral bush grows from the bottom of the *mihrab*. Faint glimmers of the colourful bands (ivory, yellow, crimson, blue and green) can be seen in the plain ivory surface. The crimson spandrel is adorned on both sides with symmetrical floral patterns – vines, leaves and poppy blossoms. As is typical of flower style rugs, the major border of the rug contains lotus flowers against a dark blue ground and is enclosed in ivory field minor borders.
b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.provenance: Kashmir or Lahore, North India or Pakistan

b5e98c52-08ad-5e05-97c5-2071372ff0ed.short_description: An offset pattern of lancet ovals is structured against a red background. b5eeb317-b1a2-5710-8891-111d70b464e6.name: Ewer for Zamzam water
b5eeb317-b1a2-5710-8891-111d70b464e6.description: Pear-shaped ewer with strap handle and serpentine spout. b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.name: Gospel cover of Dorotheos Proios from Edirne
b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.short_description: The gospel comes from Adrianople, but a handwritten note on the second page notes that: "…it was crafted and decorated here in Smyrna". From around the mid-eighteenth century Smyrna was the second most important port of the Ottoman Empire, and an important part of its economic life was in the hands of Greeks. The “Frankish quarter” and the preponderance of large-scale, foreign trade gave o cosmopolitan air to Smyrniot society. There is strong western European influence on this impressive silver cover made for Dorotheos Proios. Scrolled cartouches, thronging garlands of roses and conch shells in high relief make it a triumph of Rococo art, at least after the fashion in which it was understood in the Ottoman Empire. Smyrna was an important centre of silver production, but the designs were in general circulation and compositions were put together to fit the circumstances.
b65922f4-01d3-5457-a9bc-98f6df701f87.author: Ballian 1992, 86-7, no.46
keywords: Adrianople; Smyrna; Greeks

b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.name: Zamzam Water Bottle
b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.short_description: This simple, circular Zamzam bottle has been constructed from copper-alloy sheet and decorated with hammered and incised decoration. A very narrow cylindrical neck gives access to the body of the vessel, and a chain secured to its shoulder allows it to be carried. Every pilgrim to the Holy City of Makkah will make a point of drinking and collecting water from the sacred well of Zamzam, located near the Ka’bah within the precinct of the Holy Mosque at Makkah al Mukarramah. Its never ceasing flow is considered a miracle, and its properties are believed to aid good health and wellbeing. To this day, pilgrims to Makkah make a point of taking as much Zamzam water as they can back with them, not least to distribute it to loved ones and treasured friends in order to allow them to partake in the water's beneficial properties.

b81f4192-674c-5d84-b11c-20c80e67d288.name: Box
b81f4192-674c-5d84-b11c-20c80e67d288.short_description:
This Syrian bronze box is inlaid with silver and copper wire, displaying geometric patterns, interlaced six-pointed stars and Arabic calligraphy. Four legs ending in stylized paws elevate the casket to create suitable storage for a Qur’an.  
  
The ninety-nine beautiful names of God known as *al-Asma al-Husna* cloak the box in the *maghrebi* calligraphy style. The names of God add a protective layer to the Qur’an chest.  
  
This particular copper-alloy container resembles the Mamluk metalware from Syria in the 13th to 16th centuries with prominent features including silver-inlaying, palmettes and sumptuous geometric patterns. This type of Mamluk Revival art became increasingly popular in Egypt, Syria and Europe during the 19th century, at a time when the Syrian economy witnessed enhanced dependence on foreign merchants. As Damascene revivalist metalwork appealed to Europeans with Orientalist attitudes, local craftsmen attempted to emulate the older pieces.

ba8fded9-1679-518f-9ec9-6179d462f308.name: Prayer rug
ba8fded9-1679-518f-9ec9-6179d462f308.description: The composition of the central field recalls the triple-arch design of certain Ottoman court rugs; only this time the lateral niches are merely suggested and the columns are made up of decorative floral bands. The column bases also feature floral patterns, and, instead of the lamp evoking Sura An-Nur (“The Light”), a flower garland is hanging from the apex of the centre niche. The main border of alternating palmettes and rosettes is reminiscent of classical carpet borders (16th–17th centuries). Compared to these, the layout of the present rug is lacking in accuracy, which accounts for the incomplete motifs in the bottom left corner. The rug is however remarkable for the balanced palette of warm and cool hues and its exquisite workmanship, qualities not to be found in later Kula carpets which will resort to a more subdued colour range and a rather coarse weave.

bbc8f1e6-fdee-507b-9bb8-8b0201e8ff87.name: Recycled prayer rug
bbc8f1e6-fdee-507b-9bb8-8b0201e8ff87.short_description: On this recycled Moroccan prayer rug, a prayer niche indicates the direction of prayer towards Mecca. A mosque lamp makes reference to the verse of light in the Qur'an: "God is the light of heaven and of earth. His light [comes] as if from a niche, in which a lamp stands." (Sura 24, Verse 35). Two stylised hands indicate to those praying where their hands should come to rest. Uppermost is the invocation to God: "Allahu akbar" – "God is the greatest". The open hand symbolises the five fundamental obligations of Islam (confession of faith, prayer, charity, fasting, pilgrimage). At the same time, the hand provides protection against negative influences and evoke happiness and fertility.

bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.name: Mosque lamp for the mausoleum of Amir Aydakin al-‘Ala'i al-Bunduqdar
bc55917f-d0f7-5bd8-a131-1a210f5df63d.short_description: Mamluk amirs adopted emblems, often connected to their ceremonial roles at court, which decorated the objects and buildings they commissioned. Here the two gold crossbows against a red shield indicate that the patron of this lamp held the high-ranking office of *bunduqdar* (keeper of the bow) at the Mamluk court. The inscription states that the lamp was ordered for the mausoleum of Aydakin al-‘Ala’i, who died in Cairo in 1285.

bc7e3eae-5354-5ec9-bfb6-2bdb12fdb9ce.name: Gördes Prayer rug
bc7e3eae-5354-5ec9-bfb6-2bdb12fdb9ce.description: Gördes, in the Manisa Province, Anatolia was an important rug producing town during the 17th and 18th centuries. The name “Gördes knot” was coined for the symmetrical knot technique after the fame and popularity of the region’s rugs. However, the “Gördes knot” technique is older than the town and wide‒spread geographically. This example is a prayer rug. The niche corners are decorated with two trees of life. The head band is composed of rose and rosebud motifs. Various flowers motifs are used on the borders as an expression of heavenly gardens.

bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.name: Monstrance
bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.description:
The monstrance is by the Graz goldsmith, Hans Georg Pfisterer. The shaped oval base has enamel medallions showing scenes from the Passion of Christ and continues into a knob, shaped like a Baroque vase, from which rises the top part of the monstrance of the so-called sun type. Bands and foliate ornaments completely cover it intertwined with filigree and jewels. The opening of the ostensory has a six-sided moulded frame made up of wavy and angled sides and surrounded by airy filigree ornamentation of entwined scrolls and jewels that form flowers. Above the ostensory is a richly decorated canopy under which God the Father, holding the globe, hovers in clouds. Above the canopy is the dove of the Holy Ghost. At the foot of the frame, two adoring angels kneel on narrow decorated bases. The bottom edge of the monstrance has a lambrequin motif from which pearls hang.  
Bishop Juraj Branjug of Zagreb acquired the monstrance. He was one of Croatia’s most active bishops in 18th-century in the field of religious art building a new palace in Zagreb and renovating and building many churches. He had his own woodcarving workshop at Kaptol whose master craftsmen made altarpieces and pulpits adorned with the bishop’s arms for many churches. He bought and donated first-class liturgical objects to the cathedral.
bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.short_description: A so-called sun monstrance covered with filigree work, a series of bands and foliate ornaments, jewels and enamel medallions showing the Passion of Christ. Made by the Graz goldsmith, Georg Pfisterer, it was acquired by Bishop Juraj Branjug for Zagreb Cathedral.

bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.name: *Minbar*.
bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.description: This *minbar* is a mobile pulpit with eight steps supported by vertical walls ending with lateral arcatures linked by a ramp. Both the internal and external sides are decorated. The entire Andalusian decorative repertoire – vegetal, floral, geometric and epigraphic – has been employed. The sides and the back are framed with *kufic* inscriptions (Qur'anic text, pious formulas and three foundation texts). The characters are embossed, sculpted or inlaid. Marquetry and bone and ivory inlay have been used on the sides for chequered geometrical knotwork and the floral designs, in the shape of trees of life, crowned by arcatures that decorate the back and the risers. The variously shaped small polygonal wooden panels that fill the interstices of the geometrical knotwork are sculpted and carved with floral and vegetal motifs with an outstanding level of delicacy and precision that is reminiscent of and even surpasses the work on Umayyad ivory boxes. In addition to the sculptures and carving, the palette of colours and shades of the valuable woods make this liturgical object a masterpiece of the genre. One of the inscriptions says that 'Ali ibn Yusuf commissioned it from a workshop in Córdoba in AH 532 / AD 1137 for the Great Mosque of Marrakesh. The Almohad 'Abd al-Mu'min spared the *minbar* when he razed 'Ali's mosque in AH 542 / AD 1147. He put it in his mosque, the original Kutubiya and then transferred it to his second, current Kutubiya, where it was used until the 1950s.
bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.short_description: Made in Córdoba for the Great Mosque of 'Ali ibn Yusuf in Marrakesh, it was spared by the Abbasid 'Abd al-Mu'min and placed in his mosque, the Kutubiya. The meticulous, precise and subtle crafting of this item make it the only *minbar* to have survived to our times, a masterpiece of its type.
bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.initial_owner: The Almoravid monarch ‘Ali ibn Yusuf commissioned it for his Great Mosque of Marrakesh.
bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.dimensions: Height 386 cm, length 346 cm, width 87 cm.
bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.method_for_datation: The inscription engraved on the last upright on the left side reads: 'This *minbar* was made in Córdoba, God protect it, for the Great Mosque of the city of Marrakesh, God protect it, and its construction began with God's help on the first day of the month of Muharram in the year 532 (AD 1137), may God glorify the reward of its commissioner'. The inscription on the back arcature reads: 'May God help the prince \[of the faithful, 'Ali ibn Yusuf\] ibn Tashufin and his heir'.
bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.method_for_provenance: The place where it was made, (Córdoba) and its original location ('Ali ibn Yusuf's mosque) are mentioned in the inscription engraved on the back arcature: 'This *minbar* was made in the city of Córdoba, God protect it, for this great venerated mosque, may God help it to endure with the word of Islam. It was finished …' The name 'Aziz' engraved on the structure, discovered during restoration, could be that of a craftsman or foreman.
bde1bb31-4ed9-500e-8ed0-c80c51d8d0cd.obtention: Removed from the Kutubiya Mosque for preservation in 1962 and restored. Since 2005 kept in a room in the Badi Palace.

bf855ca5-82b9-5496-8eb9-62a39c53ba92.name: Cope of signed Safavid silk fabric
bf855ca5-82b9-5496-8eb9-62a39c53ba92.short_description: The cope, an important element in the array of Christian liturgical vestments, was fashioned out of precious Iran silk. At the time, the silk manufactories of the Safavid Empire were ranked among the highest-quality production centres in the world; their products were coveted export articles. This textile presumably found its way to Europe via the trade routes and was processed after its arrival. The fact that the silk is signed indicates the how highly it was valued by those taking part in its production.

bfdbe8a5-e335-5014-a461-8cecc5b16445.name: A complete cover for a Damascus *mahmal*, with the name of Sultan Mehmed IV
bfdbe8a5-e335-5014-a461-8cecc5b16445.short_description:
The *mahmal* was a ceremonial palanquin that represented the authority of the Sultan over the Holy Places. The Mamluk sultan Baybars (r. 1260 – 1277) is reported to be the first to have sent a mahmal with the caravan of pilgrims from Cairo, and the custom was continued under Ottoman rule and almost without interruption until the early 20th century. This, the earliest of seven mahmal covers in the Khalili Collections, is an example of a second mahmal which left Damascus with the caravan of Syrian and Turkish pilgrims. The Egyptian and Syrian mahmals were occasionally joined by a third mahmal from the Yemen.  
  
The embroidered Qur’anic verses are apposite: the text on the pyramid top is Qur’an, *sura* *al-Ahzab* (XXXIII), verse 56, which mentions the Prophet; the band around the lower part has al-Baqara (II) verse 127, which refers to Abrahim and Isma‘il raising the foundations of the House, that is, the Ka‘ba. At the very top, below the finial, is *sura* *al-Nahl* (XVI), verse 7: ‘And they carry your heavy loads to lands that you could not otherwise reach except with souls distressed’.

c13c410a-cc43-5e8b-8251-2f9bd6a4319e.name: Kula Rug
c13c410a-cc43-5e8b-8251-2f9bd6a4319e.description: Kula, Manisa Province was an important rug producing centre. During the 18th and 19th centuries they supplied the demand of international rug companies. Most Kula rugs, including this example are prayer rugs. The main component of prayer rug decoration is the *mihrab* and can be described as a stylized arch surrounding the prayer area. This is a double *mihrab* Kula rug with band stairs on both sides. In double *mihrab* rugs there are two *mihrab*s, one at the bottom of the image and the other at the top. This Kula rug with a double *mihrab* has eight borders, four wide bands and four narrow bands. It is decorated with an image of flowers in a vase.
c13c410a-cc43-5e8b-8251-2f9bd6a4319e.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

c147d8a2-97a3-5021-88ab-e73c8c00b9c1.name: Traveller's Qur’an Scroll
c147d8a2-97a3-5021-88ab-e73c8c00b9c1.short_description:
This parchment encapsulates the entire Qur’an. Tear-shaped leaf-patterns frame the holy book, which stretches across five showcases. The 114 chapters are written with horsehair with scripts illegible to the naked eye.  
  
Due to its shape and weight, Muslim travellers, in particular pilgrims, would carry this type of Qur’an, ensuring lighter luggage than traditional books. However, it is believed that Qur’an scrolls like this sample would function as a talisman or good-luck charm on long journeys rather than a book for reading.  
  
Today, smartphone applications make holy books accessible at your fingertips, while many global hotels provide religious texts for their guests.

c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.name: Parts of the St. Mary and St. Ladislaus altarpieces from Zagreb Cathedral
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.alternate_name: St. Mary and St. Ladislaus altarpieces
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.description:
The museum's altarpiece composition comprises parts of two altarpieces, that of St. Mary and St. Ladislaus. It has a central niche from the altarpiece of St. Mary – decorated with acanthus leaves, putti and bunches of fruit – within which the statue of Mary with the Child Jesus in her arms is standing on a half-moon entwined by a serpent. In front of the niche stand the statues of St. Ladislaus, the King, and St. Emeric, the Duke, which belonged to the altarpiece of Ladislaus.      
The composition, flanked by carved consoles attached to the wall, has the same ornamental decoration as seen in the central niche of the altarpiece of St. Mary; the consoles used to support painted altarpiece wings. Above them are the statues of the four evangelists, which were originally in the niches of the predella panel of the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus.  
In a contract of 1686, the sculptor from Ljubljana, Ivan Komersteiner, agreed to make the altarpiece of St. Mary for the apse of the north aisle of Zagreb Cathedral. In another contract of 1688, he agreed to make its pair, the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus, for the apse on the south aisle. Komersteiner was already a citizen of Zagreb with a workshop in Zagreb's Kaptol.    
The two altarpieces were identical in design: winged altarpieces with painted panels showing scenes from the Life of Mary on the altarpiece dedicated to her, with statues distributed on two levels and in the attic. Painted panels depicting scenes from the Life of St. Ladislaus decorated the altarpiece dedicated to him, with appropriate statues. While the wings from the altarpiece of St. Mary were destroyed those from the altarpiece of St. Ladislaus are kept in Zagreb City Museum.     
St. Ladislaus, the King of Hungary, was responsible for the foundation of the Zagreb Diocese.  
Komersteiner was responsible for the statues and woodcarving. Ivan Eisenhort and Bernardo Bobić collaborated on the painting and gilding of the altarpieces, while Matijaž Erlman began the work on the architecture for the altarpiece of St. Mary.  
The arrival of the sculptor, Komersteiner, to Zagreb marked the final entrance of the Baroque in the sculpture of continental Croatia. He brought with him as a novelty the ornamental decorative motif of Baroque acanthus, so-called Italian leaves, and his statues anticipate a new style expressed in the mobility of the slender figures of saints in characteristic counterpoise, freeing them from dependence on altarpiece niches.      
Komersteine's expression in his work has no direct analogies either in Croatia or in neighbouring territories, but the indirect influence of Italian art in his work is undeniable.  
During renovations in 1882, both altarpieces were removed from Zagreb Cathedral.
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.short_description:
A “composite” altarpiece composition comprising parts from the Altarpieces of St. Mary and St. Ladislaus originally designed for the apses of the north and south aisles of Zagreb Cathedral.  
During renovation of the cathedral in 1882, both altarpieces were removed and partially destroyed in the process. They were made by Ivan Komersteiner, a sculptor who worked first in Ljubljana and then in Zagreb. His arrival in Zagreb marked the final entrance of the Baroque to continental Croatia.
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.method_for_datation: Contracts from 1686 and 1688 in Acta capituli antiqua fasc. 101
c148a3a5-ac87-5785-bf74-013a0b3503df.obtention: In 1921, the Commission for Education and Religion gave the order to transfer parts of the altarpieces to the Museum of Arts and Crafts to protect the cultural heritage.

c2097e9b-56b2-56db-8332-8b268a5e48e1.name: Gördes double niche carpet
c2097e9b-56b2-56db-8332-8b268a5e48e1.description:
The rug-weaving areas of Anatolia are conventionally divided into western, central and eastern regions. Western Anatolian centres such as Uşak, Gördes, Kula and their vicinity have a long tradition of carpet and rug production. Carpets from these centers were very popular in Europe. Ghiordes is an Anatolian town northwest of Uşak. Rugs in this area have been woven at least since the 18th century and perhaps long before.  
This type of rug is often called Kiz Gördes. *Kiz* is a Turkish word for a girl or a bride, so these types of rugs were intended as a gift from a bride to her husband on their wedding day. In the central field there is a double niche with central hooked diamond medallion on a red background. Spandrels are fields with diagonal rows of florets on a light blue background. Above and beneath the arches there are two oblong fields with cloud band shaped flowers. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border is decorated with large motifs of flowers and leaves. The inner border is decorated with geometrical motifs. The outer border is the leaf and blossom meander border.

keywords: medallion carpet; double niche; prayer rug; Ghiordes; Anatolia
materials: Cotton, wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.name: Mosque lamp.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.description: An enamelled glass and gilt mosque lamp with a wide funnel-shaped neck and a rounded rim. The lamp has a squat body, steeply sloping shoulder and a flattened base, and a tall pedestal foot with a pronounced pontil mark on the underside. Six trailed suspension loops are placed around the body at regular intervals. The lamp is decorated comprehensively with enamel decoration executed in red, blue and light-green, embellished with gilding. Around the neck is a wide band of *thuluth* script executed in blue enamel, surrounded by a floral border. An excerpt from the Qur’an (*Sura* 2; verse 256), the inscription is interrupted by decorative roundels rendered in gold, red and green, each of which contain a little cup in the centre. The lower neck and upper body are decorated with floral bands interrupted by roundels with individual floral motifs. On the main body, another inscription in *thuluth* script gives the titles of the official who commissioned the lamp: Zain al-Din Mubarak who, according to the blazon above, was cupbearer to the sultan, al-Malik al-Salih, who is also named in the inscription. There were two rulers with the same titulature, both of whom were the sons of Nasir Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun: the first, al-Malik al-Salih Isma’il (r. AH 742–5 / AD 1342–5); the second, al-Malik al-Salih Salih (r. AH 751–4 / AD 1351–4).
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.short_description: Glass mosque lamps with enamelled decoration were commissioned in large numbers by the Mamluk elite in Egypt and Syria. Decorated with Qur’anic inscriptions and the titles of the patron, they were destined for the numerous mosques and *madrasas* endowed by the Mamluks throughout Cairo and the empire.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.method_for_datation: The appearance of the name of al-Malik al-Salih on this mosque lamp assigns the piece to the reign of either al-Malik al-Salih Isma’il (r. 742–5 / 1342–5) or to al-Malik al-Salih Salih (r. 751–4 / 1351–4).
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.method_for_provenance: Mosque lamps of this type were made in large numbers in both Egypt and Syria during the 8th / 14th century.
c3101633-812c-5595-969c-ee2b57886090.obtention: Purchased by NMS from the Major W. J. Myers Collection in 1900.

c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.name: *Bust of a Saint*
c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.description:
The bust, on an original volute pedestal, arises out of a relatively narrow base widening into a compact chest. The bearded head is that of an old man, with a cloak thrown loosely over the right shoulder. The figure might be St. Hieronymus, one of the church fathers. The pedestal shows that the object was a reliquary.  
*Bust of a Saint* demonstrates the artist's broad creativity seen not only his technical craft but also in his ability to capture mental states. The ecstatic expression of desire and submission to God is not rough-hewn, but has an elegant, court-like nature manifest in the figure's S-shaped movement and the soft shaping of the volume.  
Lengelacher may have familiarised himself with bust-making in his native Bavaria, or during a stay in Vienna through Giovanni Giuliani, who provided the gallery pews in the Heiligenkreutz Monastery, Lower Austria, with a whole series of busts. Lengelacher probably met Giuliani while working on the decorations of the Belveder in Vienna.  
In 1719 Lengelacher settled in Mikulov, where as sculptor to Walter František of Dietrichstein, he created sculpted interior decorations for several south Moravian churches. Lengelacher's *Bust of a Saint* is part of a series of original decorations for altar tables in the Church of St. Michael, Dolní Věstonice, which Lengelacher embellished with stuccoes and carvings. The artist worked there from the 1720s in relation to one of his first major commissions, the Benedictine church in Rajhrad (1727–1734).
c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.short_description: *Bust of a Saint* demonstrates both the artist's skill as a sculptor and his ability to capture mental states. The ecstatic expression of desire and submission to God is not rough-hewn but has an elegant, court-like nature. The reliquary bust is part of the original altar decorations in Dolní Věstonice.
c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.initial_owner: Church of St. Michael in Dolní Věstonice
c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.method_for_datation: The authorship and dating of the sculpture have been determined by its provenance and confirmed by an analysis of the style.
c37ef84c-4918-5c4a-89b2-3c585804a510.obtention: The bust and its counterpart were purchased in 1913 from a private vendor. It comes from the Church of St. Michael in Dolní Věstonice in South Moravia.

c4ba74ec-5d96-5dd1-9cc3-a2a1553b4630.name: The Solovetsky Monastery
c4ba74ec-5d96-5dd1-9cc3-a2a1553b4630.description: Savvaty, a monk from the Kirilov Monastery, founded a small commune on the island of Solovki near the White Sea in 1392. He left the inhospitable island in 1435 and died later the same year. The next year, the monk Zosimas moved to Solovki and built the first monastic cell, which eventually became a splendid and wealthy monastery thanks to a lucrative salt trade and plentiful gifts. Zosimas remained the abbot until his death in 1478.  The monastery, with its numerous towers and thick, fortified walls, is depicted in the lower half of this icon, and Saints Zosimas and Savvaty are depicted above the monastery, flanked by two angels. This icon’s large scale and thematic content suggest that the image was produced at the Solovetsky Monastery.
c4ba74ec-5d96-5dd1-9cc3-a2a1553b4630.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2006. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

c5864634-4eda-5afc-9805-0634535b6407.name: Religious coloured print: Protective hand with eye
c5864634-4eda-5afc-9805-0634535b6407.short_description: The raised hand with outspread fingers is universally understood by all people, regardless of language and culture: "Stop!" The protective hand and eye are inextricably associated with each other, in particular when it comes to defending against the evil eye, the envy of others. Material barricades, a symbolic eye or a repelling hand, should deflect danger and secure the continued existence of one's own family. A Turkish house blessing of the palm of a hand with an inscribed eye promises well-being and protection against the evil eye: "*Allahın dediği olur*"– "God's will be done."

c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.name: Tile Bowl
c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.description:
The bowl has a round and flaring rim. Its round body narrows towards the ring base. It is decorated with dark blue, green, red and yellow gilding on a white glazed ground. On the external part of the bowl, there are Surahs of al-Falaq and al-Ikhlas in medallions.  
Produced in China for the Ottoman market.
c5b5daa1-000f-54c3-95f9-2872725c902d.owner: The Republic of Türkiye Ministry of Culture and Tourism

c8a7c58e-d37a-5d59-9506-320c260a750e.name: Saint Nicholas of Zaraisk with Various Scenes
c8a7c58e-d37a-5d59-9506-320c260a750e.description: Saint Nicholas, a 4th-century bishop from modern-day Turkey, is one of the most venerated saints in Russia. He is known as a protector of the weak and poor. Stories of Saint Nicholas giving gifts to the needy and protecting children spread far and wide as people traveled or emigrated from Russia to other countries. In this icon, Saint Nicholas is shown full-length, giving a blessing with his right hand while holding the Bible with his left. He is flanked by images of the Mother of God and Christ. The images in the border depict important moments from his life.
c8a7c58e-d37a-5d59-9506-320c260a750e.obtention: From the private collection of Dr. Andreas Pittas. Purchased by Gordon Lankton from the Temple Gallery, London, in 2011. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

c9f822c3-3474-5596-90db-ee77387c77fd.name: *Cintamani* carpet
c9f822c3-3474-5596-90db-ee77387c77fd.description:
The *cintamani* carpet is one of the most impressive objects of the National Museum in Kraków collections and not just for its artistic features, but because of its huge dimensions (10m x 4m) as well. The central field is decorated with *cintamani* motifs: two golden wavy stripes combined with three white balls. In the background are small dark-blue multi-leaf medallions ornamented with “leaf” and “shield” palmettes grouped around the rosette motif. Medallions as well as *cintamani* motifs are arranged in net-like patterns – such a composition makes an impression of harmony. In the main border are white shields with bouquets of roses; among them are delicate, sinuous tendrils with palmettes interwoven with cloudbounds. Colouristically, the composition is balanced: the red ground contrasting with the white, yellow, blue and green pattern.  
Cairo was already a well-known carpet-weaving centre in the 15th century during the Mamluk dynasty. In 1517, the Ottomans captured the city and the style of the carpets woven there changed. The influence of the Turkish Tabriz and the Anatolian workshops became visible. This *cintamani* carpet, probably made in the second half of the 16th century, combines the graceful floral motifs of Persian-style carpets with a *cintamani* pattern characteristic of Ottoman Turkey. The *Cintamani* symbol originates from the Buddhist tradition. Adopted by the Timurids, it was known as the “Badge of Timur”. In the Ottoman Empire the *cintamani* motif was widely used in the decoration of everyday objects, i.e. garments, carpets, ceramics, symbolising the power derived from the pattern of the leopard- and tiger skins worn by rulers. The high artistic and technical quality of this carpet allows us to presume that it could have been made in one of the sultan’s court workshops.  
This *cintamani* carpet comes from the Corpus Christi church in Kraków. It was certainly used for the decoration of the church, probably on the floor. Oriental art was very popular in Poland during the 16th and 17th centuries, and textiles served to decorate both secular and sacral interiors.
c9f822c3-3474-5596-90db-ee77387c77fd.method_for_datation: Stylistic features, as well as the technique of execution (the asymmetrical, so-called “Persian” knot) allow us to suggest Cairo as the possible place of production

cba9697e-4726-5cc0-9a64-80be790a931d.name: Fragment of an interior Kiswa Cover for the Ka'ba in Makkah
cba9697e-4726-5cc0-9a64-80be790a931d.short_description: For four hundred years, the Ottomans sent money and gifts to Makkah and Medina with the Surre procession. The gifts included covers for the Ka’ba, made in Cairo and Istanbul, which were replaced every year. Old covers were returned to the palace in Istanbul, distributed to the faithful or sometimes reused.Textiles like this one were made in Istanbul and Bursa from the 10th century H/ 16th century to the early 14th century H/ 20th century. Woven in red and beige silk, they were intended for draping either the inner walls of the Ka’bah in Makkah or those of the Tomb of the Prophet in Madina. Their zig-zag design echoes that of the main kiswa but the religious inscriptions vary according to the textiles’ intended use. Here, the combination of texts with their emphasis on the Prophet suggests that this fragment was part of a hanging intended for the Prophet’s tomb chamber, which also houses the cenotaphs of his first two successors, the caliphs Abu Bakr and Umar ibn al Khattab.

keywords: Ka'bah; kiswa
materials: Lampas woven, red and beige silk

cbadcbe0-3272-59a1-a3b3-967703ee5993.name: Alms Vessel
cbadcbe0-3272-59a1-a3b3-967703ee5993.short_description:
Known as the Prophet’s *mudd* vessel, this bronze pot would collect and measure the alms given as charity by the people of Medina in Saudi Arabia. The cylindrical jar features the *basmala* or Muslim invocation and Qur’anic verses in *thuluth* and *naskh* script.  
  
Commissioned by the Naqib al-Ashraf, Mohamed Jamal Allah, the pot represents a replica of the original *mudd* vessel employed by Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) to gather and distribute charity money. Inhabitants of Saudi Arabia would quantify money using the Abbasid Islamic economic measure called *mudd*.  
  
With *zakat* (charity) as one of the pillars of Islam, wealthy Muslims are obligated to donate alms. Muslims base the amount of *zakat* on a surplus of wealth, rather than one’s income, while a minimum amount prevents the application of this tax. This minimum amount called *nisab* akin to the modern-day minimum wage determines who should give and receive charity. *Zakat* meaning "purity" or "purification" enacts a reciprocal gift-giving exchange, where the recipient and charity-giver accept blessings from God.

cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.name: Sacramento Monstrance
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.description:
An exceptional example of Baroque workmanship during the period of King João V, the Sacramento Monstrance – also called the *Anjo Custódia* “Angel Monstrance” – assumes the form of an Atlantis angel, a figure that is sometimes incorporated into the lower part of gilded wooden altarpieces. In this particular case the Atlantis angel appears free; instead of the usual representation as a pillar sustaining a globe the angel holds a radiant sun. Theatrical tension is undoubtedly achieved with the decoration of the piece itself, but the monstrance would have been surrounded by the gilded wood of the sacred space of the high altar and the aim would have been to increase the emotional and devotional fervour of the congregation and lead them to contemplate the divine light of truth and its beauty.  
Symbol of the Church Triumphant, the monstrance is a splendid composition of contrasting effects: dynamic lines and imposing shape – the result of which sees the elegant sculptural angel in polychrome and gilded wood – and the resplendence of silver, colour and glinting of both the enamel and glass.  
The kneeling angel holds a spherical, smooth and polished monstrance enveloped in a corona of silver rays. Surrounding the *luna* – the space where the host is kept and exhibited – are Eucharistic symbols enhanced by brightly coloured enamel work, and mounted over a circular base with eight ornamental silver-gilt cherubs. Vegetal motifs and coloured glass form flowers to complete the decoration. The monstrance presents a municipal contrast between the silver from Lisbon (L), in use since 1690, and the incomplete hallmark of an unidentified goldsmith from Lisbon, whose initials were LRP, and who was active between the end of the 17th century and the first half of the 18th century.
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.short_description: Holding the solar sphere made out of silver – glowing with the true Word of God – the Atlantes angel is supposed to increase the emotional and devotional fervour of the congregation and lead them to contemplate the divine light of truth and its beauty. This piece was probably the highlight of the gilded wood high altar at Sacramento Convent in Lisbon.
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.owner: Museu Nacional Machado de Castro, Coimbra
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.method_for_datation: This goldsmith’s hallmark first appeared in the early part of the decade of 1690 and continued to appear throughout the first decades of the 18th century. The technical and stylistic affinities of both the figure of the Atlantis angel and the polychrome allow the monstrance to be placed within the Baroque style during the reign of João V (1707–1750).
cbb6bbe3-72b1-5d00-b8a3-fc74f38248d4.obtention: The monstrance came originally from the Santíssimo Sacramento Convent in Alcântara, Lisbon. Founded in 1612, the convent belonged to the female branch of the Dominican order and was closed after the death of the last nun in 1897. The monstrance was transferred to Coimbra in 1914 where it became part of the gold and silverware collection of the National Museum of Machado de Castro.

cbc34421-cbf1-565d-b4bd-d91bdc792930.name: Rosette shaped part of the *minbar* of the Mosque of Ibn Tulun
cbc34421-cbf1-565d-b4bd-d91bdc792930.description:
The mosque of Ibn Tulun was built in Cairo in the 9th century AD, and was restored and renovated during the reign of the Mamluk Sultan Hosam al-Din Lajin in 1296. One of the most important items of the equipment of a mosque is the *minbar* – originally a raised seat – used as a pulpit, but having also a symbolic meaning as the "Throne of Muhammad". The *minbar* was decorated with stone or wood inlays.  
  
The *minbar* of the mosque of Ibn Tulun was one of the most precious. Its wooden decoration was exhibited at the World Trade Exhibition of 1867 in Paris as one of Egypt’s most significant craft works. After that, important pieces of the *minbar* reached numerous European collections.

cd8363f9-fa9a-5f8b-942e-3c9d931124ec.name: Saint Paraskeva
cd8363f9-fa9a-5f8b-942e-3c9d931124ec.description:
Saint Paraskeva was born to Christian parents during the reign of Emperor Hadrian. She was given the name Paraskeva (Greek for “Friday”) since Friday was the day of Christ’s crucifixion as well as the day of her birth. She was arrested during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius for preaching Christianity. He offered her great wealth and even proposed marriage if she renounced her faith, but she refused. The enraged emperor placed her in boiling oil, and when she did not show any pain, demanded to know whether she had used magic to cool the oil. She responded by throwing the hot liquid at the emperor, instantly blinding him. He asked Paraskeva for help and she healed him with water from a nearby stream. Antoninus Pius set her free, converted to Christianity and stopped persecuting Christians. The inscription on the scroll in this icon reads as follows:  
  
\[H\]ighly praised is thy name – of Father and Son and Holy Spirit, my Lord God – now and forever. For thou forgave me and did not reject my humility nor my prayer; and thy being pleased by me is incomprehensible.
cd8363f9-fa9a-5f8b-942e-3c9d931124ec.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2006. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.name: Pair of Torchères
cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.description:
These two grandiose torchères were ordered for the Chapel of Saint John the Baptist to be installed in São Roque church in Lisbon. With a triangular base, in gilt bronze, they form a pyramid held by titans. Above, a cornice developing into a dome is finished with Rocaille-inspired shells and a D. João V shield on each of the three surfaces of the torch holders. In niches below the dome, forming an oratory, the Doctors of the church are seated: St Jerome, St. Thomas Aquinas, Sr. Ambrose and St. Bonaventure, St. Augustine and St. Leo the Great. The hybrid ornamentation develops upwards in fluid volutes – wing, acroterion, cymatium – flowers in the shape of garlands, phytomorphic elements – rope, laurel and acanthus – and zoomorphic elements, as well as a variety of *putti* inspired by the Roman Baroque.  
They were conceived and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi with the cooperation of the metalworker Fellice Schiffone, the carpenter Lucano Celladini, Agostino Ancidoni another metalworker, and Lorenzo Morelli a silversmith and founder. Following the death of Giuseppe Gagliardi minor finishing and the lamination were concluded by his son, Leonardo Gagliardi, who like his father was a master silversmith.
cd9c5acc-6762-581c-8259-b6b3a0d9e694.short_description: A splendid pair of torch holders in gilt bronze and chiselled silver, they form part of a royal commission for the Chapel of St. John the Baptist. Designed and produced by Giuseppe Gagliardi, the metalworkers Fellice Schiffone and Agostino Ancidoni collaborated with him on the project. Lucano Celladini was the carpenter and Luciano Morelli was the silversmith and founder.

cdb915c1-3659-5399-a392-93205b57fd30.name: Carpet
cdb915c1-3659-5399-a392-93205b57fd30.description:
Following the 1834 abolition of Portuguese religious institutions, most of their portable heritage was transferred to the Portuguese State. The incorporation of textiles, including carpets, into State property is particularly relevant to the history and the creation of national museums and collections such as the National Museum of Ancient Art. This carpet, which has been in the NMAA’s collection since 1888, comes from the former convent of Estrela for which it had been commissioned by Princess Maria I (r.1777‒1816) after the birth of her son.  
Although building began in 1779, well after the date of this carpet’s production, its incorporation in the convent can be attributed to two reasons: as an offering from the Royal Portuguese House, owner of an impressive collection of Oriental carpets, to encourage offers from other donors, or even a transfer from another religious institution.  
The lack of documentation makes it difficult to ascertain its original function. These carpets were much appreciated and used as important decorative furnishings both in sacred and profane interiors, where they were meant to define spaces. One such example of physical delimitation lay in the use of carpets to cover the stairway and higher elevated daises that became an Iberian tradition within the female universe and lasted well into the 19th century.  
This carpet has undergone several restorative interventions, with its original size having been approximately a metre larger than at present; of almost eight-metres in length, this carpet shows a very balanced design and colour. It presents the classical ornamental motifs characteristic of this category, along with the field filled with “vine scrolls” alternating with palmettes and S-shape cloud scrolls (*tchi*). It also exhibits the characteristic contrast of colours between the field and the border (red/blue), both filled with palmettes and chinar leaves.
cdb915c1-3659-5399-a392-93205b57fd30.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by Jessica Hallet and Steven Cohen

cdc27ae7-3a64-5545-a795-1006d1e99c9e.name: Gördes Prayer Rug
cdc27ae7-3a64-5545-a795-1006d1e99c9e.description: This rug is an outstanding example of a Gördes prayer rug. The knot technique is not well suited for such detailed decorations. Nevertheless, complex stylized floral motifs are skilfully woven on the *mihrab* corners and borders expressing heavenly gardens. In contrast, the *mihrab* area is decorated simply.

d04a23e2-0c3a-5d55-be53-ebac7989ba2d.name: Gördes prayer rug
d04a23e2-0c3a-5d55-be53-ebac7989ba2d.description:
This prayer rug was made in Gördes, one of the best-known carpet production centres in Anatolia. Rugs from Gördes were very much appreciated in the West as well, because of their high quality and splendid, vivid colours. The rug preserved in the National Museum in Kraków is a fine example.  
At the centre of the Kraków rug, a bright-red *mihrab* indicates the direction of the Kaʽba in Mecca. A horseshoe arch is supported by the two delicate columns constructed from diamond shapes. Elegantly shaped ewers with flowers rising from them serve as the bases of columns. The vessels are another religious reference to recall the ablutions preceding prayers. In the capitals another significant motif from Islamic art is recognisable in the *cintamani*, meaning power and happiness.  
The ornamental and colouristic composition of the carpet is balanced. The most striking feature is the plain-red niche under turquoise-blue spandrels, which is filled with a scrolling ivory vine with contrasting red buds. The cross-panel above the *mihrab* is decorated with small palmettes much differentiated in colour (ivory, yellow, blue and red), against a dark-indigo background. The border is also highly decorative. The central, wide, dark-indigo border is filled with a rhythmical composition of large roses and palmettes, surrounded by smaller roses and carnations on leafy stems. The central border is flanked by the thinner ivory borders decorated with tendrils with flowers.  
Similar rugs are preserved in Austrian collections, the Wawel Royal Castle Kulczycki Collection and in the Ballard Collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
d04a23e2-0c3a-5d55-be53-ebac7989ba2d.method_for_datation: The floral ornaments that decorate this rug are rather realistic and elaborate, with a soft, fluent line; the presumption is that it dates from the 17th century

d0932db7-f1ba-5774-8b6f-19506abedc69.name: Ramadan lamp
d0932db7-f1ba-5774-8b6f-19506abedc69.short_description: During Ramadan, night becomes day. The silhouettes of the mosques shine with neon light. All of Cairo is lit up. The ninth month of the Islamic moon calendar is a festival of lights. It is the time of fasting and of religious reflection, of commemorating that at this time the Qur'an was sent down to man. From sunrise to sunset, believers are called upon to refrain from eating, drinking, smoking, and sexual activity. At sunset, the breaking of the fast is celebrated within the family circle with a lavish celebratory meal. Up until the final mealtime before sunrise, every house, mosque, and café is decorated with garish lamps. Afterwards, fasting begins again until evening. Individual objects which were once made of metal from tin cans and coloured glass have meanwhile been replaced by cheap plastic competitors "made in China."

d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.name: Prayer rug.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.description: A prayer rug that is typical of those produced in Ladik, a village near the city of Konya in central Anatolia. The rug has a red, central niche surrounded by three decorated frames. In the centre of the niche is an abstract tree-of-life motif springing from a stylised water-vessel. Above the vessel there is a rectangle with illegible text; above the tip of the niche there are a crescent and another rectangle with the date according to the hegira calendar, '1217' (1802) woven sideways. Made by the women in the village on a domestic handloom, the design for this type of prayer rug is inspired by the columned, court prayer rugs of the AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries. The women also reared the sheep, sheered the wool, spun it and dyed it. Ladik lay on the main pilgrimage route from north to south, and these rugs were made to supplement the villagers' income, and were, subsequently, presented to mosques and shrines in the area and beyond as pious offerings. One such rug appears in a 17th-century European painting, a still life by Nicolaes van Gelder, dated 1664.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.short_description: This prayer rug is an example of those produced in the village of Ladik near Konya in Anatolia. Made by the women in the village, on a domestic handloom, the rugs were sold to pilgrims who passed through on their way to Mecca. They in turn donated them to mosques and shrines on their return.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.method_for_datation: Woven into the rug is the date according to the hegira calendar, '1217' (1802) positioned in a rectangle above the tip of the crescent on top of the niche.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.method_for_provenance: Artistic analysis and comparison with other prayer rugs made in Ladik.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

d0d2ab0e-7d90-5e08-89b9-cfab8bae0d85.name: Section from the *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba
d0d2ab0e-7d90-5e08-89b9-cfab8bae0d85.short_description:
The pattern consists of zigzag bands alternately enclosing the *shahada* (‘There is no god but God, Muhammad is the Messenger of God’) and the invocation ‘O! God, May his Majesty be exalted’, the latter in mirrored script. It is possible that the calligraphy was designed by the master calligrapher, ‘Abdallah Zuhdi, who was known as *katib al-haramayn* (‘the calligrapher of the two holy sanctuaries’).  
Egypt had been supplying the *kiswa* of the Ka‘ba on a yearly basis, and almost without interruption, since Fatimid times. Since the early 1970s, however, the *kiswa* has been woven in a special workshop in Mecca.

d0d6c9d5-6ebd-5af5-9fa7-3367e09d88aa.name: Curtain for the door of the Ka‘ba, with the name of Sultan Ahmed I
d0d6c9d5-6ebd-5af5-9fa7-3367e09d88aa.short_description:
In her study of the Ka‘ba door curtains in the Topkapı Sarayı, Hülya Tezcan has identified four main styles. The earliest is that of a curtain bearing the name of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent and the date AH 950 / AD 1543–4. The second style, to which this curtain belongs, apepars to have been popular for a long period, as known examples date from the late 16th to the late 18th century.  
  
Characteristic features of this style include the five arches at the top, as well as the zigzag panels and the reciprocal ogival cartouches at the bottom. The commisioning order and date are in the two panels immediately above the latter. This curtain was commisioned and presented to the Ka‘ba by Sultan Ahmed I.

d199debb-1836-5a98-80c3-90ef128b824b.name: Glass Mosque Lamp
d199debb-1836-5a98-80c3-90ef128b824b.short_description: This mosque lamp may have been made in 19th century Hebron, a century-old Palestinian centre for glass manufacture that managed to survive despite the increasing influx of cheap, mass-produced goods from Europe. While its shape continues a style already popular in Mamluk times, its etched and gilt decoration relates closely to other neo-Mamluk artefacts produced for European tourists at the time.

d27da85e-f180-5ec8-90d7-7fdfc02299ee.name: Kırşehir Multiple‒niche prayer rug
d27da85e-f180-5ec8-90d7-7fdfc02299ee.description: This is a rug from Kırşehir Province, an important rug producing centre famous for its prayer rugs. This type of prayer rug ‒ locally called *saf*‒ has multiple niches that are side by side allowing three or more people to communally pray. There are examples of *saf* carpets as early as the 15th century. They were produced all around the Muslim world, but they were never in high production so they remain very rare.

d2a1fca5-7efb-5323-927c-0aaad478f6c1.name: Transylvanian prayer rug
d2a1fca5-7efb-5323-927c-0aaad478f6c1.description:
Turkish rugs arrived in Transylvania through trade. Almost all types of small-format Turkish classical rugs can be found in this region. The most numerous are the so-called “Transylvanian” group – prayer rugs with an undecorated field are widely dispersed throughout Transylvania. The term Transylvanian prayer rug is mostly used by Romanian authors such as Stefano Ionescu, Mircea Dunca, Andrei Kertesz and Alexandra Zigura, since it avoids specific reference to any weaving centre.  
The Transylvanian prayer rug from the Museum of Arts and Crafts is one of the oldest rugs in the museum collection. In the central field of the carpet there is an undecorated red *mihrab* (prayer niche) field. Delicate floral ornaments appear at the edge of the upper part of the *mihrab*. Spandrels are decorated with flowering-stems on ivory ground. The main border is in Ottoman style with rosettes and pine cones on yellow ground. Minor borders are vegetal on blue and red ground.

d2e14578-6d14-5f7d-85be-43b1df94ecf2.name: Mary with child
d2e14578-6d14-5f7d-85be-43b1df94ecf2.description: The Madonna, originally from Zurich and reminiscent of antique statues in posture and clothing, was imported from Northern Italy. It is an example of the reinterpretation of a sacred sculpture after the Reformation. It was used to represent the Haus Zum grossen Weissen Fräulein (house of the large white maiden) at Obere Zäune 12 in Zurich. The collection of stone sculptures in the Swiss National Museum is modest. Whereas sculptures south of the Alps were mainly carved from stone, wood was the preferred material north of the Alps.

d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.name: Font.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.description: Font with eight lobes. The inside is hollowed out, with the rim moulded on the top and on the outside. It has a hole at the bottom. The base is truncated, with a base or foot missing. The exterior moulding has a decoration of small engraved geometric patterns (lozenges, squares and circles). The upper rim has an Arabic inscription in *kufic* script running all the way round, in which it is possible to read the expression ‘al-Mulk’, repeated in a chain.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.short_description: The evidence for the prolonged presence of a Muslim community in Lisbon is supported by this octagonal ablutions font sculpted from local *pedra lioz* (lias) limestone. It was found during restoration work in Lisbon’s Moorish quarter, to whose mosque it belonged.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.method_for_datation: External, historical dating. The mosque in the Moorish quarter, to which it is supposed to have belonged, was dismantled in the early 16th century, in the reign of Dom Manuel I of Portugal.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.method_for_provenance: Found during urban regeneration work, re-used in the masonry of one the walls of the building on no. 67 Rua João do Outeiro (Moorish quarter, Lisbon). The building probably dated originally from the 16th century.

keywords: font; lias stone; Kufic script; al-mulk

d5063c4c-2fb6-5145-80ab-45cf9cbda6d3.name: Section from the *kiswa* of the Prophet’s tomb
d5063c4c-2fb6-5145-80ab-45cf9cbda6d3.short_description:
This section from a *kiswa* of the Prophet’s tomb belongs to a small group of fragments in which the finely calligraphed *thuluth* inscriptions are woven in silver-wrapped silk thread on a deep raspberry-pink ground. Selin Ipek has suggested that, given the amount of silver used in its weaving, the *kiswa* from which they come must have been a special commission.  
  
The vertical repeat consists of four wide zigzag bands alternating with four narrower ones; there are two horizontal repeats per loom width. The first wide band at the top of the textile has a supplication to God for blessings and peace upon Prophet. In the narrow band below that is *sura al-Ikhlas* (CXII), followed by the *shahada* in the wide band. Next is *sura al-Ahzab* (XXXIII), verse 56. The third wide band has *Allahu wala siwahu* (‘God and there is none equal to Him’), with a small flower under each of the words, Allah. Inscribed in the last narrow band in the repeat is *sura al-Qasas* (XXVIII), end of verse 88.

d56fbc83-d137-562e-8b49-e4ffd202595c.name: Censer
d56fbc83-d137-562e-8b49-e4ffd202595c.short_description:
The Chinese burner rests on three legs with Arabic calligraphy, reading the Muslim declaration of faith called *shahada*. During the Qing dynasty, this bowl would cradle incense to scent the air of a Chinese mosque.  
  
Although many regional Muslims could not read Arabic, the calligraphy endured as a decorative element. Because there are no Chinese characters to express the concept of a single God, Arabic words offer an effective medium to convey religious messages. As seen on the seal on the bowl’s bottom, artists utilized Chinese calligraphy to remark the ownership or production. The seal at the bottom of this censer reads "Ming Dynasty, Manufactured by Wu Bang Zuo, of Public Works in the 5th year of the Xuande Emperor." While the inscription alludes to the production in 1430, numerous incense burners have been produced with the apocryphal mark.  
  
Today, the Muslim-Chinese minority seeks to preserve their heritage including rare objects such as the Qing-metalwork, which have been lost or destroyed over time.
