d709dc46-d56e-5b96-833d-47202bfed1b4.name: Prayer rug
d709dc46-d56e-5b96-833d-47202bfed1b4.description: A lamp stands out against the indigo field of the prayer niche (*mihrab*) shown on this high-pile rug. Featuring a foliated scroll pattern, the olive-green spandrel is supported by two columns. Carnations decorate the upper level of the niche. A series of rosettes and palmettes interspersed with arabesques covers the ivory ground of the main border. This rug, which has 4,200 symmetrical knots per square decimetre, was made in Turkey during the first quarter of the 20th century. Positioned facing Mecca, the rug ensures the purity of the place of worship and creates a separate space for praying. Long ago, Muslims kneeled down and prostrated themselves on palm-frond mats or sheepskins. The field of a prayer rug usually shows a stylized representation of a *mihrab*, a niche made in the wall of a mosque indicating the direction of Mecca, towards which the faithful turn to pray.

d75b8026-c7bc-5c73-aacc-00b073b4d618.name: Double niche ‘Transylvanian’ rug
d75b8026-c7bc-5c73-aacc-00b073b4d618.description: The term “Transylvanian” rug designates 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in Transylvanian Saxon churches, which, once considered being of Transylvanian origin, were in fact made in western Anatolia. Some have a *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs, while others feature two opposing arches. Here, the red ground of this double niche is decorated with stylised floral motifs connected by geometric scrolls. A mosque lamp is featured at one end of the central field. Scalloped edge cartouches on ivory-white ground decorate the main border. At an early stage, the bright colours of this surprisingly well-preserved rug raised doubts about its authenticity. Still, a few other carpets from Transylvanian churches display a similarly vivid colour range; at the same time, over the past 100 years (ever since it was sent to Moscow in 1916) the rug has only been exhibited once, in 1994, which explains its excellent state of conservation.
d75b8026-c7bc-5c73-aacc-00b073b4d618.holder: The National Museum of Art of Romania

d75b8026-c7bc-5c73-aacc-00b073b4d618.obtention: Partial return of the Romanian treasure sent to Russia for safekeeping during the First World War

d7af68b8-a735-58da-b119-51e16cb51bde.name: Gilt copper candlestick
d7af68b8-a735-58da-b119-51e16cb51bde.short_description: This candlestick was possibly made for a religious context, judging by its curious inscription all along the vertical facets of the neck and around its base. While Arabic in appearance, it merely repeats individual letters and letter sequences. Such pseudo-inscriptions are not uncommon in Islamic metalwork, and some may have mystical significance.

keywords: Pseudo inscriptions; calligraphy

d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.name: The *Annunciation*
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.description:
Initially composed of four panels, this piece was originally of a different size. Recent tests have proved that its lower section has been cut on both sides. Prior to this recent modification, the work underwent further changes. The Virgin Mary is represented in the second condition of the Angelic Colloquium of the Mystery of the Annunciation, by Friar Roberto Caracciolo de Lecce (1425‒1495). That is to say, this is the moment of *cogitatio* or reflection, in which the Virgin considers the Angel’s words and demonstrates her prudence.  
Similar to other paintings alluding to this theme, the work bears witness to symbolism characteristic of representations of the Annunciation: the book that lays opened before Mary; the vase with lilies; the Angel’s sceptre; the bed, topped by its canopy and with its prominent front curtains, upon which the knots are formed; the column between the two characters, and the mat on which Mary is found standing.  
In recent years, the study of textiles through paintings, in its manifold categories, has proved to be very useful. Aside from documental sources and extant objects, paintings provide important visual evidence concerning an object’s trade and usage throughout time. In this particular painting, representing a Portuguese domestic interior, the Virgin Mary stands on a mat. Following the Islamic presence in the Iberian Peninsula, which stretched well into the 16th century, floors were commonly covered with mats, mainly in the summer, when they replaced carpets.  
Although this mat could be of Portuguese manufacture (Lisbon, Oporto or the Algarve) it has been associated with the mats woven with palm fibre and decorated with geometric patterns from sub-Saharan Africa, particularly those from the Congo (and Benin and Niger).
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.holder: Museum of Portuguese Decorative Arts – Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva Foundation
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.method_for_datation: Authorship was attributed to the Lourinhã Master (active between 1500 and 1540) by Luís Reis Santos in his work dedicated to this artist and published in 1963. This attribution has been rejected in more recent studies, thus it is classified here as the work of a follower of the master.
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.obtention: This was one of Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva's first pieces towards his collection of primitive artworks; donated by Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva in 1953.

Saldanha, Nuno, *Tesouros das Imagens, colecção Museu-Escola de Artes Decorativas Portuguesas – Pintura*, Lisbon: FRESS, 1996.

keywords: Portuguese painting; 16th century; School of the Lourinhã Master; the Annunciation

d97e8889-9ee3-5eb8-9ea9-a6732fa73dbd.name: The Mother of God Smolenskaya
d97e8889-9ee3-5eb8-9ea9-a6732fa73dbd.description: This Mother of God icon is known as a *Hodegetria* icon (Greek for “one who shows the way”). It is recognizable by the solemn expression of the Mother of God and the frontal position of the Christ Child delivering a blessing. The Christ Child sits on his mother’s left knee and holds a tightly rolled scroll. A copy of the original *Hodegetria* icon was brought to the Assumption Cathedral in Smolensk from Byzantium in the 12th century. In the 15th century, it was transferred to Moscow before being returned to Smolensk. The icon has a silver *repoussé basma* (hammered metal ornamentation) nailed to its surface, as well as a Kremlin School *cloisonné* raised halo dating back to the 17th century.
d97e8889-9ee3-5eb8-9ea9-a6732fa73dbd.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2001. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography
materials: Egg tempera on wood with silver basma, enamel

d9a8677b-3869-5fcc-91d3-50b6d8a59c46.name: Mosque lamp
d9a8677b-3869-5fcc-91d3-50b6d8a59c46.short_description: Mosque lamp with a cursive inscription reading: “This was made for our Lord the Sultan al-Malik al-Kujuk, may God protect him with his Grace and illuminate his mausoleum”. This lamp was made for the tomb of the Mamluk sultan al-Ashraf Ala` ad-Din Kujuk, ibn al-Nasir, ibn Qalawun, who reigned as a child for six months in AH 746 (AD 1341-42). In September 1345 he was murdered by his younger brother Sha`ban and his mausoleum was erected in Cairo in 1346-1347.
keywords: Lamp; Tomb; Al-Ashraf Ala` ad-Din Kujuk; Glass; funerary object
materials: Glass with gilded and enamel decoration

dd51c631-efa7-5621-9c17-104499a84fde.name: Textile fragment from a dalmatic of the so called *Heinrichsgewänder* (vestments) in the Alte Kapelle chapel in Regensburg
dd51c631-efa7-5621-9c17-104499a84fde.short_description: This fragment came into the MAK textile collection through a purchase of textiles negotiated by the Aachen Canon Franz Bock in 1865. Beforehand, it was part of the so called *Heinrichsgewänder* (vestments) in the Alte Kapelle chapel in Regensburg. The longitudinal, variously wide stripes detectable on the fragment, its interior structuring with rectangular fields and different patterning of the latter, lend credence to a provenance from Central Asia.

dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.name: Safi ibn Vali’s Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’)
dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.short_description:
Written during the year-long pilgrimage undertaken by the author, Safi ibn Vali, in 1676–77, the Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’) gives advice to prospective pilgrims on every aspect of the journey: which ships to choose, how to stay healthy, the places to visit, the rituals to be observed and the people one is likely to encounter. Safi ibn Vali’s own pilgrimage (he commenced his journey on 12 Rajab 1087/ 20 September 1676) was made possible through the financial help of Zib al-Nisa, a daughter of the Mughal emperor Awrangzeb, for whom he had written a commentary on the Qur’an.  
  
This manuscript belongs to a long-established tradition of guides to the Holy Places (see MSS 1038), although the illustrations here differ in that they combine the diagrammatic views normally found in such guides with vivid and colourful scenes of the pilgrims and their caravans. The illustrations are simple in their conception yet their attention to detail is acute. They provide a cogent picture of camp life of pilgrims in the late 17th century.  
  
The illustrations:  
  
View of the port of Surat and the ships carrying pilgrims (folio 2b). Surat, on the Western coast of India, north of Bombay, was one of the main points of departure to Arabia. The view is oriented to the south.  
The pilgrims’ ships crossing the Sea of Oman (folio 3b). The two larger ships carry pilgrims; one, on the right, appears to be casting (or raising) anchor. The smaller vessels may be fishing boats.  
The mish‘ar al-haram and the ritual of collecting pebbles (folio 10a). The painting shows the pilgrims in the region of Muzdalifa, in a state of ihram (ritual purity), collecting pebbles.  
The pilgrims in the town of Mina, being shaved, making sacrifices and casting pebbles at the Devil (folio 10b). This day corresponds to ‘Id al-Adha on 10 dhu’l-Hijjah, the feast commemorating the Sacrifice of Abraham. By this stage, the pilgrims, who are in a full state of ihram indicated by their white garments, have already completed their initial circumambulation of the Ka‘bah (the welcome tawaf); the ritual of running between the hills of Safa and Marwa (sa‘iyy) recalling Hagar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma‘il; the day of prayer at ‘Arafat – a most holy time when every pilgrim stands alone with God; and the gathering of pebbles at Muzdalifa in preparation for the stoning of the Devil at Mina. This recalls yet another chapter in the Abrahamic narrative in which Isma‘il stones the Devil seven times (the ritual is illustrated in the upper right-hand corner of the painting). After this a sacrifice is made. The pilgrims are released from most of the restrictions imposed by the state of ihram; men shave their heads and beards; women have their hair clipped. Pilgrims can now wear their normal clothes and leave for Mecca, where they perform another essential rite, a further circumambulation of the Ka‘bah known as the tawaf al-ifadah, which takes place on the same day.  
The birthplaces of the Prophet Muhammad; Fatimah; Abu Bak al-Siddiq; as well as the Madrasah of Sultan Sulayman, and a Bektashi lodge (folio 11b). These are shrines to visit in the vicinity of Mecca, which are not part of the hajj rituals.  
Plan of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca with the Ka‘bah (folio 12a).  
The camp of North African caravan of pilgrims (folio 15a).  
The camp of Egyptian caravan of pilgrims (folio 15b).  
The camp of the Syrian caravan of pilgrims (folio 16a). Unlike the pilgrims from North Africa and Egypt, the Syrian pilgrims are richly dressed and carry swords and gold daggers. Ahmad Pasha, the Syrian Amir al-Hajj, is identified by a caption (top left).  
The camp of the desert Arabs and the people of Najd (folio 16b).  
The camp of the caravans of the Indian (top) and Iranian pilgrims (folio 17a).  
Officials, scribes and secretaries (folio 17b). This is a small illustration, which is not captioned.  
Sharif Barakat, hakim haramayn sharifayn (‘Governor of the two Holy Sanctuaries’), riding to meet the envoy of Sultan Mehmed \[IV\], the Emperor of Rum (folio 18a).  
‘Abdi Pasha, the Amir al-Hajj of the Egyptian caravan, on his way from Mecca to Medina (folio 18b).  
The port of Mucha, in the Yemen (folio 21a). The illustration shows the pilgrims’ ships departing from the port as well as Sayyid Husayn, the Governor of Mucha, riding his horse (bottom right).  
The port of Jeddah (folio 22b). This view is very similar to that of Mucha (folio 21a) in that it combines views of the city and the pilgrims’ ships with one of the Governor of the city, Sunjuq.  
Man attacked by a lion (folio 21b); Man saved from the jaws of a lion (folio 23a); A feast (folio 23b). The three small-scale paintings are illustrations to a parable about a very poor woman taking pity on some beggars passing by and feeding them; her act of generosity was rewarded when a stranger saved her son from being eaten by a lion. The feast is probably in celebration of the son’s safe return to his mother.  
Script:  
  
Persian text copied in nasta‘liq; with 23 lines to the page.

df2d65a4-48bc-5ed0-b535-bf708ffef329.name: Set of Two-Sided Mineia Icons
df2d65a4-48bc-5ed0-b535-bf708ffef329.description: The *mineia* icons record important dates in the calendar year of the Orthodox church. Feast days and saints are arranged by date and labeled. The icons are usually painted in miniature, and a typical day can commemorate up to ten feasts and saints. This two-sided *mineia* was once part of a set of 12 with each tablet featuring one month. The Museum of Russian Icons has ten icons from the original set.
df2d65a4-48bc-5ed0-b535-bf708ffef329.obtention:
Collection of the late artist Petros Sasaki, who purchased the tablets in Finland in the 1960s to early 1970s. Sold by Christie's Auction in June 2008 to a private collection, USA. Sold by Macdougall's Auction in 2009 to a private collection, USA.  
Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Chelsea Auction (private sale) in 2014. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2021.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

dfeaa5f1-63bf-55dd-a784-98bce952f149.name: Minbar.
dfeaa5f1-63bf-55dd-a784-98bce952f149.description:
A wooden *minbar*; a double door (surmounted by a *muqarnas* frieze with traces of painted floral decoration) opens to a staircase of seven steps, at the top of which is a small landing topped by an onion-shaped dome. Almost all the exterior surfaces of the minbar are decorated with geometric patterns using wood inlaid with ivory plaques like a mosaic. Some of these patterns are quite bold, such as the 16-pointed stars and polygons on the triangular side panels, while others are more dense and complex, such as the pattern on the twin doors of the entryway. The *minbar* bears several inscriptions on carved wood or ivory panels. Some are Qur'anic verses; for example, 33:56 and 16:90 (respectively) are found above the front and back of the *minbar* doors. Other inscriptions praise Sultan Qaytbay and wish him a long reign.  
  
This *minbar* would have been used in one of the many mosques that Qaytbay either had built or renovated during his sultanate, although it is not known which one. This is one of the last Mamluk minbars to use ivory, as economic conditions made it a prohibitively expensive material in the final years of the dynasty.
dfeaa5f1-63bf-55dd-a784-98bce952f149.short_description: A wooden *minbar* (pulpit) with extensive all-over decoration including geometric patterns formed of inlaid ivory. This was probably used in one of the many mosques founded or renovated by Sultan Qaytbay, who presided over a period of great economic and artistic revival in the Mamluk lands.
dfeaa5f1-63bf-55dd-a784-98bce952f149.dimensions: Height 708 cm, width 113 cm, depth 304 cm
dfeaa5f1-63bf-55dd-a784-98bce952f149.method_for_datation: Inscriptions on the *minbar* name Qaytbay as Sultan and imply that he is still alive ('may God extend his rule'). Thus the *minbar* is dated to his regnal dates, AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96.
dfeaa5f1-63bf-55dd-a784-98bce952f149.method_for_provenance: How was provenance for object established: Cairo was the Mamluk capital and thus the likeliest place that an object of such quality would have been made.

e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.name: Monstrance of the Golden Sun of Moravia
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.description:
This vessel, used for carrying the Host – the embodiment of Christ's flesh – the presentation of which constitutes the spiritual climax of a mass, is one of the most precious specimens of the goldsmith's craft in Moravia. An oval incised base supports a vase-like *nodus* bearing a sunburst with an aperture lined with a cartouche, accentuated by a crest motif. The typically Baroque, intricately undulating ornamentation with faggoting encircles a case with a lunette, a crescent for holding the Host.  
The sun as the source of life, light and Divine truth lent its name to a whole group of “solar” monstrances contrasting with medieval monstrances which were spire-shaped with Gothic pinnacles.  
The decoration features certain older elements originally associated with objects now lost. The most interesting of them is an enamel label set into the back of the monstrance leg. It depicts St. Wenceslas on a Gothic throne – the emblem of the Olomouc Chapter – with the coats-of-arms of Emperor Ferdinand III (1637–1662), brother of Leopold I Vilém of Habsburg, Bishop of Olomouc and Archduke of Austria. The Gothic-style throne in the chapter emblem, supplemented with Dietrichstein wine-maker knives, possibly represents the actual “throne of St. Wenceslas” in the Olomouc cathedral, commissioned by Bishop František of Dietrichstein.  
The origin of the monstrance was once associated with Cardinal Wolfgang Hanibal of Schrattenbach, Bishop of Olomouc, who bequeathed a significant amount of money for its creation. In fact, the monstrance was commissioned by the Olomouc Chapter, headed by Dean Kašpar Florentin of Glandorf and Canon Jiří Jindrich Mayer of Mayerswald, who also commissioned a missal decorated with wrought silver (1733). In recognition of its high artistic value, the monstrance remained Chapter property even after an imperial decree issued after the Napoleonic wars ordered that all objects with precious stones be transferred to Vienna.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.short_description: This vessel, for carrying the Host, the embodiment of Christ's flesh, is one of only a few gold monstrances in Europe. The typically baroque, intricately undulating ornamentation encircles a case with a lunette, the crescent for holding the Host. The sunburst symbolises the source of life, light and Divine truth.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.method_for_datation: Marked with hallmarks, it is the only known work by a Brno goldsmith demonstrating close contacts between Brno and Olomouc, the two main centres of Moravia. Although goldsmiths of the same name were also active in Augsburg and Linz, their family ties have not yet been proven.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.obtention: Following extensive restoration, the monstrance, from the treasury of the Cathedral of St. Wenceslas Olomouc, is exhibited at the Archdiocesan Museum, Olomouc.

e1cf8f81-916a-549e-812c-671899736546.name: Prayer rug
e1cf8f81-916a-549e-812c-671899736546.description: The prayer niche is merely suggested here by two diagonals that do not meet. The field of the niche features two hands and above them, a floral motif, which is repeated all over the purple ground of the spandrels. The spandrels and the three narrow borders with a rich decoration of *boteh*s or tiny flowers connected by scrolls are in sharp contrast to the large beige *mihrab* field. Popular belief associates the hand motif with the hand of Fatima, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, and as such, it is often used to decorate talismans. Sometimes, the hand motif also appears on prayer rugs, mostly on Caucasian and Baluch rugs.

e2301ec1-c5b6-5d83-a402-0bf32d43fab0.name: Section from the belt of the Ka‘ba
e2301ec1-c5b6-5d83-a402-0bf32d43fab0.short_description:
The *hizam* (‘belt’) is an inscribed band that encircles the upper part of the Ka‘ba. During the Ottoman period, it was made up of eight sections – two on each wall – and this section would have been on the south side. It is embroidered with *sura al-‘Imran* (III), verses 95–97. The text refers to ‘the religion of Abraham’; ‘the first house of worship that was in Mecca’; and ‘the Station of Abraham’.  
The *kiswa* and its various components had been supplied yearly, and with very few exceptions, since Fatimid times. An incident at Mina during the Hajj of 1926 led to a break in the relation between Egypt and Saudi Arabia. As the season of Hajj approached the following year, and with no *kiswa* arriving from Egypt, King ‘Abd al-‘Aziz al-Saud ordered one to be made in haste at Dar al-Kiswa in Mecca. Due to the shortness of time, the *hizam*, of which this is a section, had to be machine-embroidered.

e2a17074-8d98-5cbe-9a65-83b0164d6179.name: Lamp
e2a17074-8d98-5cbe-9a65-83b0164d6179.short_description:
This mosque lamp is one of the oldest extant metal lamps in the Islamic world. Older lamps of silver and gold existed, but they were melted down long ago. A glass bowl held the wick and oil.  
The lamp’s decoration consists of an openwork, scale-like pattern surrounding a text from the Koran written in monumental *Kufi* calligraphy decorated with foliage.
keywords: Lamp; Kufic; Brass; mosque interior decoration

e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.name: The *Annunciation*
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.description:
The beginning of the second quarter of the 16th century marks the emergence of the representation of “Lotto” knotted carpets in Portuguese painting. These carpets, their name derived from the Venetian artist Lorenzo Lotto, who represented them in his paintings, are characterised by their geometrical, angular aesthetics lined up in a repetitive scheme. The Lotto carpets of Turkish origin probably reached the high-end Portuguese market through the Venetian export trade.  
The presence of these carpets in Portuguese interiors is mostly evidenced through representations in paintings, in particular those of the court painter Gregório Lopes (active 1513‒† 1550). In this representation of the *Annunciation*, the Virgin Mary stands on a Turkish carpet with a yellow, meandering arabesque pattern on a red field and a pseudo-*kufic* border. It’s relevance in the painting is reinforced by the artist, for he captures the very moment when the Archangel, as if suspended in time, places one foot on the carpet, and thus enters the sacred domain of the Virgin Mother. As such, the carpet is used as a device in the painter’s masterful depiction to mark the passage from one space to another, as though through a gateway.  
Interestingly, the opposing end of the same carpet is represented in another of Gregorio Lopes’s paintings, the *Presentation of the Head of Saint John the Baptist*, of around 1539 to 1541, a painting encompassing a ceremonial banquet in an aristocratic setting. In the *Annunciation* the artist takes the contrary approach, emptying the space of the splendour of the banquet, and replacing pageantry with a bare, peaceful interior befitting of the unfolding scene.
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by José Alberto Seabra de Carvalho
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.obtention: Transferred, an original altarpiece-painting from the church of the Monastery of Santos-o-Novo, Lisbon, Portugal, in 1911
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.bibliography: Hallett, Jessica and Pereira, Teresa Pacheco, *The Oriental Carpet in Portugal: Carpets and paintings, 15th‒18th centuries*, Lisbon: MNAA, 2007.
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.author: Ana Kol
keywords: painting; Annunciation; Portugal; Gregório Lopes; Lotto carpet

e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.name: Mosque lamp.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.description: A large glass mosque lamp with a flaring mouth, flattened lower section, and low folded foot. Six glass rings are attached for suspension chains. The lamp is decorated with gilding and enamelling which forms a design in several registers. The top section of the neck features a large inscription in bold blue letters. The inscription, which is divided into three sections by circular medallions praising the sultan, includes the beginning of the famous Light Verse from the Qur'an (24: 35): 'God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The likeness of His Light is as a wick-holder wherein is a light …'. This verse was a popular inclusion on lighting implements such as mosque lamps. The lower part of the neck has a band of sketchy decoration in red, punctuated by small blue medallions. The main part of the lamp's body features a dramatic network of fine interlacing patterns outlined in red against a blue background with floral elements. The interlacing is left clear, so that when the lamp was lit the patterns would have glowed. The bottom section of the lamp, the area above the foot, repeats the circular medallions from the neck.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.short_description: A mosque lamp of typical Mamluk shape, decorated with a bold inscription around the neck and a complex interlace pattern on the body. The interlace pattern is in outline, so when the lamp was lit – supposedly in the mosque of Sultan Hasan in Cairo – the interlacing bands would have glowed.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.initial_owner: Thought to have been made for the mosque and *madrasa* of Sultan Hasan (r. 748–52 / 1347–51 and 755–62 / 1354–61).
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.dates: Probably between hegira 757 / AD 1356 and AH 762 / AD 1361.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.method_for_datation: The lamp is said to have come from the mosque and *madrasa* of Sultan Hasan, which was built between 757 / 1356 and 762 / 1361.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.method_for_provenance: It is assumed that glass lamps like this were made in Cairo, as it would have been easier and safer than making them elsewhere and then transporting them.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.bibliography: Stanley, T., with Rosser-Owen, M. and Vernoit, S., *Palace and Mosque: Islamic Art from the Middle East*, London, 2004, p.28 and plate 14.
e36d1815-45d9-51df-ac24-e2a59050461b.author: Barry Wood
keywords: religious object; Mosque interior decoration; calligraphy; inscription; floral decoration

e3b0645a-dca5-537b-86d7-5a168c647274.name: Mineia, February
e3b0645a-dca5-537b-86d7-5a168c647274.description: The *mineia* icons record important dates in the calendar year of the Orthodox church. Feast days and saints are arranged by date and labeled. The icons are usually painted in miniature, and a typical day can commemorate up to ten feasts and saints. This February icon was once part of a set of 12 *mineia*, with each panel featuring one month in the church calendar.
e3b0645a-dca5-537b-86d7-5a168c647274.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from the Temple Gallery, London, in 2007. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Saints; Religious iconography

e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.name: Konya prayer rug with pelt
e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.description: Rugs with animal skins are a specialised category within Turkish carpet weaving. The earliest examples are seen in Anatolia from the 17th century. This rug has three borders. The first and third borders are identical. A sequential hooked “s” motif on white ground fills the interior. The main border is in the form of a band, with blue *Rumi* on red ground arranged in two winding rows. The branches of these *Rumi* are enriched with tiny palmettes. The animal pelt is stretched in a way to form the prayer niche of this rug with a red main ground. A ram’s horn motif on the top part of the spotted pelt design is on white ground that resembles red and brown panther spots. The same motif is found on the bottom short edge of the prayer rug.
e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

e6e39016-a178-5040-afd2-919c26cefc8e.name: Fertek‒Niğde Prayer Rug
e6e39016-a178-5040-afd2-919c26cefc8e.description: There are several towns around the Niğde Province including Taşpınar, Maden, Yahyalı, Yeşilhisar, Karapinar, Karaman, Bor and Fertek which were important rug production centres. Niğde was the regional market place, and rugs produced in these towns became known as “Niğde rugs”. This is an excellent example of a Fertek rug. It is distinguished from other Niğde rugs by simple but nice looking floral motifs. The head band of the prayer rug is decorated with stylised tulips. Eight point star motifs appear on the niche corners.
e6e39016-a178-5040-afd2-919c26cefc8e.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
e6e39016-a178-5040-afd2-919c26cefc8e.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

e750697b-0787-548a-a9e2-a530da438063.name: Mosque lamps
e750697b-0787-548a-a9e2-a530da438063.short_description: From 1356 to 1363, Sultan an-Nasir al-Hasan commissioned a mosque to be erected in Cairo. He decorated it most luxuriously with mosque lamps made of enamelled glass. The most magnificent of them were produced in the workshops of Aleppo and Damascus. In the mosque, they are suspended on fine bronze chains from the ceiling, reminiscent of the star-spangled heavens. They decorate the space more than they illuminate it. In accordance with the religious surroundings, their ornamentation is modest: some elegant arabesques, the initial lines of the famous verses of light from the Qur'an and a dedication to the renowned benefactor. Together with his crest, the mosque lamps announce his generosity and his wealth. In 1855, it is believed that two of these precious mosque lamps were brought out of Egypt by the Austrian archduke Ferdinand Max, the future Emperor of Mexico; he decorated one of the splendid halls of his pleasure palace near Trieste with them.
e750697b-0787-548a-a9e2-a530da438063.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
e750697b-0787-548a-a9e2-a530da438063.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.
e750697b-0787-548a-a9e2-a530da438063.obtention: Miramar Collection of Archduke Ferdinand Max, brother of Emperor Franz Joseph I, which was officially incorporated in 1878 into the Imperial Collection in Vienna.

e77d0bf1-58c8-5972-8f5a-b708fbd506b7.name: The Mother of God Umilenie
e77d0bf1-58c8-5972-8f5a-b708fbd506b7.description: The *Umilenie* (tenderness) Mother of God icons display touching images that depict the Virgin caressing her Child. The distinctive feature of this icon type is that the Christ Child has his face pressed against her cheek and one arm around her neck. Finely executed and balanced in line, color and composition, this icon, the earliest in the Museum of Russian Icons collection, is a particularly beautiful example of this motif.
e77d0bf1-58c8-5972-8f5a-b708fbd506b7.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from a private collection in 2000. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography

e79d0da8-0e74-53d4-8df3-5ad805dd038d.name: High Choir, Organs
e79d0da8-0e74-53d4-8df3-5ad805dd038d.description:
The dioceses of Braga and its archbishops was very important within the Catholic Church since the early Middle Ages, before the foundation of the Kingdom of Portugal, as well as throughout the Portuguese history namely in the Baroque period.  
In the North of Portugal during the 18th century there was an active workshop that provided important clients in accordance with the splendour and dignity of the court and religious life. Facing the need to replace the old choir stalls from the 16th century, Braga Cathedral commissioned Marceliano de Araújo and Miguel Francisco da Silva to design the monumental High Choir, the choir stalls and the gilded, carved wood organ cases in 1737.  
The whole set of the choir stalls made of carved and gilded wood includes two rows of seats, the cathedra for the Archbishop and in the centre a remarkable choir stand with the same decorative programme. Due to the major role of music within the Baroque Roman Catholic liturgy, Simão Fontanes was commissioned to build the mechanics of two impressive Baroque organs (1737-1738) with thousands of copper pipes, which are encased in magnificent cases made by Braga's woodcarver Marceliano de Araújo.  
The ceiling painting also belonging to this phase of the cathedral redecoration was executed by Manuel Furtado de Mendonça.  
The organs of the Braga Cathedral, commonly included within the category of the Iberian organs, are installed in two balconies over the central nave. The abundance of sculpture ornaments distributed from the base of the building to the top of the Cathedral allows us to include this artwork as one of the finest examples of the Baroque woodcarving in Portugal.
e79d0da8-0e74-53d4-8df3-5ad805dd038d.short_description: The choir is located at the west end of the nave and includes two encased organs and choir stalls. They are an example of the work produced in the 18th century by the Northern Portuguese workshop to supply important clients in accordance with the dignity of the court and religious life.

e8943284-2319-51c2-91bf-636b5313c45d.name: ‘Transylvanian’ prayer rug
e8943284-2319-51c2-91bf-636b5313c45d.description: The term “Siebenbürger” or “Transylvanian” rug recurs frequently in Oriental carpet literature. It is used to designate 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in large numbers in the Saxon churches of Transylvania, whose provenance has not been yet definitively established. Certain experts have indicated Transylvania as a possible source, whereas according to more research that is more recent they were produced in western Anatolia. Many “Transylvanian” rugs feature the *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs; in most cases though, the niche becomes a purely decorative element devoid of its original meaning, a fashionable motif popular with carpet buyers outside the Islamic world. This rug is a fine example of exquisite craftsmanship. The white field of the *mihrab* is decorated with floral motifs intertwined with geometric scrolls; a mosque lamp is hanging from the apex. Above the red spandrels decorated with similar geometric scrolls, a narrow rectangular panel features alternating tulips and cypress trees. Polygonal cartouches alternating with octagons fill the main border.

e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.name: Niche carpet
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.description: This carpet is among the most famous in the Berlin collection. As early as 1871 it was acquired by Wilhelm von Bode for the painter Heinrich von Angeli, but it was not until 1905 that Bode was able to buy it from his heirs and donate it to the Museum. Von Angeli and some of his colleagues depicted this carpet several times. The charm of this carpet lies in its depth of colour, its high, dense pile and the impressive sheen of the wool. On a dark blue ground, two red-ground spandrels are separated in the form of niches by a strong white line. Unusually, the spandrels blend into each other at their tops. The lower half of the niche field is filled with a light blue cloud band, in whose arc a large blossom forms a fixed point. This cloud band is reminiscent of delimitations in the so-called keyhole or Bellini carpets. Their often angular arch forms are associated with fountains, which were needed for the ritual cleansing before prayer. Because of the Persian appearance of the blossoms, the origin of the cloud band from East Asian cultures, and the use of depressed warps, this carpet has occasionally been ascribed to Persia. However, not only the colour palette and the reference to the keyhole motif, but also the use of a symmetrical knot, speak in favour of a location in Turkey.
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.method_for_datation: The carpet has been radio carbon dated. The carpet has been dated on stylistic analysis of its pattern, due to its colours and knot-technique
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.method_for_provenance: The carpet has been located on stylistic analysis of its pattern, due to its colours and knot-technique
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.obtention: Bought by Wilhem von Bode in 1871 for the painter Heinrich von Angeli; 1905 gifted by Wilhelm von Bode

keywords: Carpet; Prayer Capet; Niche Carpet; Cloudband; painting; Wilhelm von Bode
materials: Wool; knotted pile carpet, symmetrical knot

e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.name: Prayer rug with a row of niches.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.description:
This is one of three 'row' carpets of an early date in the collection of the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts which have survived from the 9th / 15th century to the present day. The composition has been organised into *mihrab* niches which provide a distinct space for worshippers in the mosque to pray in well-defined rows. It has survived as a fragment; the original dimensions of the complete rug are not known. The ground is white (cream). Within the sections outlined by dark-blue borders are five *mihrab* niches, two of them green and three dark-blue. The influence of the monumental *kufic* borders of AH 7th- / AD 13th-century Konya rugs of the Anatolian Seljuq period can be seen in the design of the rug's *mihrab*s. Each of the *mihrab* niches are crowned with a stylised ram's-head motif, while their corners have corner-pieces with dark-blue chequer patterns and red 'stalactites' hanging off them. In each *mihrab* there are three mosque-lamp motifs, one in the centre and two at the sides, hanging downwards. Four of the *mihrab* niches have diamond-motifs in their lower section, ornamented with motifs like arrowheads pointing in four directions. In contrast, the central niche has a diamond-motif in its lower section which is plain, as if the element of symmetry is meant to show the centre of the prayer rug.  
  
The pattern reminiscent of a double ram's-head in blue on a red ground, while it makes up the main border, is at the same time used to separate the rows from each other.  
  
The motifs on the narrow yellow-ground border which surrounds the main border resemble a chain of plaited yellow and blue rosettes. The geometric motifs carry on Seljuq tradition, especially their arrowhead-like corners which resemble *kufic* script. These, as well as the mosque-lamp and eight-pointed star motifs, prepare the way for the transition to Ottoman prayer rugs.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.short_description: The earliest Ottoman prayer rugs with multiple niches are dated to the AH 9th / AD 15th century. They were produced for use in the mosque to help the congregation to pray in straight lines. The prayer rugs (*seccade*) of this period with their geometric compositions and *kufic* borders are a transition to classical Ottoman prayer rugs.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.method_for_datation: Chemical analysis carried out on the original dyes used for this rug, together with analysis of the motifs and composition, point to a date of production in the 9th / 15th century.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.method_for_provenance: Rug-making is not widespread in the Eskişehir-Sivrihisar region. Moreover, in this period Konya was the most important centre for rug production, and since this example continues the Seljuq tradition, it is thought that it was woven in the Konya region.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.obtention: The rug was transferred from the Sheikh Baba Yusuf Mosque in 1911 as a result of a countrywide initiative to collect up artworks in order to prevent theft and plunder. The aforementioned mosque was built in 903 / 1498 in Sivrihisar, one of the first large sites settled by the Turcomans (Türkmen). Sheikh Baba Yusuf (d. 918 / 1512) was a religious scholar descended from Haci Bayram Veli (753–834 / 1352–1430), founder of the Bayramiyya branch of Sufism.

eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.name: Magic cup
eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.description:
The bowl is lined with inscriptions inside and out – verses from the Koran, the most beautiful names of God, religious and talismanic expressions – alternating with magic squares. On the outer perimeter, images of the zodiac and planets engraved inside medallions were scrupulously obscured at a later date with floral motifs, no doubt in order to avoid the association of the Koranic text with representations of living creatures.  
Consuming drinks or food in such cups, thus closely connecting religion, medicine, and astrology, permitted one to resist the effects of poisons, fevers, and other physical ailments. *The Thousand and One Nights* invoked a divinatory purpose too.
eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute
eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.dates: Hegira 11th - 1st quarter of 14th century / AD 17th and 19th century
eb9313ce-3a64-5d73-bea2-13a7a7012be8.bibliography:
Delpont, E., et al., *Album du musée*, Paris: Somogy éditions d'art, 2012: 295.  
  
Roux, J-P., *Arts de l'Islam: des origines à 1700*, Paris: Musée national de l'Orangerie, 1971: 112.  
  
Welch, A., *Calligraphy in the arts of the Muslim world*, Austin: University of Texas Press, 1979: 186-187, Fig. 80.

ebe4dfb5-2c91-5b48-9947-a44e4359f085.name: Daghestan Prayer Rug
ebe4dfb5-2c91-5b48-9947-a44e4359f085.description:
A 19th century Caucasian prayer rug with a knotted pile. Its directional design consists of a single-plane lattice design crowned by an angled arch with a pointed summit, laid out on an ivory-coloured background and framed by a wide red and blue border.  
  
The lattice design of the centre field contains diamond-shaped compartments, each of which holds a single multi-coloured flower. The horizontally arranged rows of multi-coloured flowers contain repeats of three flowers, symmetrically distributed. The flower repeat arrangement is staggered across the succeeding rows, creating a diagonal uniformity of colour and shape distribution. Below the right edge of the prayer niche arch, and to the right side of the centre-field, near the edge of the border, is a figure of a quadruped, possibly a dog, rendered in pink and yellow with black outlines. This little animal, with its long curled up tale and long stretched back ears, has been inserted in place of a flower.  
  
The border of the carpet consists of a dark green/blue background overlaid with a red scroll of Arabesque design – a version of the Caucasian border scrolls inspired by Arabic *kufic* script.  
  
Such carpets are made for use in performing the daily prayers in Islamic culture. The arch end of the carpet indicates the side upon which the worshiper lays his forehead in prostration.

ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.name: The Mother of God Smolenskaya with Oklad
ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.description:
This is a *Hodegetria* (Greek for “one who shows the way”) Mother of God icon, recognizable by the solemn expression of the Mother of God and the frontal position of the Christ Child delivering a blessing. The Christ Child sits on his Mother’s left knee and holds a tightly rolled scroll. The original icon was brought from Byzantium in the 12th century and kept in the Assumption Cathedral in the city of Smolensk. In the 15th century, the icon was transferred to Moscow before being returned to Smolensk.  
This icon has four additional figures, two on each border: a guardian angel and Venerable Basil the Confessor on the left, and Saint John the Baptist and Saint Anne the Prophet on the right. The *oklad* (covering) is solid silver under mercury gilding with no apparent hallmark. The *oklad* has a large nimbus containing sculpted angels with openings for their faces and hands, as well as many gems and a raised floral and fruit design. An inscription on the bottom border reads as follows:  
  
At the Alenskiy-Skete in the area of Kerzhenets, the Schemamonk Filaret the icon painter, had painted this icon for the Schemamonk Iosif. At the year 7250 \[1740\] this icon was given to the treasury of the Schemanun Irinarkha. The Abbess, the nun Anafoliya donated this icon in the year 7376 \[1868\], at the third day of February to the Archbishop Antonij of Moscow and Vladimir.
ed13e6c9-1b55-5025-a832-f8d710bb6ff1.obtention: Purchased by Gordon Lankton from Ikonen Galerie, Germany, in 2011. Gifted to the Museum of Russian Icons by Gordon Lankton in 2013.
keywords: Virgin Mary and Child; Religious iconography

ed9865de-73ac-57f6-ade6-ad41f83cd57d.name: Section from a chasuble with ogival medallions
ed9865de-73ac-57f6-ade6-ad41f83cd57d.short_description:
The fabric is of very high-quality weave, and is datable on the basis of its technique and design to the early years of the classical era of Ottoman silk lampas (*kemha*) in the 1550s, when the designers and weavers, encouraged by state patronage at the very highest level, were establishing themselves in competition with Italian silk weavers. The tiny scale of the stylized blossoms, the precision of their drawing and their symmetrical arrangement are all indications of a fairly early date.  
Fabrics of this sort, exported to western and central Europe, were frequently fashioned into ecclesiastical vestments, the chasuble being the most common genre to incorporate both Ottoman *kemha* and Ottoman velvet.  
The two halves of the other side of this chasuble are in the Textile Museum, Washington, DC, inv. no.1.51; and the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York, inv. no.08.109.24.

ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.name: Mosque lamp.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.description: A mosque lamp of typical size and shape for Mamluk lamps, with flaring neck, wide body and high foot. Thick glass loops are attached for the suspension cords. The body is decorated with a large inscription which reads, 'This is what was made a *waqf* by the servant yearning for God the Exalted, hoping for the pardon of his generous Lord, Qijlis, \[officer\] of al-Malik al-Nasir'. The neck carries a verse from the Qur'an (9:18) and three medallions with the Mamluk blazon indicating the owner's rank, in this case a sword telling us that Qijlis was *amir silah* (arms-bearer) to the sultan. The lamp is said to have come from a monastery in Seidnaya, a village near Damascus.
ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.short_description: A mosque lamp of typical Mamluk form, with bold inscriptions and three medallions with the patron’s blazon, a sword. The patron was one Amir Qijlis, arms-bearer to the sultan, who commissioned this lamp as a pious donation to an unknown mosque.

ee03a75d-9b6a-5031-8a38-a31dc82d9b98.method_for_datation: The inscription mentions Sayf al-Din Qijlis al-Nasiri, who was promoted to *amir silah* of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad in 716 / 1317 and died in 731 / 1331.

f0e2d598-8e69-5768-bd25-d9db967e1292.name: Painting Entitled ‘al-Rihlah al-Hijaziyyah/ Sacred Pilgrimage Journey’
f0e2d598-8e69-5768-bd25-d9db967e1292.description: According to a plaque below the images, the painting depicts the pilgrimage of ‘Abbas Hilmi II, the Khedive of Egypt, which he performed in 1909. His portrait is on the left; on the right is that of Mehmed V Rashad, the contemporary Ottoman sultan. To the left and right of the Ka‘bah, which occupies the centre of the painting, are depictions of the Mosque of the Prophet in Medina and the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. Many of the remaining images are based on photographs of the hajj published in the July 1953 issue of National Geographic.

f0fbf3fe-1168-5514-90da-4ae1a4c94a50.name: Brocade.
f0fbf3fe-1168-5514-90da-4ae1a4c94a50.description:
The aesthetics of this fabric is based on a repetitive design of large medallions and a well-balanced use of only three colours. Finely drawn silver arabesques fill the centre of each medallion, surrounded by a narrow poly-lobed frame of red silk. It follows a row of circles alternately coloured red and silver. A zigzag encloses this inner pattern. Red contoured trefoils and leaves on a golden background form the outer border. A detail which also proves the skill of the designer is the small silver point emphasising the middle of each trefoil.  
This brocade is part of a larger piece formerly used as an antependium (altar frontal). Many of the ecclesiastical textiles made in Sweden include fabrics imported from Persia and Turkey.
f0fbf3fe-1168-5514-90da-4ae1a4c94a50.short_description: Brocade with a repetitive design of large medallions. The design shows a well-balanced use of colours: silver for the arabesques which fill the centre of each medallion and red for the surrounding poly-lobed frames. This brocade is part of a larger piece formerly used as an antependium (altar frontal).

f3f71340-4ba9-56b9-bb2e-aa39656b9630.name: The *Annunciation*
f3f71340-4ba9-56b9-bb2e-aa39656b9630.description:
Aside from the *Annunciation*, the *Mass of St Gregory* is one of the most common and important painting subjects in which representations of carpets can be found. Into one of the crucial moments of Christian iconography, artists transposed aspects of the typical Portuguese feminine interior spaces of the 16th century, with the marked presence of the female dais (*estrado*). Its use appears associated with the context of Islamic presence in the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages.  
In this painting, the Virgin Mary appears kneeling on a mat: this, along with other similar representations bear witness to the past presence in Portugal of these types of small carpets that are non-existent in collections today. Such is the case of these “mats”, used during the summer as an alternative to the dense knotted carpets of the winter months, as well as of the tapestries, which alternated in the summer period with the *guadamecis*.  
The artist’s decision to include a mat, rather than an Oriental carpet, may be down to the painting being commissioned for a convent of the Order of Saint Claire, where the strict rules called for austerity. This appears in opposition to Gregório Lopes’s painting intended for a wealthy clientele.  
In addition, it all goes to prove the absorption and influence of African artistic production in Portuguese contemporary life and art since the 15th century, when mats, but also other objects such as saltcellars and ivory spoons, began to be imported to Portugal from Benin.
f3f71340-4ba9-56b9-bb2e-aa39656b9630.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by José Alberto Seabra de Carvalho

f445365e-28d3-5b5f-869c-11cd87fe18f8.name: The *Circumcision*
f445365e-28d3-5b5f-869c-11cd87fe18f8.description:
We are witnessing the representation of one of the most important episodes of Jesus’ childhood, in which, according to Jewish law, the Child gains its identity.  
The scene has been re-created in the interior of a Renaissance-style temple where the Holy Family and several figures cluster around the table where a priest is about to carry out the circumcision.  
Covering the altar there is a white towel, in turn, this covers a carpet, of which only the border, filled with “vine scrolls”, palmettes and foliage, is visible. This variant in the use of carpets in a painting makes this a very interesting document.  
Alongside its use as a floor-cover in paintings, when its symbolism is associated with dignity and spatial boundaries, carpets were used widely as a cover for altars in churches as well as in civil settings as furniture covers, as several Portuguese inventories attest.  
In the *Circumcision*, a so-called knotted “Holbein” carpet can be seen. It is put to the same use here as the carpet represented by Hans Holbein, the Younger (1497/8‒1543), in his famous portrait *The Ambassadors*, which thereafter gave this specific compositional structure the name “Holbein”.

f4ea69e8-9de2-5382-aca9-484c574fcf53.name: Konya Prayer Rug
f4ea69e8-9de2-5382-aca9-484c574fcf53.description: This rug is known as the “prayer rug with a high estrade”.It was woven specifically for the midday religious service in mosques on Fridays. The Kaʽba and its surrounding  buildings are portrayed. Kaʽba  motifs and foot marks at the bottom side indicate the direction of the prayer, as one must turn his/her face to the Kaʽba during prayer. There are hanging candle motifs symbolizing the holy (eternal) lights of the prophet along the right and left side of the Kaʽba motifs. The floral decoration on the borders are typical for its origin and date.

f50bd176-bda6-5419-b0f2-72d317a0f0f5.name: Prayer rug
f50bd176-bda6-5419-b0f2-72d317a0f0f5.description: At the centre of this prayer rug there is a *mihrab*, which indicates the *qibla* ‒ the direction of the Kaʽba in Mecca. The Kraków example is especially attractive because of its vivid colours: a warm-red niche, closed with an arch of bizarre shape, contrasts with yellow borders. Inside the white spandrels is a black arabesque ornament. In the cross-panel there are rosettes inscribed in lozenges. The most striking feature is a wide border with a pattern of rhythmically turned rosettes and pomegranate motifs. Such a border reflects the style of Ottoman court rugs attributed to Bursa. Similar rugs can be found in many churches in Transylvania.
f50bd176-bda6-5419-b0f2-72d317a0f0f5.method_for_datation: Geometrisation of the motifs as well as simplification of the design dates this rug to as late as the 18th century

f50ec732-f02a-5c81-8530-9953b2cc241a.name: Prayer Box with Cover
f50ec732-f02a-5c81-8530-9953b2cc241a.short_description:
This silver prayer box encompasses rich engravings suspended from a neck chain. In Iranian, Omani and Yemeni tradition, these types of necklaces treasure a secret wish.  
  
Rolled paper amulets would fulfil wishes, alleviate pain and defend against the evil eye. It remains uncertain whether people wear the prayers on their chest to be read or locked away forever.  
  
By holding or handling the box, a person enacts the power of the amulet for themselves, a loved one, or even against someone as a curse. Like engraved charms in modern jewellery, magical signs may cast a mystical aura, with Islamic phrases often written in reverse.

f52af067-edfe-5f5e-95b7-9a131fd3f4f1.name: Kula prayer rug
f52af067-edfe-5f5e-95b7-9a131fd3f4f1.description:
This prayer rug was probably made in Kula. It is decorated with a terracotta-red *mihrab* closed with a stepped arch, the spandrels of which are light blue. The bordure, which consists of 23 thin stripes, is divided into three colouristic areas of green and yellow, ivory and dark-brown, and red and blue. Every space of the carpet is filled with minute motifs: four-petal rosettes in the niche, upside down tulips in the spandrels, and flowers on leafy stalks in the bordure. The big red, yellow and ivory carnations in the cross-panels beneath and above the niche, contrast with the other flora. The colouristic and ornamental composition gives an impression of delicacy and lightness.  
Carpets made in Kula were strongly influenced by the Gördes production, but the multi-striped borders can be more often found in Kula rugs. In addition, the choice of minute floral motifs is very characteristic of this production centre. It is worth noting just how differentiated the floral motifs used to decorate the carpet are, especially in terms of the colour scheme.  
Prayer rugs were very popular among the 17th- and 18th-century nobility in Poland. Taste for Oriental art was one of the characteristic features of Polish culture at the time, and prayer rugs were widely used for interior decoration.  
The Kula rug was obtained by the very famous Polish collector Feliks Jasieński ‒ called Manggha (1861–1929) ‒ and formed part of his extensive and precious collection. Part of this collection was donated to the National Museum in Kraków in 1929, according to Jasieński’s last will and testament.

f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.name: *Conversion of St. Paul* Altarpiece
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.description:
A Rococo type of *reredos* (retable) with ornamental pilasters instead of columns, and a wealth of Rococo ornamentation in compact form. At the centre is the *Conversion of St. Paul*, flanked by two female saints without attributes. Two angels kneel at the corners of the cornice. The central, upper section of the altarpiece holds the coat of arms of the Halper-Sigetski family.  
Initially, the altarpiece stood in St. Mark's Church in Zagreb, near the triumphal arch. Like most altarpieces in the church, this one was commissioned by a particular guild, the boot-makers' guild. Its production was part funded by a donation from Anna Gerlichich in 1760, as an inscription on the altarpiece details.  
The altarpiece is by an accomplished master, showing a high level of design and technical skill. The influence of Vid Königer (one of the greatest Styrian sculptors of the second half of the 18th century) is apparent, seen in the female saints in particular.  
During restoration of St Mark's at the end of the 19th century, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, at that time owned by Baron Halper-Sigetski, who placed his baronial arms on it.
f5ef250e-6f10-578b-9290-9c8967a2f518.short_description:
A richly carved Rococo altarpiece: two saints stand either side of twisted pilasters and two angels decorate the attic, while the central scene of the *Conversion of St Paul* is in high relief.  
Commissioned for St Mark's Church by the boot-makers' guild in 1760, it was part-funded by a donation from Anna Gerlichich, as an inscription on the altarpiece details.  
During restoration of the church at the end of the 19th century, the altarpiece was moved to the chapel of Zajezda Manor in Hrvatsko zagorje, at that time owned by Baron Halper-Sigetski, who placed his baronial arms on it.

ANNA SAN(C) NATA DE GERLICHISCH 1760". Anna Gerličić, whose name appears on the coat of arms, probably sponsored some of the work for this altarpiece, such as the gilding.

f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.name: Triple-arch prayer rug
f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.description:
Triple-arch rugs, sometimes also described as six-column rugs, were very popular in Transylvania – there are several interesting examples preserved in the collections at the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts and the Brukenthal National Museum in Sibiu, and in a number of Austrian collections as well. It is very probable that in this case the niche doesn’t represent the *mihrab*, but derives from mosque architecture.  
The red niche at the centre of the rug is divided into three pointed arches supported by six columns, on bases in the form of polygonal turrets, with the so-called “precious stones” decoration. The large carnation flower is suspended from the pick of the central arch, and much smaller flowers hang from the lower arches. The dark-blue spandrels are decorated with a mainly yellow ornament of rosettes, and lanceolate leaves flanking them. The main, wide border, filled with an ornament of hexagonal cartouches enclosing lozenges with carnations rising from them, is placed between two narrower borders with flower ornament. The main colours of the carpet are red, yellow and dark-blue, with details in white, red and blue.  
Some characteristic features distinguish the Kraków carpet from other examples of this type: the ornaments are rather simplified, and a clear, precise outline is almost lost especially in the spandrels; the paired central columns rise from the bases as one column, which is quite an unusual solution. Worthy of note also are the delicate, small flowers rising from the central part of the columns. The left arch has a bizarre shape, which is probably the result of an error made by the maker.
f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.method_for_datation: The composition of the rug and also its stylistic features prove that it belongs to the group of triple-arch carpets traditionally connected with the Anatolia workshop of the 17th century
f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.method_for_provenance: Both composition and technique suggest that it could have been made in Ladik, Anatolia

f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.name: Cross chain
f9783bd6-7a5b-5ca2-8a70-781a2af32872.short_description: A cross of silver on a silver chain known with the folkloric name “heal of gazelle”, worn by Christian women. Silver was the most common jewellery; only rich people used gold. The dowry of silver and gold jewellery was given by the groom to the bride, reflecting the financial status of the groom. This object illustrates the variegated religious composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It also demonstrates personal attire, fashion, local costumes and rites.

fa052673-5ed9-5255-bc4c-8cacacef21c2.name: Kaaba *Kiswah* (Covering)
fa052673-5ed9-5255-bc4c-8cacacef21c2.short_description: Prior to Islam, regional tribes competed to cloak the Kaaba, a religious sanctuary. Every year on the ninth day of the Pilgrimage month, a new *Kiswah* (covering) reveals the Kaaba’s new face in a ceremony while concealing the building’s appearance. Sewn by Egyptian craftsman in 1910, this fragment of the *Kiswah* to the Kaaba in Saudi Arabia represents the curtain covering an architectural door adorned with calligraphy. A generous 220 kilograms of gold and silver embroider the 670 kilograms of black-dyed silk. The year-long manufacture, considered a religious duty, requires precision and laborious processes to create a fitted garment that can withstand the hot sun. Egyptian rural production centres produced the *Kiswah* for centuries. Today, modern media helps witness the production and ritual replacement worldwide with livestream coverage.

fabf4535-e263-529b-9b2c-f09555375400.name: Mosque Lamp
fabf4535-e263-529b-9b2c-f09555375400.short_description: Glass mosque lamps such as this splendid example were made in abundance during the Mamluk period in Egypt and Syria. Free blown, enamelled and gilded, these lamps contained oil and were suspended from the ceiling of mosques, madrasas and palace complexes, illuminating the buildings with their beautifully executed decoration, including Qur’anic verses, proverbs, sultanate titles, or geometric and floral patterns. This particular lamp, with a rounded body and long sloping curved shoulder with a flared, conical mouth and trumpeted foot, has six applied loop handles around its body from which it would have hung. The lamp’s body and mouth are both decorated entirely with blue floral medallions outlined with white strapwork, set against loosely drawn red floral motifs. This example, although comparatively small in height, relates to a known set of other mosque lamps attributed to the reign of the Mamluk Sultan Hasan (AH r. 747-762 / AD 1347-1361). These lamps were most probably made for the madrasa of Sultan Hasan in Cairo, which was completed in 763-764 AH / 1362-1363 AD. Like many other examples, this lamp remained in its original structure until the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries AH / nineteenth century AD, when many were sold and entered into museum collections worldwide.

fafb3812-1969-5e3a-b9d0-22446066efee.name: Chest for a Portable Altar
fafb3812-1969-5e3a-b9d0-22446066efee.description:
Portable altars in the form of chests were an element of religious furniture, epitomising Portuguese maritime travel to different parts of the world.  
This type of furniture developed from the 16th century onwards as Portuguese maritime voyages, in particular to India and China, increased.  
These voyages often involved both regular and secular clergymen embarking on missionary activities, aristocratic families, the backbone of the administration in the Portuguese empire, or those who set out for diverse corners of the world in the quest for new commercial markets.  
The need to reduce the volume and weight of the cargo transported on these voyages resulted in the construction of furniture that was light and easy to handle and store.  
This piece of furniture is built of wood and covered with black-painted leather. It is adorned with engraved plant motifs and a pattern made out of tacks. On the outside it is fairly plain. The exuberance of the piece is revealed after it is opened and assembled. The internal lining in red silk is further embellished by gold trimming. The fittings that frame the lid were inspired by incised motifs, a decorative mode that flourished during the period.  
The liturgical implements (chalice, crucifix, pyx, cruet, paten and bell), all of which were necessary to celebrate mass, were stored in a drawer below the altar table, in customised, made-to-measure indentations.  
Many masses were celebrated aboard the carracks on altars such as this one, as well as on land, at sites that did not have suitable facilities for religious worship.  
Mass could only be celebrated on altars that contained an altar-stone – a stone that had been blessed – upon which was placed the chalice and the host. In this altar, the altar-stone is found in a concave indentation within the table.  
During voyages, priests were obliged to celebrate mass every Sunday and on holy days. A particular feature of masses celebrated on board ship was that they did not have the consecration and consequently did not have communion. They were thus called “dry masses”.  
In his work, *As* *Cartas Ânuas da China: 1636, 1643 a 1649,* a compilation of letters from China written to the Jesuit General in Rome annually, the Jesuit priest António de Gouveia described the presence of altars in the houses of Portuguese settlers. He relates that it was a common practice to “assemble the altar” in the largest room so that mass could be held.
fafb3812-1969-5e3a-b9d0-22446066efee.short_description: A chest containing a portable altar, it was designed to be transported long distance on Portuguese maritime voyages to enable those on board to celebrate Mass both while on board the ship and, on arrival, in foreign lands.

fbd001b0-41f7-592f-b717-94dbb55470d2.name: Curtain for the door of the Ka‘ba, with the name of Sultan Abdülmecid ['Abd al-Majid] I
fbd001b0-41f7-592f-b717-94dbb55470d2.short_description:
The curtain for the door of the Ka‘ba – known also as *sitara*, *burda* or *burqu‘* – was by far the most elaborate part of the *kiswa* and was replaced annually. Since Mamluk times, they were made in Egypt, and left Cairo with the *kiswa* accompanied by the caravan of pilgrims amidst great pomp and circumstance.  
  
The design of this curtain is typical of those made at the Dar al-Kiswa in Cairo during the 19th century, and it continued to be used until the early 20th century. Curtains of this type were usually made in four sections which were embroidered and then sewn together, the heavy wire embroidery almost completely obscuring the seams. The silk fabric was backed with heavy canvas which helped support the weight of the wire, which on a heavily embroidered example like this, can weigh anything up to 60 kilograms. With its heavy use of embroidery, this curtain could have easily taken 20 or more embroiderers two months to complete.

fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.name: Oil lamp.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.description: A glass lamp composed of three sections: base, body and the neck, and completely covered with vegetal decoration beautifully and skilfully executed. It is painted with a variety of colours, with enamel and with profuse gilding. In addition it is adorned with written inscriptions and the blazon of the endower. The neck of the lamp is wide and narrows as it moves in closer to the body, thus taking the form of a conic glass. The neck is adorned with both vegetal motifs that fill the surface, and with an inscription band in Mamluk *thuluth* script. The inscription, 8 cm high, rendered in dark-blue, includes part of a verse from the Qur'an, “al-Tauba” (“the Repentance” 9: 18): “The Mosques of Allah shall be visited and maintained by such as believe in Allah and the Last Day”.The verse is intercepted by three circular medallions with a red circle at the centre, within which is a gilded goblet, the blazon of Amir Tankaz al-Nasiri. A decorative band is located between the body of the lamp and its neck formed from eight consecutive lotus flowers. The body is decorated with a relatively large gilded inscription band, against a dark-blue background, it reads: “This has been ordered by the Sublime, our lord, the *amir*, al-Saifi Tankaz supporter of the honourable and protected Mamluks in al-Sham \[Syria\]”. The inscription is interrupted by six suspension loops that are used to attach the chains for hanging the lamp. There is decorative band below that containing the inscription this is adorned with vegetal motifs. The lower area of the body, before transferring to the base, contains six medallions, three of which contain blazons and the remaining three of which are filled with vegetal motifs. The base of the lamp is 4 cm high; it is wider at the bottom than the top. The base is adorned with three bands filled with gilded vegetal decoration.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.short_description: The glass lamp is completely covered with intricate and skilful vegetal decoration and is painted in a variety of colours, with enamel and gilding. The body bears a gilded inscription and the blazon of its endower, Amir Tankiz al-Nasiri, against a dark-blue background. The lamp has a number of decorative medallions.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.holder: Islamic Museum, al-Aqsa Mosque / al-Haram al-Sharif.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.initial_owner: Amir Tankaz al-Nasiri who occupied the position of a representative of the Sultanate in al-Sham (Great Syria) region in AH 712–40 / AD 1312–40. This was during the rule of the Mamluk sultan, al-Nasir Muhammad bin Qalawun (who ruled three times: AH 693–4, 698–708 and 709–41 / AD 1294–5, 1299–1309 and 1309–40).
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.method_for_datation: The lamp was dated based on the written inscriptions on it, which mention the name of its owner, Amir Tankaz al-Nasiri.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.method_for_provenance: Lamps, similar to that exhibited here, were renowned during the Mamluk period. They were typically produced in either Cairo or Damascus, so it is likely that this piece was made in Damascus in view of the fact that Amir Tankaz was a deputy there.
fc210313-c572-52b3-ab9c-6ec080f0812a.obtention: The lamp was transferred from al-Haram al-Ibrahimi (the Ibrahimi Mosque) in Hebron (al-Khalil) to the Islamic Museum in Jerusalem in 1967.

fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.name: Tomb
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.description:
The tomb, which is made of gilded silver shaped like a reliquary, holds a casket within which a figurine of Christ lies. Resting upon a trilateral base and supported on the backs of three ivory dragons, the tomb is decorated with embossed and chased foliate and *rocaille* ornaments and jewels. Enamel tablets hold within them scenes from the Life of Christ. From the base, a halo rises surrounded by a border of double rays. Attached to the base are allegorical figures of Faith, Hope and Love, flanked by St. Peter and St. Paul, and above them the figures of the Fathers of the Church Saints Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory. The centre of the sunburst halo holds an enamelled painting of the Virgin and Child in a jewelled frame. It is decorated with foliate and *rocaille* ornaments, supported by two gilded angels. Above the frame is a splendid jewelled crown with a pendant pearl, flanked by two small ivory angels.  
Made in Augsburg and bought for the treasury with money bequeathed by Cardinal Juraj Haulik (the first Archbishop of Zagreb enthroned in 1853) a great patron of the arts and patriot whose ideas reflected the Enlightenment spirit.
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.short_description: A gilded silver tomb shaped like a reliquary, which holds a casket within which a figurine of Christ lies. It rests upon a trilateral base supported on the backs of three ivory dragons. The tomb is decorated with embossed and chased foliate and *rocaille* ornaments and jewels. Enamelled tablets hold within them scenes from the Life of Christ.

fe134b50-319c-5411-b2af-fb5d9bcfd6cf.name: Ladik Prayer Rug
fe134b50-319c-5411-b2af-fb5d9bcfd6cf.description: Ladik town of Konya Province was one of the most important rug producing centres of Anatolia. From the 17th to the 19th centuries many kind of carpets including large ground rugs, hall rugs, floor mats and cushions were produced in Ladik. Prayer rugs from the region are the most famous group. The distinctive feature of a Ladik prayer rug is a *mihrab* with a triple niche and stylized columns. Ladik prayer rugs are popular in Transylvania. Rugs were exported to the region and this type became known as a “Transylvanian rug”.

febb9b50-5023-54dc-aba9-74d232d247aa.name: *Mihrab* from the Damsaköy Taşkınpaşa Mosque.
febb9b50-5023-54dc-aba9-74d232d247aa.description:
The *mihrab* is made of walnut. The geometric and vegetal motifs and inscriptions which make up its decoration are executed with deep carving with round surfaces, double-level carving and bevelling. The *mihrab* exhibits outstanding craftsmanship. Its niche is framed by two wide borders. The outermost border from floor level up to 68 cm is decorated with a vegetal composition featuring palmettes and *rumi* (split-palmette) leaves. The second border is covered up to about 100 cm with a geometric network. Both borders continue at these respective heights with inscription bands containing verses from the Qur'an (10:255, 59:20–23, 46:31).  
  
The *mihrab*'s lobed niche is framed with thin borders of various widths comprised of vegetal decoration featuring palmette and *rumi* (split-palmette) motifs. The form of the niche hood, as well as the fact that its interior is empty, suggests that this part is a restoration. The niche interior itself, which is semi-circular in profile, is decorated with an intricate vegetal composition.  
  
The spandrels of the *mihrab* niche have round medallions containing inscription bands. The frames of the medallions feature deeply carved vegetal motifs which give the impression of having been executed in openwork. The right medallion has the word 'Allah' in the centre, surrounded by a verse from the Qur'an (59:22); the left medallion has the word 'Muhammad' surrounded by part of verse 59:23.  
  
The large rectangular panel on the upper section of the *mihrab* contains a geometric network made up of 12-pointed stars. The *mihrab* has no pediment crowning it.  
  
Although buildings outside Anatolia and from various historical periods feature wooden *mihrab*s, such as the Azhar Mosque (AH 360–62 / AD 970–2) and Sayyida Nafisa Mosque (AH 532–3 / AD 1138–45) in Cairo, the Iskodar Mosque in West Turkistan (5th–6th / 11th–12th century), and the Halawiyya Madrasa in Aleppo (end of the 6th / 12th to beginning of the 7th / 13th century), the *mihrab* of the Damsaköy Taşkınpaşa Mosque is the only one in Anatolia made of wood. For this reason it is of special importance.
febb9b50-5023-54dc-aba9-74d232d247aa.short_description: The only example of of a wood-built *mihrab* in Anatolia, this *mihrab* is an exceptional work of art displaying excellent craftsmanship and rich geometric, floral and calligraphic decoration.
febb9b50-5023-54dc-aba9-74d232d247aa.method_for_datation: The Damsaköy Taşkınpaşa Mosque has no foundation inscription. However, the tombs found in the courtyard there have inscriptions dating to the 8th / 14th century, so it is accepted that the mosque was probably built in the mid-14th century. In addition, in the 8th / 14th century it was common for geometric and vegetal compositions to be used together with inscriptions, especially in tile-mosaic and stucco *mihrab*s. This decorative programme was used on the wooden *mihrab* of the Damsaköy Taşkınpaşa Mosque.
febb9b50-5023-54dc-aba9-74d232d247aa.method_for_provenance: Although the exact place of production for this *mihrab* is unknown, both its stylistic characteristics and the motifs used on it point to a local (Anatolian) provenance.
febb9b50-5023-54dc-aba9-74d232d247aa.obtention: The wooden *mihrab* that once belonged to the Taşkınpaşa Mosque in Damsaköy was transferred, along with the *minbar*, to Ankara Ethnographic Museum on 23 October 1940.
